The seller’s financials were a little messy, the client base was sticky but aging, and there was a key employee who had been threatening to leave. But the price was a steal, the market was growing, and the buyer had a clear plan to stabilize operations post-close. Their lawyer kept circling back to one phrase: “too many unknowns.” And they were right. That’s what risk looks like. But business is about taking calculated risks—not eliminating them. So the question wasn’t “Is there risk?” It was: “Is this a risk worth taking, and can we price it in?” That’s a business decision—not a legal one. Business Requires Risk. Good Business Requires Choosing It. This is the paradox of entrepreneurship: you can’t grow, invest, or acquire without risk. The entire job is about identifying risk, deciding which version of it you can live with, and taking the leap with eyes wide open. Lawyers are trained to flag risk, not greenlight it. So when you ask your lawyer, “Should I do this deal?” don’t be surprised when the answer sounds like: “Not unless we get these seventeen things tightened up.” They’re not wrong. But that’s not the full picture. The Best Use of Legal Advice Here’s how to get the most value out of your lawyer: Have them spot the landmines What are the worst-case scenarios? What’s buried in the fine print that could bite you later? Have them quantify the risk How likely are those risks to materialize? Can they be mitigated through terms? Have them help structure solutions Can we rewrite this clause? Add a rep? Cap a liability? Move something from the purchase agreement into a consulting agreement? Do not ask them if you should take the risk. That’s your call. The Gut Check That Matters Most Your lawyer is one voice in the room—and an important one. But it’s your gut, your goals, and your risk tolerance that should drive the decision. Not theirs. I’ve seen great lawyers talk clients out of great deals because they were approaching the situation like a legal exam instead of a business opportunity. I’ve also seen great clients walk away from bad deals, not because of the contract, but because they knew the seller wasn’t trustworthy—even though the agreement looked bulletproof. That’s why you need both: legal clarity and business instinct. Final Word: Don’t Let the Deal Die on Someone Else’s Risk Report In the end, the best deals are made by people who know when to defer to their lawyer—and when to thank them for the memo and move forward anyway. So yes, get legal counsel. Get smart, sharp legal eyes on everything. But when it comes time to say yes or no? Put the lawyer down, and pick your gut back up. That’s the real job of a business owner: not to avoid risk, but to choose the right kind. Bankers How to Make Sure Your Banker Is the Best you Can Get If you are relying on a bank to close your deal, your banker will make or break your transaction. And yet, a lot of people treat the bank like a vending machine: push a button, get a loan. That’s not how it works. Behind every good small business acquisition loan is a human—or several humans—making judgment calls. So you need to know exactly who you’re dealing with and how they work. Let’s start with the BDO, or Business Development Officer. That’s the person who sells you on the bank. Their job is part lender, part sales rep. Because they’re in sales, they’ll often tell you exactly what you want to hear. But they’re not the ones issuing the final thumbs-up or thumbs-down. That’s the underwriter’s job. So here’s what matters: you want a BDO who has a strong, trusted relationship with their underwriter. Ideally, one where the underwriter trusts the BDO’s judgment and there’s a real feedback loop. That loop is crucial. Why? Because if the BDO slings loans all day without regard for what underwriting will approve, you’re going to end up on a conveyor belt to nowhere.

Why You Absolutely Want an SBA Preferred Lender If you’re planning to use SBA financing—and for many small business acquisitions, it’s the most accessible capital on the table—you need to work with an SBA Preferred Lender. Full stop. Why? Because not all banks are created equal under the SBA program. A Preferred Lender has earned the ability to process, approve, and close loans entirely in-house. That means no waiting for the SBA to sign off, no outside review delays, and no guesswork. They’ve got the authority to move quickly—and that’s a massive advantage in a deal environment where timing matters. Now contrast that with a non-preferred lender. They have to package up your deal and send it off to the SBA for final approval. You wait. They wait. And sometimes you get a surprise “no” weeks down the line, when you’ve already spent money on diligence and legal. That’s not a timeline you want to bet your deal on. Industry Experience Matters, Too Beyond preferred status, you want a banker—or a bank—that has actual experience financing deals in your industry. That’s especially true for professional services like accounting or financial advisory firms, which can confuse generalist lenders. A banker familiar with professional services knows how to evaluate recurring contracts, seasonality, and discretionary, knows the staffing models, and probably won’t freak out when they see owner comp baked into SDE. A banker who doesn’t know your space? They might try to apply a restaurant or retail underwriting lens to your deal—and that can send things sideways fast. Remember, you’re not borrowing money. You’re building a relationship with a financial institution that has to understand what you're buying to say yes, and say it efficiently. What About Bank Brokers? Now let’s talk about bank brokers—these are folks who act as matchmakers between you and a lender. They usually take a small percentage of the loan proceeds, and yes, a lot of them refer to the same handful of banks over and over again. That can feel a little cookie-cutter, but don’t write them off entirely. Here’s where they can be very valuable: Translation and Packaging: A good bank broker knows what the bank wants to see—and how they want to see it. They can help you package your deal in a way that maximizes your odds of approval. Think of it like applying to college with someone who used to sit on the admissions committee. Access: They often have existing relationships with specific BDOs or underwriters. That means when they say, “This is a strong deal,” the bank is more likely to listen. Heavy Lifting: If you don’t have a bank broker, you are the one pulling together all the seller’s financials, organizing them, and explaining them to the bank. A bank broker can do some of that work for you—and they’re often better at chasing down documents from a seller than you are, because that’s literally their job. That said, not all bank brokers are created equal. Some are hands-off and drop your deal like a referral code. Others are actively involved, shoulder-to-shoulder with you through the entire financing process. If you’re going to work with a bank broker, ask how engaged they’ll be, and whether they’ll help with packaging, underwriting calls, and follow-ups. She’s a smart, driven CPA who finally found the accounting practice she’s been searching for—solid recurring revenue, loyal clients, and a seller ready to exit. The cash flow was a bit tight, but with SBA financing, the numbers worked. Barely. But they worked. Here’s where things went sideways. While Amy was searching for the right acquisition, she decided to get the ball rolling and launch her own small accounting firm. She only operated it for a few months before finding the right deal, but during that time, she invested about $50,000 into startup activities—going to a couple of industry conferences, building a website, setting up some tech, branding, and trying to land her first clients. So when the bank started reviewing her application, they saw that $50K loss on her personal P&L and asked: “How much of this was startup cost?” Amy, thinking like a good accountant, responded: “About $5,000.” Why? Because that’s what the IRS allows you to deduct in the first year for startup costs. But the bank wasn’t looking for the tax-deductible number—they were trying to understand how much of that $50K was one-time, non-recurring spend. Instead, her answer made it sound like $45,000 of the loss was operational—and likely to continue. That wrecked the bank’s cash flow projection and broke the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) they needed to approve the loan. The deal was denied. Not because the business wasn’t strong. Not because Amy wasn’t qualified. But because she answered a question literally—and no one helped her frame the narrative. Enter: The Bank Broker Who Could’ve Saved It This is exactly where a bank broker earns their keep. A good broker would’ve stopped the conversation and said, “Hold up—when the bank asks how much was startup cost, they’re not talking about what the IRS lets you deduct. They want to know how much of that $50K isn’t coming back next year.” Then they would’ve helped her reshape the response: “Roughly $45K of that loss was one-time, upfront spend—conferences, brand development, tech setup, etc. The core business is now running lean and is either breaking even or close.” That shift in language? It changes the whole financial picture. It tells the bank, “This isn’t a red flag—it’s a ramp-up.” And that could’ve kept the DSCR intact, and the deal alive. What This Means for You Bank underwriting isn’t about numbers—it’s about interpreting those numbers through the lens of risk. And the people best equipped to help you translate your story into the language banks speak? Great bank brokers. They don’t send your deal into the void. They help: Reframe confusing numbers Position your story in the best light Anticipate questions before they blow up your deal Amy’s story is a classic example of what happens when there’s no translator in the room. She wasn’t wrong—she wasn’t answering the right question. Let’s go. 1-Managing Deal Fatigue Embarking on an acquisition—especially in the small to mid-sized space—isn’t only a business transaction; it’s a mental, emotional, and logistical endurance sport. It starts with a burst of excitement—kind of like the first mile of a marathon when you believe you're a runner. But as negotiations drag on, timelines stretch, and your inbox fills with follow-ups marked "URGENT" from people you’ve never heard of, reality kicks in. Welcome to the long, sweaty middle miles. This is where deals go to die. Recognizing that your counterparty’s attention span, patience, and emotional bandwidth are limited resources is the first step. Treat them like gold. Whether you’re buying or selling, the goal is to preserve goodwill, pace yourself, and create an environment where people want to answer your emails three months in. 1. Understanding Deal Fatigue and Its Implications Here’s the thing nobody tells you until you’re in it: getting a deal across the finish line is another full-time job. And unfortunately, most people already have one. The seller is running their business—keeping clients happy, managing staff, keeping the lights on. The buyer might be juggling diligence and financial modeling while working a full-time W-2 job, fielding banker calls during their lunch break and reviewing legal docs at midnight. No one’s sleeping. Everyone’s over it. And that’s when deal fatigue sets in. Deal fatigue isn’t “we’re getting tired.” It’s more like an emotional version of running out of gas in the middle of nowhere—with no cell reception and a hungry raccoon staring at you. In mergers and acquisitions (M&A), deal fatigue shows up as disengagement, missed deadlines, abrupt radio silence, or tense Zooms where someone says “per my last email” with a little too much heat. It’s the feeling that you’ve been “close” to signing for weeks—but nothing’s moving (except the projected closing date). Deal fatigue tends to track closely with how long the process drags on. The more time that passes without a clear, focused path to closing, the more likely it is that one or both sides start to lose steam. Energy fades. Enthusiasm cools. And the deal starts to wobble. Put simply: the longer it takes, the shakier it gets. 2. The Finite Nature of Deal Stamina Most sellers of sub-$5M businesses don’t have a team of advisors and analysts backing them up—they’re doing it themselves while also running their business. Same for buyers. One minute they’re prepping a diligence request list, the next they’re troubleshooting payroll software. There’s no bandwidth fairy coming to save anyone. That’s why deal stamina—your capacity to keep making thoughtful, engaged decisions—is finite. It’s a real, measurable resource, like money or calories. And once it’s gone? You’re at the mercy of stress, shortcuts, and worst of all, bad assumptions. If you’ve ever tried to negotiate while sleep-deprived, hangry, or at the end of a long week, you know how quickly good intentions can unravel. When both parties are depleted, what used to be a reasonable question (“Can we clarify this working capital adjustment?”) starts sounding like an attack. It’s a recipe for retrading, resentment, or worse, walking away. 3. Proactive Strategies to Build Deal Resiliency So how do you keep everyone engaged, aligned, and moving forward—even when the process stretches longer than anyone wants? The following tactics are not good ideas—they’re what help people close. Set Clear Expectations Early Before you dive into diligence, set expectations. Everyone should know the timeline, the communication flow, and what’s considered “urgent.” If you skip this step, don’t be surprised when someone’s “quick update” derails a whole week. As CW Law puts it, "Setting appropriate expectations from the outset, based on transparent and clear information, will help limit client frustration and promote a productive attorney/client relationship" (cwlaw.com). It’s not about professionalism—it’s about managing mental load. Surprises drain stamina. Clarity builds it.

Maintain Momentum After the Letter of Intent (LOI) is signed, there’s usually a burst of energy. Everyone’s optimistic, ready to collaborate, and the inbox is on fire with helpful updates. Ride that wave. It’s essential to ride that initial wave of energy. Early momentum is one of the most valuable assets in a deal—use it to push things forward while both sides are engaged and optimistic. Respond quickly. Keep meetings short and purposeful. Make it easy for people to say yes to the next step. Foster Open Communication You don’t need daily calls, but you do need consistent check-ins. Regular updates, even when there’s “nothing major,” prevent the buildup of unspoken concerns. Encourage people to flag potential issues early, before they become crisis-level problems. And remember, tone matters. People are more likely to raise concerns if they trust you won’t bite their head off. Recognize and Address Emotional Factors There’s no such thing as a 100% rational deal. Buyers worry about overpaying. Sellers worry about regret. Both sides worry about losing face. Acknowledge it. “This is a big step—I get that it’s not about numbers” can go a long way. Showing empathy isn’t weak. It’s strategic. It builds trust and keeps people showing up. BOX Something to keep in mind-Every small business under $5 million is, whether it says so on paper or not, a family business. At that scale, the lines between work and home blur fast. Your spouse might be helping out with invoicing or taking client calls when you’re in the field. Your kids have probably done everything from stuffing envelopes to hauling recycling. Your family knows what kind of year you’ve had before your accountant does. It’s all deeply interwoven—emotionally, financially, logistically. I know this firsthand. My dad’s construction business was a standalone profitable company but it was also a family operation. My first job in elementary school was checking the mail and carrying it up to him and his business partner in the attic-turned-office. Later, in high school, I cleaned the office on Sunday nights—a fantastic job for a teen. You don’t forget that kind of closeness to a business. And when it comes time to sell, those threads don’t untangle themselves. There will be emotions. The Power of Being Likeable: Why Rapport Might Be the Most Important Deal Term Deals aren’t closed by spreadsheets. They’re closed by people. And people are messy, emotional, and prone to wanting to work with folks they trust, like, and respect. Rapport isn’t fluff. It’s the glue. When due diligence hits a snag (and it will), rapport is what keeps people on the phone instead of lawyer-ing up or ghosting. When the deal hits friction, the human connection makes it easier to work through the mess. When parties like each other, they pick up the phone. They listen. They brainstorm. They collaborate. When they don’t? Every issue becomes a battle. Emails get colder. Lawyers start cc’ing more people. And suddenly, that minor tax question is now “a fundamental breakdown in trust.” So be someone they want to work with. Be transparent. Be a great communicator. Be curious. Ask about their goals. Care about their team. Treat the deal not like a transaction, but like a transition. Especially if you’re a seller—remember, the buyer is watching closely. They’re deciding if they want to inherit you. Show them you’re someone who collaborates, not someone they’ll have to unravel. Being likeable doesn’t mean being fake. It means showing up with emotional intelligence, grace under pressure, and a sense of humor. You don’t need to be everyone’s best friend—but you do need to be someone worth partnering with. That’s why it’s so important to build real rapport before diving into the deep end of due diligence.

And here’s a tip that’s worked wonders for me: Before every tough call, I take a moment to find something I like about the other person. Maybe they remind me of someone I admire. Maybe they’re funny without trying. It warms me up—and almost every time, they respond in kind. People can feel when you’re genuinely engaged. They tend to mirror it back. But if you can’t find anything you like about them? Oh my gosh, run. Half-kidding. But only half. The deal process is hard enough with rapport. Without it? You’re in for a long, expensive, painful slog. Trust me. BOX Navigating Generational Differences in Negotiations When you're negotiating across generations, you're not just speaking different languages—you’re practically negotiating across time zones. Each generation brings its own set of expectations, communication styles, and deal-breaking triggers to the table. If you’re not paying attention, those subtle misalignments can turn into full-blown deal fatigue. The Unspoken Bias You Should Always Expect (and Work Around) Here’s a hard truth that’s part joke, part survival tip: older business owners often think younger business owners are lazy. Is it true? Not really...but maybe. Is it a wildly unfair overgeneralization? Absolutely. But is it something you should keep in mind if you’re the younger party in a deal? Without question. This perception isn’t about facts—it’s about feelings. And in deals, feelings move faster than facts. Maybe they see your flexible schedule and assume you’re not serious. Maybe you mention that you don’t go into the office daily, and they picture you lounging in pajamas until noon. Or maybe you automate 90% of your back office and they assume you don’t understand what it means to “put in the hours.” Example: I’ve had sellers ask buyers in their 30s, “So... who’s going to run the business if you aren’t keeping a physical office space?” To which the buyer responds, “Uh... me... from my home office” The seller’s question is not an attack—it’s a reflection of a generational gap in how “hard work” is pictured. Another one I’ve seen: A Gen X seller was suspicious that a younger buyer wouldn’t “respect the grind” because he mentioned he’d take Fridays off to be with his kids. The irony? The business had 80% of its revenue recurring and ran like a well-oiled machine. But old mental models die hard. So what do you do with that? You over-communicate your seriousness. You don’t get defensive. You show up buttoned-up, prepared, and with a plan. You demonstrate through action (not argument) that you’re not here to “hack” your way through their legacy—you’re here to earn it, evolve it, and honor what they’ve built. It’s not about pretending to be older. It’s about anticipating the perception gap—and proactively closing it. When in doubt: say what you’re going to do, then do it. That alone will set you apart.

They want to know the “why” behind the work, expect feedback (soon and often), and prioritize purpose over perks. They’re fluent in memes and multitasking, expect diversity and authenticity, and have no patience for outdated tech or rigid systems. Negotiation Style: Digital-first and to the point. You don’t need to be a shapeshifter. You need to recognize when the other party is bringing different assumptions to the table—and meet them halfway, wherever they are on the generational timeline -- When a deal falls apart, it’s rarely because of some exotic legal clause. It’s because the parties didn’t care enough about each other to bridge gaps and keep going. Rapport and Respect Will Save Your Deal Conversely, some of the best terms I’ve ever seen have been proposed by the parties working together in collaboration. When Collaboration Becomes the Best Deal Term on the Table Some of the best deal terms I’ve ever seen didn’t come from lawyers, spreadsheets, or negotiation books. They came from two people sitting down, having a real conversation, and solving problems like grown-ups who trust each other. Here’s one of my all-time favorites: Donna and Jeff: A Collaborative Win-Win Donna and Jeff had been circling each other for years. Not romantically—professionally. They were friendly competitors in the same market, each quietly respecting the other's work while occasionally stealing a client or two. Classic small-business frenemy energy. Eventually, Jeff decided it was time to retire and, rather than go to market, he went straight to Donna. He trusted her. She knew the industry. She wasn’t going to gut the company he’d spent 25 years building. So he offered her a deal—entirely seller financed—with terms that frankly looked more generous than you'd expect for that size and quality of business. Donna was interested, but nervous. There was a specific employee she had her eye on—someone with influence over a chunk of the client base. Donna didn’t want to wake up six months post-close with that person gone and her recurring revenue limping. She came to me and asked, “Can I get a non-compete on this guy?” Here’s where I got to be the fun police. I had to break it to her: unfortunately, no. She didn’t have a legal relationship with the employee, wasn’t providing consideration, and had no contractual hook to hang it on. Without that nexus, she couldn’t slap a restrictive covenant on him.

When there’s a foundation of trust, logic and empathy become the best negotiating tools in the room. Tommy and George: When Rapport Doesn’t Have to Be Earned On the other end of the spectrum—where the logic breaks down but the deal closes—I had a front-row seat to one of the strangest transactions I’ve ever worked on. The buyer, we’ll call him Tommy, was young. And not just young—young and brash. He was sharp, sure. But he had a knack for putting his foot in his mouth like it was a daily vitamin. If there was a way to say the wrong thing in a meeting, he’d find it. If there was a tactless comment to make about how the business “really needed to modernize,” he’d say it. Loudly. Twice. I was representing the seller, George, who was in his late 50s. Experienced. Thoughtful. The kind of guy who had built a steady, profitable firm and earned every bit of his market reputation. And I’ll be honest: I kept expecting him to walk. Every time Tommy misstepped—and there were many—I waited for George to say, “You know what? I don’t need this.” But he never did. In fact, he kept extending Tommy grace. Not just patience, but real kindness. He’d soften harsh feedback. He’d give the benefit of the doubt. He even covered for him once in front of staff. Then we closed. Smoothly. George agreed to stay on post-close to help with the transition. It was, frankly, kind of heartwarming—if slightly confusing. It wasn’t until weeks later, in an unrelated conversation, that I found out the missing puzzle piece: George had a son. Same age as Tommy. Same name. Same rough-around-the-edges energy. Sometimes rapport isn’t earned—it’s imparted. Sometimes it’s not about how well you show up in the deal room; it’s about what you unintentionally remind someone of. A son. A younger version of themselves. A chance to pass the torch to someone who, yes, has rough edges—but also has heart. Now, does that mean you can be rude, unpolished, and get the deal? Definitely not what I’m saying. But it’s a good reminder that not all goodwill is transactional. Sometimes it’s personal. And when that happens, the deal gets a little magic dust sprinkled on it that no LOI can capture. Bottom Line Trust beats perfection. Empathy trumps tactics. And rapport—whether earned or instinctively granted—can carry a deal through bumps that would tank a more brittle negotiation. The next time you’re structuring a deal, remember: the best terms aren’t always written by lawyers. They’re born out of trust, human connection, and a genuine desire to create something that works for both sides. 2- Practicing Calculated Empathy: The Art of Understanding What the Seller Cares About (Or: There’s a Lid for Every Pot) Here’s something I say all the time—so much so that clients can probably recite it back to me like a mantra: “Good deals are made, not found.” There’s a myth out there—especially among first-time buyers—that great deals are waiting to be discovered, like some hidden gem buried under a pile of mediocre listings. But here’s the truth: good deals are made, not found.

But turning it into a good deal—that comes from the work you do after you find it. The diligence you dig into. The relationships you build. The structure you negotiate. The risks you manage. I’ve seen buyers walk away from great businesses because the headline number felt too high—without ever doing the work to see how terms could shift the economics. And I’ve seen average businesses become great buys because the buyer knew how to shape the deal to fit their needs and protect their downside. The best deals are rarely perfect when you first spot them. They become great through careful planning, creative structuring, and smart negotiation. So don’t wait around for the unicorn. Learn how to build one. You don’t stumble into a good deal like you find a twenty-dollar bill in your coat pocket. You build one. Piece by piece. With strategy, care, and—believe it or not—empathy. And not any empathy. We’re talking about calculated empathy. This isn’t about being soft or sentimental. It’s about being smart enough to understand what the seller cares about, and using that insight to create alignment, craft better terms, and ultimately get to a deal that works for both sides. Because here’s the thing: you can’t tell whether a business is a “good deal” by looking at a listing. A listing shows you the shell—gross revenue, location, headcount. That’s like picking a spouse based on height and hair color. What makes a deal “good” is the intersection of the business’s features, the terms of the offer, and the emotional and strategic fit between buyer and seller. Which brings me to my grandmother, Irene. She lived to be 97.5 years old—and yes, the half-year mattered. “After 90,” she’d say, “you start counting like you're a toddler again.” She also had a phrase she loved, and it’s been lodged in my brain ever since: “There’s a lid for every pot.” She wasn’t just talking about dating (though she was also definitely talking about dating). She meant that every person, and every situation, has a complementary match—if you’re patient enough to find it. That’s what calculated empathy is in the world of business acquisitions: the practice of finding the fit, not just the numbers. What Does the Seller Care About? Spoiler: it’s rarely just the money. Yes, sellers want to get paid. Of course they do. But very few walk away from a business they’ve built with their own two hands thinking, “Hope the check clears, peace out forever.” They care about what happens next—to their team, to their clients, to their legacy. They care about whether you’ll treat the business with respect. Whether you’ll change the software their team has finally gotten used to. Whether Karen at the front desk, who brought them soup during their divorce, still has a job. Your job as the buyer is to pay attention. Listen for the subtext. Ask the second question. If the seller keeps telling you how long their bookkeeper has been with them, that’s a flag. Not a red one—a gold one. That’s someone who matters. Your deal should reflect that. If they mention they go to lunch every Friday with their original client from 1987, ask if they want to keep that client relationship going post-close as a carveout to the non-compete. These are the details that don’t make it into CIMs or spreadsheets—but they’re what the seller’s heart is anchored to. If you can address them sincerely, you immediately become a more compelling buyer. For the seller, your core concerns usually boil down to two big ones: Get paid. Limit liability. Simple enough, right? But—surprise—those two goals are the foundation. Sellers almost always have specific, personal, often quirky deal terms they care deeply about. Some of them are economic, many are not, and a few will make you pause and say, “Wait, what?” And for the fun part: real-life examples of actual seller requests I’ve seen negotiated, written into LOIs, and in some cases—yes—enforced. Real Requests from Real Sellers: “You must hire Karen at the front desk.” Why? Karen was the seller’s deceased mother’s best friend. This wasn’t about operational efficiency—it was personal legacy. The seller didn’t care if Karen answered the phones or watered the plants. She wanted to know Karen was taken care of. “You can have the jukebox, but I keep the records.” Yep. Seller was emotionally attached to the vinyl. Buyer got the machine. Everyone won. “I’ll keep doing work for these nine clients—for free.” You read that right. No revenue, no split. These were longtime relationships the seller wasn’t ready to let go of. (Buyers: flag this—it could create weird boundaries post-close.) “I want to come in every Wednesday and get a free muffin.” This was a bakery deal. Seller built the business from scratch. All they wanted post-sale was to swing by once a week, chat with staff, and walk out with a muffin. No cash involved—just ritual and closure. “You can have the aquarium, but I keep the fish.” This one made sense once you knew the fish had names and the seller had raised them from tiny little pet-store fry. Again, emotional legacy. “You must rent the office space from me for the next seven years.” The seller owned the real estate. Keeping a stable tenant (a.k.a. the buyer) was part of their retirement income plan. Not optional. Non-negotiable. “You must buy the commercial property as part of the business deal.” No leasing allowed. Seller didn’t want to play landlord. They wanted a clean break, and that meant selling the business and the building in one transaction. “I need to keep access to a private office to store my watercolor paintings.” Yes, the business was being sold. But that office? That was the seller’s creative sanctuary. They wanted to keep using it a few days a week to paint, quietly and peacefully. And they asked for it. “I want to keep using the firm’s tax software to file my returns...forever.” Not for clients. Just for themselves. Free lifetime tax prep tools as a retirement perk. “You can’t change the software the team uses.” The seller was fiercely protective of their staff. They didn’t want the buyer to come in and throw everyone into a new system—especially not in month one. For them, this was about respecting the culture they’d built. These might sound eccentric—but they’re not rare. They’re human. And while they may not show up on a balance sheet, they can carry more emotional weight than a few extra points on the purchase price. Buyers: Don’t Sleep on the Non-Economic Terms As a buyer, it’s easy to zero in on the dollars. What’s the EBITDA? What’s the multiple? How quickly can we close? But if you stop there, you’re missing the point—and potentially missing the deal. Sellers want to know that they matter. That what they’ve built matters. And that you see the whole picture, not the P&L. A well-crafted LOI that speaks to their specific concerns—however odd, sentimental, or minor they may seem to you—sends a powerful message: “I’m not just blasting this out to 30 people. I’m writing this for you.” It builds trust. It builds momentum. And sometimes, a thoughtful, human-centered LOI with a slightly lower purchase price will beat out a cold, generic offer at full price. Because here’s the truth: sellers don’t pick the highest bidder—they pick the one who makes them feel like they’re leaving their baby in good hands. So the next time you’re writing—or reviewing—an LOI, slow down. Ask what matters. And remember that sometimes, the key to getting the deal done isn’t another $50K on the table. It’s letting someone keep their fish. Empathy as Leverage This isn’t about being manipulative. It’s about being strategically human. If you can show up with emotional intelligence and a solid business plan, you will consistently win deals over higher bidders who lack tact, timing, or self-awareness.

One of the biggest tactical mistakes I see in negotiations—especially from first-time buyers—is trying to resolve each term one by one like it’s a checklist at a hardware store. Don’t do that. In complex negotiations, you should not lock in each miniature term in isolation. Instead, leave them all on the table until they can be resolved as a cohesive package, and then take them off together, all at once. This approach—called “package bargaining” in negotiation theory—gives you flexibility to make trade-offs that get the deal done. Maybe you give a little on the seller note, but you get shorter consulting obligations. If you resolve terms too early, you lose leverage, because you’re shrinking your deal toolkit before you know which tools you'll need. Harvard’s Program on Negotiation has long advocated for multi-issue negotiation strategies, noting that “negotiators who consider issues simultaneously, rather than sequentially, are more likely to reach win-win outcomes”—and a 2021 MIT Sloan study confirmed that package negotiators were 26% more likely to close deals than their piecemeal counterparts. Translation? Keep all the terms live until the deal comes together like a final puzzle snap. Otherwise, you’ll spend all your leverage solving for the corners, and have nothing left to finish the picture. You can’t look at each piece of the transaction—price, structure, seller financing, employment agreement, lease terms—as if they’re isolated Lego blocks. They’re more like a plate of spaghetti. Tug on one noodle, and the whole thing shifts. That’s why I’m constantly coaching buyers and sellers to resolve as many terms as possible at once. Because if you don’t? You end up in a never-ending game of term-by-term Whack-A-Mole. Raise the seller-financed amount? The seller now wants more post-close involvement. Lower the seller note interest rate? Suddenly they want more salary. They push for a quick close? You ask for a longer transition window. On and on it goes. Why Package Bargaining Is a LOI Power Play (And Why You Lose That Power After It’s Signed) The annoying part about package bargaining is you only really get to do it before the LOI is signed. After that? You're no longer building a deal—you’re coloring inside the lines of one. Here’s why. The LOI Locks In the Frame—Even When It’s "Non-Binding" Everyone loves to say that LOIs are “non-binding,” and legally, sure—that’s true. But functionally? Once both sides sign that letter, it sets the tone, structure, and framework for the rest of the deal. It becomes the working contract, even if it’s not enforceable in court. People get emotionally and mentally anchored to what’s in it. So if you come back after the LOI and say, “I want to tweak the purchase price, reduce the seller note, and add a consulting agreement,” the other side hears: “I’m trying to renegotiate what we already agreed on.” Now, they’re defensive. The energy shifts. And you’ve lost your flexibility. Before the LOI: All the Levers Are on the Table LOI is your golden window. It’s the only stage where: You’re exploring. You have multiple trade-offs available. Nobody’s committed yet. And both sides are more open to creativity because nothing feels “final.” That’s when you can say: “If you need that higher topline number, maybe we shift some of it to an earnout.” “If you’re worried about staff retention, let’s make that part of the consulting arrangement.” “If cash at close isn’t where you want it, what if we sweeten the seller note with a higher interest rate and shorter term?” This is where package bargaining lives—not in legal docs, but in strategic conversations between two people trying to make the puzzle fit.

Translation: Use the LOI Stage Like It Matters (Because It Does) This is why I tell buyers: don’t rush the LOI to “get it signed.” The LOI isn’t a formality. It’s your last and best chance to think holistically about the deal. Because once that letter goes out with a price and a basic structure, you’ve taken a hundred other structures off the table. You’ve told the seller, “Here’s the shape of what I’m offering,” and anything that doesn’t fit inside that shape now feels like a problem. So before you send it, do your packaging. Build your trade-offs. Think like a chef, not a short-order cook. Mix the ingredients in a way that makes the whole thing work, not one piece at a time. And trust me—you’ll never wish you waited until the APA to get strategic. Example 1: The Seller Note Squeeze If the bank is only willing to finance the deal if there’s at least a 10% seller note involved. But the seller’s allergic to that idea—“I’m not your bank,” they say, rolling their eyes across the conference room table. Here’s a potential solution: You sweeten the seller’s consulting agreement to offset the ding. Maybe you increase their monthly rate. Maybe you give them a guaranteed six-month runway post-close with a clear scope of work. That turns the sting of the seller note into something that feels more like earned income—not deferred payment with risk attached. Want to go further? You slap a healthy interest rate on the seller note and tie it to a friendly repayment window (e.g., paid off in 18 months, not five years). That not only creates financial incentive for the seller to want the business to succeed—it also signals that you plan to prioritize paying them off quickly. Same seller note, totally different emotional experience. Example 2: The Purchase Price Bridge Radha was an attorney looking to acquire a boutique estate planning firm in Austin. The seller, Lara, had built the firm from the ground up over two decades and was proud of the client base she’d cultivated—mostly high-net-worth families and business owners with complex estate planning needs. Radha, however, was pragmatic. Based on her analysis of the financials, recurring revenue, and team capacity, she believed the practice was worth about $900,000. Lara was firm on $1.25 million, pointing to the strong pipeline of referrals, long-term client relationships, and her belief that the next 12 months were going to be her most profitable yet. Rather than argue over the valuation—or worse, walk away—they found common ground using package bargaining. Here’s how it played out: Radha agreed to pay $900,000 at closing, and they structured a $350,000 promissory note, but with a retention adjustment built in. “If the firm hits $700,000 in gross revenue in the first 12 months,” Radha said, “you’ll get the full $350,000. But if we fall short, the amount adjusts downward based on actual performance.” This allowed Lara to stand behind her confidence in the firm’s future—and Radha to protect herself from overpaying based on potential that hadn’t yet materialized. As it turned out, the firm performed well, but not quite at Lara’s forecast. Radha ended up paying $225,000 on the note—so the total purchase price landed over $1.1 million. Lara walked away feeling respected and rewarded.

Is this really about money, or is it about feeling heard? If I give ground here, can I gain it back somewhere that matters more to me? Because the best deals—the durable, high-trust, low-drama ones—are made by people who understand that you don’t win deals term-by-term. You win them by building the full picture. And sometimes, the best way to alleviate the concern about a contracting fee is to modify the interest rate on the seller note... or to offer a free muffin on Wednesdays. BOX – Concern 1 – I don’t have enough information- Realistically you will not be able to put everything into a letter of intent. You probably will not have enough information. That’s okay, but I think the exercise of going through all ten steps below and considering your position on them is incredibly valuable at the earliest possible stage. BOX-Concern 2 – I am going to scare the seller with this detail. – You might! But more often they’re going to see that you’re thoughtful and take your offer seriously. There are a lot of different brokers out there with a lot of different backgrounds and quality and there are some folks who view diligence and thoroughness as the enemy to a deal. I know it’s easy to say from where I’m sitting on the sidelines, but the letter of intent is also about weeding out brokers that are going to make your deal miserable. If a seller or their broker sees your thoroughness as a downside, that is a red flag that will certainly show up again before the deal is done. If you are very concerned, you can also initiate conversations by a much simpler Indication of Interest (IOI) – an IOI is often little more than an email with a purchase price and can kick off discussions that will allow you to get the information you need to move on to the point where you’re able to negotiate a full LOI. Letters of Intent: Make It STRUCTURED Historically, the Letter of Intent has functioned more like a wink than a contract. It says, “We like you. Let’s see where this goes.” And for billion-dollar acquirers with deal teams and deep pockets, that might be enough. They can afford to churn through half-baked LOIs and let broken deals be a cost of doing business. But for most buyers and sellers—especially in the small business world—that kind of vagueness quickly becomes a liability. It wastes time. It delays real alignment. And it often hides the “gotchas” that only surface halfway through diligence—when tempers are short and the champagne has gone flat. Worse, many standard LOIs are wildly one-sided. They often bind the seller through exclusivity, while letting the buyer keep every possible “out.” The result? The LOI becomes less of a foundation and more of a shield—protecting buyers from commitment while they keep shopping around. So how do you do it differently? You build a better LOI. Not a perfect one—but a purposeful one.

In the pages that follow, we’ll walk through each letter of the STRUCTURED acronym, piece by piece. Nail Your LOI by Making It STRUCTURED A strong LOI isn’t vague. It’s not a “we’ll figure it out later” document. It sets the tone, the timeline, and the trust level for the entire deal. That means you want to cover the key points up front. Here’s what that looks like, mapped to the STRUCTURED acronym: S – Structure Spell out exactly what’s being acquired—assets vs. equity, full sale or partial, and whether IP, brand, or real estate are included. T – Terms That Bind Clarify which terms are binding and which aren’t. Commonly binding provisions include exclusivity, confidentiality, governing law, and the agreement to negotiate in good faith. R – Retention and Price Adjustments Include any retention-based adjustments to price. Will compensation be held back if clients or employees leave? How will working capital be handled? U – Use of Employees Be explicit about employee expectations post-close—especially when the “employee” is a spouse, adult child, or a “seasonal helper.” These family-tied roles can quietly unravel deals if not addressed early. C – Covenants Not to Compete, Carveouts & the Art of Getting Specific Define the non-compete, non-solicit, and any exceptions. A vague non-compete is a lawsuit waiting to happen—or a worthless clause. Use clear terms and include carveouts where appropriate. T – Tenant Issues If there’s a lease involved, it needs real attention. What are the current rates? Are they market-based? Will the buyer assume the lease, or is a new agreement needed? Office space often becomes a surprise deal-killer when left vague. U – Use of Seller Post-Closing Outline exactly what role (if any) the seller will have post-close. Will they consult? For how long? Paid or unpaid? On call or hands-on? R – Reps, Warranties & The Legal Stuff Even if the LOI isn’t the place to draft all the reps and warranties, it should define who will prepare the purchase agreement, what laws will govern, and whether indemnification will be on the table. E – Exclusivity and Good Faith Deposits Will the seller stop shopping the deal while diligence is happening? For how long? Is there a deposit? Is it refundable? Spell it out. D – Dollars (and the Flow of Them) Don’t just put a price range—lay out the actual mechanics: Total purchase price Payment terms: how much in cash, seller financing, earnout, equity, etc. Any holdbacks, escrows, or performance-based adjustments And don’t forget the “soft stuff.” It may not show up on a balance sheet, but seller motivation and cultural fit matter—especially in a profession built on client trust. Include a paragraph on shared values and post-close intentions. If you aren’t a fit, you aren’t a fit and you want to figure that out while everyone has gas in the tank to find a better match. Chapter X: Why the LOI Is the Real Negotiation Battlefield There’s a persistent myth in the world of buying and selling businesses that a Letter of Intent (LOI) is “a placeholder”—a soft, informal gesture before the “real” negotiation starts. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard someone say, “Oh, it’s non-binding anyway.” Let me set the record straight: that’s not actually how it works. What makes a document binding or not binding isn’t the title—it’s the language inside and the way the parties act about it. In fact, if you’re doing it right, the LOI is where the real negotiation happens. This is the blueprint for the deal. Get it wrong here, and you’re in for a mess. Get it right, and everything else becomes smoother and more predictable. BOX A Quick Note on Retrades “I don’t know what to say, I guess I have to reserve the right to get smarter.” – a genius and very likeable opposing counsel telling me he wanted to change a term from the LOI Retrading — trying to change the terms after they’ve already been agreed to — is like ordering your hamburger, waiting until it hits the table, then asking the server to make it well-done instead-oh and does that bun have gluten in it? I’m gluten free. Technically, they can take it back to the kitchen, but now the chef’s annoyed, the timing’s off, and the whole experience lost its flavor. You might get what you want, but not without burning some goodwill and you’re certainly going to need to leave a bigger tip. Do it once or twice, maybe you survive. More than that and you’re going to have some serious relationship management to do. That’s why we bake as much as possible into the LOI. Reps and warranties? Those can come later. Diligence checklists? Definitely. But the terms at the heart of the deal — what everyone cares about most — should already be on the table, talked through, and agreed upon before you sign exclusivity. In fact, anything you can know up front should be known and agreed upon. If you simply do not have enough information to put something in the LOI, that’s fine, save it for later on. But most terms are actually pretty knowable at the outset. A MANIFESTO FOR ALIGNMENT Normalize hard conversations early — when they’re productive, not reactive. Build LOIs that do the heavy lifting, not just set the stage. If we do this right, the rest of the process becomes execution, not negotiation. No more games. No more gotchas. Just alignment, transparency, and velocity. If you’re selling: Don’t sign anything until the LOI says everything you want. If you’re buying: Use the LOI to test fit, reveal issues, and secure clarity. Buyers may need to recalibrate their approach and hold off on sending 30 LOIs at once. Make each one truly count and stop wasting people’s time. The LOI isn’t just the first step. It’s the moment that determines whether the deal succeeds or fails. THE TEN PARTS TO A S.T.R.U.C.T.U.R.E.D LETTER OF INTENT S- Structure - Asset Purchase vs. Stock Purchase When you're buying or selling a business, one of the first major decisions you’ll face is how to structure the deal. The two most common options? An asset purchase or a stock purchase. This choice doesn’t just shape the mechanics of the transaction—it affects risk exposure, tax consequences, and the long-term success of the deal. Next, we’ll break down what each structure really means, and why it matters. [add a drawing where someone either buys a black box or gets to open that box and choose what they want to buy out of it] Asset Purchase: The Pick-and-Choose Approach In an asset purchase, the buyer forms a new entity—let’s call it “Newco”—and purchases selected assets from the selling business. These might include physical property (like equipment and furniture), intangible property (like trademarks, customer lists, and goodwill), or contracts, inventory, and licenses. The seller retains the corporate shell—and, under the general rule, also retains the liabilities. That’s a big reason why asset purchases are the go-to choice for many buyers: they get what they want, without taking on what they don’t. But before you get too comfortable, know this: the general rule about avoiding liabilities has several exceptions, and they’re not rare. Successor Liability: What Buyers Hope to Avoid... But Sometimes Can’t In most asset deals, the legal default is that the buyer does not inherit the seller’s debts, lawsuits, or liabilities. Those remain with the selling entity. But courts can and do pop this bubble of protection (called piercing the corporate veil) under certain circumstances. Here are the major exceptions to keep in mind: 1. De Facto Merger If the transaction walks and talks like a merger—even if it’s called an asset purchase—a court may treat it as one. This can happen when: The seller’s business continues substantially unchanged under the buyer The same officers or owners stay involved in similar roles and/or There’s little separation between the old and new entities 2. Express or Implied Assumption of Liability If the buyer contractually agrees to take on certain debts—or behaves in a way that implies it has assumed them—those liabilities may follow them. This could happen with informal actions like continuing to pay off old vendor contracts or covering warranties without a formal agreement. 3. Fraudulent Transfer If a deal is structured in a way that appears to be an attempt to avoid creditors—by stripping the seller of its valuable assets and leaving it unable to meet obligations—courts can undo the transaction. This is especially risky when: No real consideration (money or value) was exchanged There is overlap in ownership or management The buyer continues operations using the same staff, location, or branding 4. Product Line Exception Some states apply the product line exception, particularly in manufacturing cases. If the buyer continues producing the same product line, they may be held liable for claims arising from products sold before the purchase—even if it was technically an asset deal. 5. Labor and Employment Law Even where general successor liability doesn’t apply, certain labor laws may impose obligations on a buyer—especially when the buyer hires a majority of the seller’s workforce and continues operating in the same fashion. Stock Purchase: Simpler for the Seller, Riskier for the Buyer In a stock purchase, the buyer acquires the ownership interests—shares, units, or membership interests—in the selling company itself. The business entity doesn’t change. Contracts, licenses, employees, and (crucially) liabilities all remain intact. That continuity can make for a smoother transition—there’s no name change, no need to re-assign leases, licenses, or vendor agreements, you can keep the same bank account—but it also means the buyer inherits everything, including unknown or contingent liabilities. This structure often appeals to sellers, since it minimizes disruption and can offer more favorable tax treatment. But buyers need to tread carefully, often with thorough due diligence and indemnity protections built into the purchase agreement. BOX Accounts Receivable Asset Purchase vs. Stock Purchase: What Happens to Accounts Receivable? One of the key differences between an asset purchase and a stock purchase comes down to what you’re buying—and accounts receivable is a perfect example of how that plays out in the real world. In an Asset Purchase The buyer is only acquiring specific assets and liabilities that are listed in the purchase agreement. Think of it like a “pick-and-choose” deal. If you’re the buyer, you might choose to buy the client list, equipment, goodwill, and lease—but usually not the accounts receivable. Why? Because A/R can be a bit messy. Some of it might be old, uncollectible, or tied up in disputes.

But buyers need to tread carefully, often with thorough due diligence and indemnity protections built into the purchase agreement. BOX Accounts Receivable Asset Purchase vs. Stock Purchase: What Happens to Accounts Receivable? One of the key differences between an asset purchase and a stock purchase comes down to what you’re buying—and accounts receivable is a perfect example of how that plays out in the real world. In an Asset Purchase The buyer is only acquiring specific assets and liabilities that are listed in the purchase agreement. Think of it like a “pick-and-choose” deal. If you’re the buyer, you might choose to buy the client list, equipment, goodwill, and lease—but usually not the accounts receivable. Why? Because A/R can be a bit messy. Some of it might be old, uncollectible, or tied up in disputes. In many cases, the seller keeps their own receivables, continues to collect them after closing, and may even pay the buyer a percentage if any work is required to help with collections. In a Stock Purchase You’re buying the whole company entity, liabilities and all. That includes the corporate shell, contracts, obligations—and yes, accounts receivable. In this case, the A/R is part of the business’s balance sheet at closing. It becomes yours, for better or worse. If there’s $100K in outstanding invoices, they’re now yours to collect. But so are any aging receivables, billing disputes, or accounting quirks that haven’t been cleaned up. Bottom line: In a stock deal, you inherit the A/R by default—so you better be confident in what you’re getting. BOX Tax Treatment: The IRS Cares How You Structure Your Deal Deal structure doesn’t just influence liability exposure—it directly affects how the transaction is taxed for both parties. Asset Purchase – Tax Implications Both parties must file IRS Form 8594, which allocates the purchase price across categories like tangible property, inventory, goodwill, and non-compete agreements. These allocations affect the buyer’s future deductions and the seller’s tax liabilities. As a general rule, Sellers are going to want as much allocated to goodwill as possible to maximize the amount of the purchase price they’ll be paying capital gains on (versus a worse ordinary income tax) Buyer’s advantage: Buyers get a stepup in basis. That means they can depreciate or amortize assets based on their fair market value, which can create significant tax deductions over time. Seller’s challenge: For C corporations, asset sales often result in double taxation—first at the corporate level when assets are sold, and again when proceeds are distributed to shareholders. Even in pass-through entities, certain assets (like depreciated equipment) can trigger ordinary income, which is taxed at higher rates than capital gains. Stock Purchase – Tax Implications Seller’s benefit: Typically, the seller pays capital gains tax on the sale of the ownership interest—often at favorable long-term rates. Buyer’s limitation: The buyer takes over the company “as-is,” including its historical basis in assets. That means less depreciation or amortization benefit compared to an asset purchase. Choosing the Right Structure Here’s the general pattern: Buyers tend to prefer asset purchases for the ability to avoid liabilities and step up basis. Sellers often push for stock sales to simplify the transition and optimize tax outcomes. But every deal is unique. The right choice depends on: The type of business The parties' tax positions The existence of contracts or licenses that are hard to assign The tolerance for risk Whether you're buying or selling, deal structure matters. A lot. It shapes risk exposure, tax liability, and how cleanly the business transitions to its next chapter. And while asset purchases are often seen as the “safer” option, they don’t provide a free pass. Courts look at substance over form. If the facts suggest the deal was a merger in disguise or designed to evade liabilities, successor liability can follow. T- Terms that Bind- What’s Binding and What’s Not? [figure of shackles on different terms] A typical LOI is a mix of binding and non-binding provisions. And the trick is being crystal clear about which is which. Courts look to the intent of the parties—what you agreed to, not what you called it. Here’s how it usually breaks down: Binding Provisions These are the parts that are enforceable immediately, regardless of whether the final purchase agreement ever gets signed. Common binding clauses include: Confidentiality This protects sensitive business information exchanged during due diligence. It means you can’t take what you learn about the other party and use it to compete, leak it, or shop it around. Exclusivity (also called a “no-shop” clause) This gives the buyer a set period of time where the seller agrees not to entertain other offers or shop the deal elsewhere. It’s binding, and violating it can tank trust—and trigger legal consequences. Governing Law This tells everyone which state’s laws will apply if there’s a dispute.

Often overlooked, but important if things go sideways. Deposit Terms / Good Faith Money If the buyer is putting down a deposit—refundable or not—the terms around it are binding. This includes when it’s due, what triggers a refund (or not), and whether it goes toward the purchase price. Duty to Negotiate in Good Faith This one’s subtle but important. If the LOI says the parties agree to negotiate in good faith toward a definitive agreement, it can actually be enforced in some jurisdictions. You can’t sign an LOI and then ghost or sabotage the deal without risking consequences. Non-Binding Provisions These are the “deal terms” that are typically up for renegotiation as the parties move through diligence. Things like: Purchase price and adjustments Employment or transition terms for the seller Financing structure Indemnity and reps & warranties Closing timeline That said—just because these are “non-binding” doesn’t mean they’re irrelevant. In practice, once something is in the LOI, it becomes emotionally and practically difficult to change. Any shift can look like a re-trade, and that erodes trust. there are court cases where Letters of Intent (LOIs) were treated as binding contracts, despite their typical non-binding language. Courts often look beyond the document’s label and evaluate the intent of the parties, the language used, and their conduct. Here’s a quick breakdown: When an LOI Can Be Treated as Binding Courts may enforce an LOI—or portions of it—if: The language indicates intent to be bound, even provisionally. Key deal terms (like price, closing date, or payment structure) are sufficiently defined. The parties acted as if they had a deal, e.g., starting performance, sharing confidential data, or excluding other offers. There’s evidence of reliance or partial performance that creates equitable grounds for enforcement (like promissory estoppel). Key Cases Where LOIs Were Treated as Binding Teachers Insurance & Annuity Association v. Tribune Co., 670 F. Supp. 491 (S.D.N.Y. 1987) The court found that the parties intended to be bound by the LOI, even though some terms were still being negotiated. Critical takeaway: A detailed LOI with agreed-upon material terms may signal an intent to be bound. Texaco, Inc. v. Pennzoil Co., 729 S.W.2d 768 (Tex. App. 1987) One of the most famous: Pennzoil and Getty had a signed Memorandum of Agreement, but Texaco swooped in before a formal contract was signed. Jury found a binding agreement existed, leading to a $10+ billion verdict against Texaco. Empro Mfg. Co. v. Ball-Co Manufacturing, Inc., 870 F.2d 423 (7th Cir. 1989) The opposite result: court ruled the LOI was non-binding, largely because it expressly disclaimed any obligation to close until a formal agreement was signed. Best Practices to Avoid Unintended Binding LOIs Use clear disclaimers in LOIs that state: “This letter is not intended to create any binding obligation...” Be explicit about which terms (if any) are binding (e.g., confidentiality, exclusivity). Avoid acting like the deal is done before it is (e.g., don’t announce it or start integration). Example: Non-binding Nature. This Letter of Intent is intended solely as a reflection of the parties' mutual interest in pursuing the potential transaction described herein. Except for the provisions relating to exclusivity, confidentiality, governing law, and any other specifically designated binding terms, this Letter of Intent is non-binding and does not create any legally enforceable obligations on either party to consummate the transaction. Both parties acknowledge that any binding commitment will only arise upon the execution of a definitive agreement. R-Retention Adjustments – Aligning Incentives & Creating a Bridge When used well, retention adjustments can offer a clean way to lower the risk of a deal without getting too far into legal weeds and without adverse tax consequences. Let’s unpack what this is, when to use it, and what you need to watch out for. What Is a Retention Adjustment? A retention adjustment is a mechanism that adjusts the purchase price down after closing if certain client or revenue thresholds aren’t met during the transition period. It’s usually tied to the retention of key clients, staff, or recurring revenue, and instead of being paid extra for hitting targets (like in an earnout), the seller takes a reduction if those targets aren’t met. In short: It’s not a bonus for performance—it’s a discount for underperformance. These adjustments are typically structured as: Reductions to the seller note principal Purchase price offsets or clawbacks held in escrow Discounts built into a final installment payment due after a short transition It’s an elegant way to align incentives during the handoff—especially when the seller insists that “the clients will stay” or “the staff loves me and they’ll be fine.” If they’re that confident, they shouldn’t balk. [Box: The SBA 7(a) Problem: No Post-Closing Seller Upside If you’re financing the deal with an SBA 7(a) loan, your options get more limited—fast. The SBA has strict rules about no post-closing seller upside. That traditionally meant: No earnouts No performance-based bonuses No “phantom equity” or backend kicker Their rationale is that they don’t want the seller continuing to influence the business in a way that might jeopardize the buyer’s ability to operate independently. It’s also about loan collateralization and repayment certainty. But downside-only adjustments? Technically allowed. You can include mechanisms that reduce the purchase price if certain conditions aren't met, as long as they’re clearly defined at the time of closing and don’t function like earnouts in disguise. That said, just because you can do it doesn’t mean everyone will like it. Why Downside-Only Adjustments Can Rub Sellers the Wrong Way Here’s where deal psychology kicks in. Even though a retention adjustment is technically fair—“If the clients don’t stay, I’m not paying full price”—it often feels worse to sellers than a traditional earnout. Why? Because it’s all risk, no reward. Earnouts say: “Hey, you could make even more!” Retention adjustments say: “We’re docking your pay if things go sideways.” And if you’re layering this onto a deal that already has a heavy seller note, consulting agreement, or SBA scrutiny? It can start to feel punitive—especially to a seller who already has to wait 3–5 years to get fully paid.] So, when you use retention adjustments, clarity and tone matter. Here’s how to do it well: How to Structure a Retention Adjustment That Doesn’t Torpedo the Deal Tie it to a clear metric. Think: “Client X, Y, and Z stay through Month 12” or “$400K of revenue from recurring clients remains billed by Month 18.” Fuzzy metrics = instant red flags. Numerator: Start with the numerator—that’s what the seller gets credit for retaining. Is it gross revenue? Specific client names? A revenue figure tied only to recurring services? You want clarity here. If it’s based on revenue, is it collected revenue or billed revenue? The more precise this is, the less room there is for misunderstanding (or manipulation) down the road. I usually prefer topline targets like gross revenue because the buyer can control the costs/overhead. As an example of how manipulatable EBTIDA or profit is, if you have a metric tied to profit margin, the buyer may be able to add a consulting fee to an affiliate entity in there to wipe out any profit. Because of this, you have to get granular on your definition of what counts as qualified overhead to keep that type of manipulation at bay. While doable, that’s a hefty negotiation point to add into a smaller deal and the attorneys’ fees can stack up. Additionally, a narrow definition of what counts as profit can have unintended consequences that keep the buyer from running the business the way they should in their best judgment. Better to stick to topline. Next, the denominator—the baseline. This is what the retention is measured against. It could be total trailing twelve months (TTM) revenue, a list of clients included in the deal, or the average of the last three years. Sellers need to ensure that the denominator reflects the actual strength of the business they’re selling—not a cherry-picked high point that sets them up to fail.

It allows a portion of the purchase price to be tied to how well the business performs after the sale—often based on client retention or revenue benchmarks. But if that’s the deal structure, it’s only natural that the seller will want some say in how the business is operated during that retention period. After all, their payout is on the line. Because here’s the thing: the seller may be picturing a six-month cruise, Mai Tai in hand, no emails, no client calls, and absolutely no staff questions. But you? You might be expecting them to sit in on every single client handoff, meet weekly for strategy sessions, and maybe even stick around long enough to help train their replacement. If those visions don’t match? Congratulations, you’re about to hit your first major post-close expectation clash. Why You Have to Talk About This Before You Sign When someone sells their business, part of what the buyer is paying for is them—or at least, the value they’ve built around their name, their relationships, and their know-how. That goodwill is baked into the purchase price. So yes, some amount of post-closing help is expected and totally fair. Things like introducing the buyer to key clients, being available to answer questions, and helping them understand how the firm runs day to day—that’s all part of the deal. No one expects a seller to hand over the keys and disappear into the sunset the next morning (well, unless that was the agreement). But here’s the important part: there’s a line. Once a seller has given a reasonable amount of time and effort to support the transition, anything beyond that should be treated as additional work—and compensated accordingly. If a seller is answering emails at midnight three months after closing, or being asked to handle shift work like they never left, it’s no longer a “transition.” It’s free labor. And that’s when things get weird. So when structuring a deal, it’s important to talk about this early. The parties should agree on what’s included in the purchase price in terms of the seller’s time and involvement, and then draw a clear boundary.

Period. An overbroad clause is not only scary to the seller—it’s also less likely to be enforceable. You’re creating fog and hoping fear does the rest. In some situations, the chilling effect of a contract can be a valid strategy, but in the context of a non-compete resist the urge to play tough guy with the language. Draft what you need to feel protected—and what a court is likely to uphold if it ever comes to that. A fair, enforceable non-compete is worth way more than a scary one that falls apart on day one. On the flip side, if the clause is too narrow, you leave the door wide open for the seller to compete with you outright—and possibly still beat you in the market while you’re stuck paying the debt service on the business you bought. And here’s the real kicker: the loans used to buy a business often last 10 years. But most non-competes max out around 5. So if your seller can take their non-solicit gloves off in year six and start calling every client they ever landed? That’s a big red flag—not necessarily for the contract, but for how you ran the business post-close. In my opinion, if they can win all those clients back after five years, you didn’t protect or grow the business—you babysat it. One common mistake? Assuming the non-compete magically covers everyone in the seller’s orbit—whether they’re part of the deal or not. Here’s the reality: a buyer can’t restrict someone they don’t have a contractual relationship with. That means if the seller’s employees are in a state where non-competes aren’t enforceable (hello, California), they may be free to walk out the door and take clients with them—unless there’s another agreement in place that limits that behavior. And what about the seller’s son who happens to be in the same business, uses the same last name, and never signed a single page of the deal documents? Yeah, he’s probably not bound either. It’s not enough to assume everyone will “do the right thing” or that the non-compete has a chilling effect by proximity. If a person didn’t sign the agreement—or can’t be lawfully bound by it—then they’re not covered. Period. So when drafting restrictions, think strategically. Who needs to be under contract? Where are they located? What limitations are enforceable? Plug the gaps before closing, because after the fact, it’s too late to wish you’d gotten one more signature. T- Tenant Issues—The Biggest Deal Killer That No One Sees Coming If I had a dollar for every seller who told me, “Don’t worry, I have a great relationship with the landlord,” I could buy the building myself. And I might need to—because that “great relationship” disappeared when it’s time for an actual lease transfer. Here’s the truth: The single biggest deal-killer that’s not a bank is almost always the landlord. Not taxes. Not reps and warranties. Not seller cold feet--The landlord. Let’s talk about why. Why Would the Landlord Say Yes? Think about it from the landlord’s perspective. Right now, they have a tenant with: A long-standing history of paying rent An existing business or personal relationship A lease they probably like (or at least tolerate) Now you’re asking them to: Let that tenant off the hook (often years before the lease ends) Replace them with a new person who has no track record in that location Agree to new lease terms, often with bank-mandated clauses they hate Pay legal fees to draft or review a lease assignment they didn’t ask for [Box SBA Oh, and if the deal is SBA-financed? But in reality? It introduces a whole new layer of deal complexity. Because now the seller is wearing two hats: Business owner (selling the business) Landlord (renting the space) And the lease becomes a key point of negotiation. Why? Because the lease rate was likely optimized for their own tax planning—not reality. Here’s what that usually looks like: Scenario A: They paid way too much in rent, shifting money into the real estate LLC to create passive income and offset depreciation Scenario B: They paid way too little, artificially juicing operating profit to impress you and your lender Neither number is useful to you as a buyer. What you need is market rent, and you need to normalize it to understand both: True business profitability Future lease burden post-close That means you’ll need a comp analysis or broker opinion—even if the deal is in LOI stage. Yes, it’s early. Yes, it’s annoying. But if the seller owns the building, this is a core deal point. Delay it at your own risk. A Note on Lease Math: Why Sellers Should Always Prefer Rent Over Price If you’re negotiating both rent and purchase price, here’s something to keep in mind: Every extra $1 in rent is 12x more valuable per year than an additional $1 in purchase price. Why? Because that $1 gets paid monthly—and over the life of a 5- or 10-year lease, that’s serious cash flow. The seller walks away with a tidy income stream, often taxed favorably. That’s why smart sellers will always push a buyer to “raise the rent a little” rather than shave the purchase price. This is exactly why we don’t take terms off the table too early. Because the lease and the purchase price are linked—you move one, the other moves too. Package bargaining at its finest. If you’re buying a business with a leased space: Get landlord engagement early. Structure your LOI with lease contingencies. Understand whether your lender needs a new lease, assignment, or SNDA. If the seller owns the building, dig into rent comps immediately. Because you might think the deal is between you and the seller—but the landlord? There’s excitement, nerves, and a long list of deal points to iron out. One of the trickiest—and most emotionally charged—topics? Employees. Who gets hired? When do you meet them? What do you promise them? Let’s break it down. When Can You Talk to the Team? This is almost always a point of tension. Buyers want to meet the employees before committing to a deal. Sellers, understandably, want to protect their team and their business until the deal is real. The typical approach? You do not get access to employees until after the purchase agreement is signed or, oftentimes, until the deal is fully closed and funded. This is non-negotiable in many deals, especially in small to mid-sized law firms and professional service practices. The seller is operating the firm, responsible for performance, and needs the staff to show up and do good work. Until the deal is locked in, access to employees remains off-limits. Instead, your first look at the team will often be a combination of: An org chart Compensation and title information Tenure summaries Performance notes (if the seller is open to sharing them) Then, after the agreement is signed—and, hopefully, before closing (but often after)—you’ll have a brief window to interview, make offers, and plan the transition. Some buyers build in a “pre-closing access” clause that allows a 1–2 week period for this exact purpose. It’s tight. It’s fast. But it’s normal. Should You Hire Everyone? Maybe not. But don’t start swinging the axe either. You’re inheriting a team that likely includes some MVPs and some folks who’ve been coasting. It’s tempting to “clean house” and bring in your own people—but gutting the staff is a recipe for chaos. These employees know the systems, the clients, the seasons. They are the muscle memory of the firm. In a small business, it is VERY challenging to know whether someone is the absolute heart and blood of the team based on their job description. At the same time, don’t hire someone you know for sure you’re going to fire. That’s cruel, destabilizing, and it puts the firm at risk. Be honest with yourself during diligence. Look at performance, attitude, and fit—and make your offers accordingly. Consider Retention Bonuses Instead of Raises One of the most common mistakes buyers make? BOX A Note on Family Members: The Hidden Landmine Now let’s talk about something even trickier: when a family member works in the business—and wanted to buy it. A broker colleague once told me: “I won’t sell a business if a key employee wanted to buy it but couldn’t. Those deals almost always implode.” Why? Because resentment poisons transitions. Now imagine that employee isn’t just a manager... it’s the seller’s daughter or son. Thanks to SBA 7(a) loans and thanks to private equity’s impact on the market, buyers can often purchase a business with only 10% down. That sounds great—unless you’re a retiring parent who’s counting on the proceeds to fund retirement. Selling to your kid means: Taking less money and funding their loan yourself, AND Asking them to shoulder millions in debt they probably can't afford. In either scenario, tensions rise. The seller can’t afford to turn down millions right at the cusp of their retirement and the family member employee can’t afford to take on millions in debt. The family member employee may stay on, but often they’re bitter. They feel overlooked. And when the buyer shows up, they’re walking into a landmine. If you find yourself in this position as a buyer, ask directly: “Was anyone in the family interested in buying the business?” If the answer is yes, don’t ignore it. Ask how that conversation went. Ask how that person feels about the transition. And have a plan—whether that’s a buyout path, a defined role, or a timeline for their exit. Sometimes she’s the de facto HR department—onboarding employees, handling payroll questions, even smoothing over office drama. Other times, she’s doing serious work that no one thought to mention. One time, it was a plumbing company where the spouse was doing all the bookkeeping—and doing it well. Another time, it was a gym where the seller’s wife was training clients several days a week... without taking a dime in salary. Here’s the issue: that labor isn’t reflected in the financials.
