(Short answer: Whoever wants the upper hand.) Now we’re getting to the part of the deal where the real power plays start—and they don’t look like power plays on the surface. They look like Word docs. Redlines. First drafts of “standard” contracts. But make no mistake: whoever kicks off the drafting process is usually the one steering the bus. And nine times out of ten, that should be the buyer. Here’s why. First, What Are We Talking About? “Definitive agreements” is the legal world’s term for the final, binding contracts that make your deal real. Not the promises, but the actual paperwork that transfers money, responsibility, risk, and assets. These usually include: The purchase agreement (a.k.a. the big one) Schedules of assets, clients, liabilities Promissory notes Consulting agreement (if the seller’s sticking around) Non-competes, IP assignments, and other guardrails Bill of sale; assignment and assumption; closing certificates, resolutions Lease or lease assignment This is where the details that really matter live—not just the headline price or closing date. Why It Matters Who Goes First Whoever drafts first frames the conversation. They get to: Choose the structure and tone of the agreement Decide what’s “included” vs. what has to be negotiated Build in subtle risk allocations—often buried in reps, warranties, and indemnities Even if the other side redlines it to death, the initial draft creates momentum. And in deals, momentum is power. I’ve seen it happen: a seller or their broker offers to “get things started” by sending over a draft. Harmless, right? Just saving time? Wrong. The buyer spends the next three weeks untangling language that subtly favors the seller—language the seller now treats as the starting point. Meanwhile, time ticks down, and everyone’s tired by the time the real negotiations begin. In the flurry of deal terms and negotiations, there’s one small section that often gets shrugged off until the very end: the governing law and jurisdiction clause. It sounds boring. It’s legal boilerplate. Who cares, right? You should care. This seemingly tiny clause can end up deciding how expensive, complicated, and winnable your dispute becomes if the deal ever blows up. Let’s break down what these two terms really mean—and why you want to think about them sooner rather than later. Governing Law: What Rules Apply? Governing law means: if there’s a dispute over the deal, which state’s laws will be used to interpret and enforce the agreement? This matters a lot more than you might think. Different states have different rules when it comes to things like: Non-competes (California hates them; Florida doesn’t mind them) Successor liability Indemnity enforceability Usury laws (affecting interest rates on seller notes) Statutes of limitations Interpretation of vague terms (some states let in a lot of parol evidence; others don’t) Confessions of Judgment Pre-dispute Jury Trial Waivers Whether employee PTO has to be paid out at closing (for an asset purchase) [Box Tip: Real Example: PTO and Governing Law Let’s say someone is drafting an LOI to buy a firm in Arizona, and they’re used to deals in states where accrued PTO doesn’t have to be paid out unless the seller’s policy says so. So they don’t address it in the LOI—they assume it’ll stay on the books post-closing, like any other accrued liability. But here’s the twist: what if it turns out the governing law is California? In California, unused PTO must be paid out at the time of termination—which includes a change in ownership where the seller’s entity is closing or employees are technically being let go. Suddenly, the seller is on the hook to write checks for every unused hour of PTO at closing, and the buyer may have to rehire those employees from scratch. If the LOI doesn’t reflect that? Now there’s a gap. Someone’s eating that cost, and it becomes a fight over whether the purchase price should be adjusted, who’s paying what, and how liabilities are being allocated. The takeaway? Always confirm the governing law early, and build key employment-related assumptions—like PTO payout—into the LOI. It might seem like a small item, but when you’re talking about dozens of employees, it adds up fast.] Jurisdiction: Where Do We Go to Argue About It? Jurisdiction answers a different but equally important question: where will the lawsuit happen if something goes wrong? This determines where someone has to physically show up and litigate the dispute—who’s traveling, which courthouse is in charge, and what rules of procedure apply. A buyer based in New York and a seller based in Georgia might choose: Georgia as jurisdiction (because the assets are there) New York (because the buyer’s likely to be the party needing to sue) Delaware (as a neutral ground, but one that both parties find equally inconvenient, and maybe that’s the point) It may sound trivial—until you realize that hiring legal counsel in another state, traveling for hearings, or being forced into a court that strongly favors local parties can shift leverage dramatically in a dispute. It’s the legal version of “you break it, you buy it.” In M&A, it usually means the seller agrees to compensate the buyer if something in the business wasn’t as represented—whether that’s a surprise tax bill, a lawsuit from a past employee, or the fact that the seller forgot to mention they’re being audited by the IRS. Think of it like buying a used car. The seller tells you the brakes are fine, but two weeks later you realize the pads are toast and it needs a full replacement.

If you had an indemnification clause, you could say, “Hey, you told me these brakes were good. You owe me the cost to fix them.” Now imagine the “car” is a $7 million business. And What’s “Survival” Got to Do With It? Survival refers to how long the seller’s representations and warranties last after the deal closes. If a rep "survives" for 18 months, that means the buyer has 18 months to discover a breach and make a claim. Some representations should die a quick death (to give the seller certainty), but others—like those related to ownership of the business or taxes—are fundamental. Those should never expire. You should be able to bring a claim for those five years later if needed, because discovering you paid millions for a business that the seller didn’t have a right to sell you doesn’t get better with time. Here’s a good rule of thumb: 12-24 months is a reasonable survival period for most reps. No limit (infinite survival is fair) on fundamental reps like: Ownership of the business Authority to enter the agreement Tax liabilities Environmental or legal compliance (sometimes) Why Survival and Indemnification Belong in the LOI (At Least a Little Bit) Look, I get it. You don’t want to negotiate every detail in the LOI. It’s non-binding, the lawyers haven’t even been hired yet, and the buyer and seller are playing nice. But that’s exactly why this is the time to plant the flag—before people get defensive. If the seller is going to demand a $10 liability cap or wants all reps to expire on the day of closing, you need to know that before you waste a dime on due diligence. Common Reps and Warranties — And Why They Matter These are the “guarantees” the seller is making about the state of the business at signing and closing. Here are the hits: Ownership of assets or stock Financial statements are accurate No undisclosed liabilities Compliance with laws No lawsuits or threatened claims Contracts are valid and assignable Taxes have been filed and paid All necessary consents have been obtained If any of those turn out to be false, the buyer can make a claim—but only if the survival period hasn’t lapsed and the breach wasn’t carved out of indemnification. [Box Tip In an asset purchase, the seller is often a company that will close up shop after the deal closes. It’ll be gutted. The assets are gone. It has no revenue. Maybe not even a bank account. The legal term for this is “piercing the corporate veil,” and courts don’t hand that out like candy. Unless you can prove fraud or that the company was never properly capitalized, you might be out of luck. Which is why you often want the owner themselves to sign personally—or at least to backstop the indemnity with a personal guarantee or an escrow holdback. This can be uncomfortable. Exclusivity in a deal usually runs one way: the seller agrees not to shop the business around while the buyer does their diligence and works toward closing. It’s not standard—or expected—for the buyer to be exclusive. Buyers are often evaluating multiple opportunities at once, and that’s generally accepted. The exclusivity is there to protect the buyer’s time and money, not to tie their hands. “You, seller, agree not to see other buyers while I, buyer, do the work and spend the money to figure out if this relationship should turn into a full-blown acquisition.” That’s the clean version. But what exclusivity really does is buy the buyer time—and signal to the seller that the buyer is serious. What Is an Exclusivity Provision? It’s a period of time (usually 30–90 days) during which: The seller agrees not to negotiate with or solicit offers from other potential buyers The buyer gets access to diligence materials and begins working toward closing The buyer attempts to secure financing Both sides attempt to finalize the terms outlined in the LOI in the definitive agreements In theory, it’s a mutual trust exercise. In practice, it’s the moment where both sides feel slightly nervous. Buyers are thinking: “I don’t want to waste money on legal fees and diligence only to lose the deal to a last-minute higher bidder.” Sellers are thinking: “I don’t want to get strung along for three months by a buyer who’s not really serious and just wants to look under the hood.” So how do you make it fair? The Great Debate: Good Faith Deposits Here’s where things get spicy. Should a buyer put down a good faith deposit during exclusivity? If I’m the seller: Absolutely. Even a small deposit ($10,000–$15,000) shows seriousness. It forces the buyer to pause before ghosting (meaning disappearing with no notice but not telling someone they’re no longer into the deal). It compensates for the risk of taking the business off the market. If I’m the buyer: No thanks. I’m not committing cash until I know the financials check out. I’ll already usually be committing time and resources, but even more money? That feels premature. Where I’ve landed, after watching enough deals implode? If there’s going to be exclusivity and I’m repping the seller, I usually want some kind of deposit—not because it guarantees anything, but because it keeps both parties honest and encourages the buyer to give notice promptly if they’re cooling on the deal. Buyers who have cash on the line are far less likely to disappear. And that alone can be worth the exercise. If someone’s going to bail, better to find out as soon as you can. Exclusivity can be a blank canvas, but here are some common—and smart—add-ons: Milestone-based exclusivity: The exclusivity period auto-extends as long as the buyer is meeting key milestones (loan application submitted, diligence completed, APA drafted, etc.) Reimbursement rights: If one party backs out in bad faith, the other can recoup a set amount of costs (legal, accounting, etc.) Liquidated damages: Rare, but in higher-stakes deals, there may be a predefined fee owed if the deal is tanked without valid cause (as you can imagine, this is a heavily debated term and, frankly, in small deals will not be worth the legal spend to negotiate it) Deposit refund triggers: The buyer gets their deposit back only if certain conditions aren’t met (e.g., undisclosed liabilities, material misstatements, inability to secure financing) I’m okay with these as long as the goal is alignment—not punishment. We’re not in the forced deal business. In small business, business is personal. If someone doesn’t want to sell—or doesn’t want to buy—you don’t want to hold them hostage. That usually doesn’t end well. A good exclusivity provision does three things: Gives the buyer a real window to explore the deal without worrying about other offers popping up Gives the seller confidence they’re not being played for time Aligns both parties around timelines, behavior, and seriousness That’s it. And if one side needs out? Let them out. There are deals that fall apart because they should—and trying to strong-arm someone into closing is the best way to make a bad deal worse. (How to Establish a Purchase Price Without Sleeping with the Fishes) When it comes to buying an accounting firm (my specialty)—or really any small business—the most common question I get from buyers is: “How do I figure out what to offer?” And my answer is always the same: you’ve got to call in the MAFIA. No, not that mafia. No one’s getting whacked here. I’m talking about the silly but memorable framework I use with clients to price deals like a professional—M.A.F.I.A. It’s memorable, it’s effective, and yes, it comes with terrible Godfather joke opportunities. So, let’s break down the MAFIA acronym: M — Market: What’s the Demand? Start with the basics: who else wants this business? You’re not negotiating in a vacuum. If this firm has a dozen interested buyers and an active broker marketing it nationally, you’re playing in a seller’s market. If it’s been sitting stale on a listing site for eighteen months with no bites and the seller changed the font on their CIM, hoping no one would notice. That’s a buyer’s market. Ask questions like: How many other buyers have signed NDAs? Has anyone already made an offer and walked? How long has it been listed? The heat in the market will tell you a lot about how aggressive—or conservative—your offer needs to be. A — Adjusted EBITDA (or SDE for smaller firms) This is the engine of your offer. Forget “gross revenue”—you want to know what the business earns after you adjust for owner perks, one-time expenses, and anomalies. SDE vs. EBITDA: Know Who You Are in the Deal Here’s a simple rule of thumb: if you’re buying the business to run it yourself, you care about SDE. If you’re not, and someone else is going to run it, then EBITDA is your metric. Most deals under $5 million in value are what we call owner-operator deals—you’re stepping into the seller’s shoes, managing the team, maybe even doing some of the client work. In that case, you look at Seller’s Discretionary Earnings (SDE) because it reflects what the business puts in your pocket. SDE adds back things like the seller’s salary, personal expenses, and one-time costs—so it gives a more accurate picture of the cash flow you, as the new owner/operator, can expect to live on. But if you’re planning to be a hands-off owner—or you’re institutional or private equity-backed—you’re going to need to hire someone to run the business. That means you care about EBITDA, which is earnings before compensation for the operator. You’ll be paying someone a salary to do what the seller used to do, so SDE isn’t a real number for you—it’s inflated. EBITDA gives you a cleaner, more scalable view of performance if you're not planning to be in the trenches yourself. Bottom line: Know who you’re going to be in the deal. The operator? SDE. The investor? EBITDA. Don’t confuse the two—it leads to overpaying and serious headaches. I — Industry Multiples: Valuation Benchmarks Across Sectors When determining a fair purchase price for a business, understanding how similar companies are valued within their respective industries is crucial. Industry multiples serve as benchmarks, offering insights into what investors are willing to pay for businesses in a particular sector. These multiples are typically expressed as a ratio of a company's enterprise value (EV) to its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA).Eqvista Why Industry Multiples Matter: Benchmarking: They provide a standard for comparing companies within the same industry. Investment Insight: Help assess whether a business is overvalued or undervalued. Negotiation Tool: Assist in substantiating your offer during negotiations. Examples of Industry Multiples Across Sectors: Industry multiples can vary significantly based on factors such as growth prospects, profitability, and market conditions. Here are some illustrative examples:Equidam Technology: Companies in the technology sector often command higher EBITDA multiples due to their growth potential and scalability. For instance, software firms may trade at multiples ranging from 15x to 25x EBITDA.FullRatio Manufacturing: Traditional manufacturing businesses might see lower multiples, typically between 6x and 10x EBITDA, reflecting factors like capital intensity and slower growth. One of the biggest early misunderstandings in a deal comes down to a deceptively simple number: the asking price. It’s important to understand that the asking price is not always the same as the seller’s “want” price. The asking price is what’s listed. It’s the number they’re putting out there publicly—sometimes to anchor the conversation high, sometimes to signal a certain level of seriousness. But the want price? That’s what the seller needs or hopes to walk away with when it’s all said and done. As a buyer, it’s worth respecting the asking price if you can—it sets the tone for the negotiation and shows you’re approaching the deal in good faith. That doesn’t mean you can’t negotiate. But anchoring way below the ask right out of the gate can derail conversations before they even begin, especially in deals where relationships matter. That said, part of your job in diligence and deal structuring is to gently work your way toward that want price—the number the seller has told themselves they have to have after taxes, fees, and financing. You’re not just trying to get a good deal; you’re trying to create one that works for both sides. Smart buyers aim for alignment—not friction.

If you can make the numbers work in a way that feels fair to you and lets the seller hit their goals, you’ve got a deal that’s far more likely to close (and succeed after). Now, here’s the nuance. The asking price is not a fact—it’s a starting point. It tells you how the seller sees the business (and sometimes, how emotionally attached they are). If it’s wildly off-base, don’t panic. Many sellers set an aspirational price because they’re hoping someone bites, or because someone once told them, “You can probably get 5x.” The Price Itself Isn’t Everything – Cash (at Closing) is King So you’ve figured out a topline number. Great. But don’t celebrate yet. Because the next question the seller’s going to ask—either out loud or silently while staring at your LOI—is this: “How much of that am I getting at close?” This is where buyers often fumble. They think the purchase price is the headline. But in reality, the structure of how that price is paid matters as much—if not more—to the seller. Rare is a seller who would prefer 3M in an earnout over 2.8M cash at closing. Put differently: 3 million dollars isn’t always worth 3 million dollars. To a seller, $2.8M cash at close might feel way better—and be way more appealing—than a $3M offer where half is in an earnout tied to three years of client retention and one mild gust of wind. Why? Because certainty matters. Finality matters. Getting paid now, not later (and not maybe later) matters. Especially for sellers who are walking into retirement, paying off debt, or emotionally trying to let go of something they’ve built for decades. So when you’re presenting your purchase price, you need to break it down clearly: Cash at closing (What hits their account day one?) Seller Note (How much is deferred, and what are the terms?) Earnout/Contingencies (What’s performance-based, and how do they earn it?) Equity rollover/Equity Grant (Are they retaining any stake in the business or getting paid in any equity of another business?) And then ask yourself: “Would I take this deal if I were them?” If your offer is heavy on future-based compensation—like earnouts, consulting fees, or equity that might pay off “someday”—you’d better have a good reason and a compelling story to sell it. Otherwise, you’re pitching risk in a tuxedo. This doesn’t mean you have to offer 100% cash. But it does mean you need to understand the emotional weight of the payout structure. Because a technically higher offer that’s back-loaded with conditions doesn’t always win. Want to close the deal? Deliver the price in a way that respects the seller’s need for clarity, dignity, and a clean break—when that’s what they’re looking for. And if they aren’t looking for a clean break? Even better. Now you can be more creative with structure. But never assume your terms are as attractive as your price tag until you show how, when, and in what form the money is getting to them. 3a. Seller Note How much is deferred, and what are the terms? A seller note is basically: “You finance part of your own exit, and I’ll pay you back over time with interest.” It’s a way to stretch the purchase price without overloading on bank debt. It often includes: An interest rate (usually 5–8%) A payment term (1–5 years) Regular monthly or quarterly payments Sometimes comes with a portion on standby to allow the Buyer to get the business stabilized post-Closing before payments begin. The benefit? It aligns incentives. The seller has skin in the game post-close and a reason to support a smooth transition. The downside (from the seller’s view)? It’s riskier than cash. If the buyer fails, the note may not get paid. Use when: The bank or investment group wants you to have more seller skin in the game You want to reduce your upfront cash burden You want to keep the seller motivated to help you with a smooth transition Pro tip: Sweeten the deal with an interest rate that makes it feel like a smart investment—not a forced concession. [Box Note on Interest Rates: Why 0% Seller Notes Aren’t Really a Thing It might sound simple and clean: “Let’s do a 0% seller note. No interest, no problem, right?” Not so fast. In the eyes of the IRS, a 0% note isn’t really a 0% note. Thanks to the imputed interest rules under Section 1274 of the Internal Revenue Code, the government assumes that any seller financing includes a minimum level of interest—even if the contract says otherwise. That minimum is tied to something called the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR), which is published monthly by the IRS. So what happens if you sign a seller note with 0% interest? The IRS steps in and says, “Cool story, but we’re going to pretend this note does have interest—and we’re going to tax the seller as if they received it.” In other words, the seller could owe taxes on income they never received. And the buyer doesn’t get an interest deduction either, because no interest was technically paid. It’s a lose-lose scenario, and that’s why zero-interest notes are not regularly used in real deals. If the goal is to keep the overall price or payments low, it’s better to work within the rules—use a low but reasonable interest rate (typically at or above the AFR), and structure the deal in a way that keeps both parties protected and tax-compliant.] 3bi Lender Protections Commonly Used in Seller Notes Seller financing can be a powerful way to bridge valuation gaps, smooth out closing logistics, or share risk—but if you’re the seller, it’s worth looking closely at the structure of the note, not the number on the page. Seller notes are not all created equal. Let’s look at the range: A contingent, subordinated, non-guaranteed, non-collateralized 10-year note? That’s a promissory note in name only. It’s long, unsecured, dependent on future events, and there's no personal guarantee if things go sideways. That’s the “you’ll get paid if everything goes well” and it’s stressful. On the flip side, a personally guaranteed, collateralized 2-year note with no contingency and no subordination? That’s real paper. It’s short-term, secured by assets, and backed by someone’s personal promise to pay. If things go wrong, you have legal recourse and leverage. It’s not cash, but it’s maybe the next best thing. Lenders use layers of protection to reduce risk, and you should too. Some of the most common protections built into seller notes include: Personal Guarantees – The buyer is personally on the hook if the entity can’t pay. Collateral – The note is secured by assets (often the business itself), giving the seller recourse if there’s a default. Shorter Terms – Less time means less risk. A two-year note is far more secure than a 10-year slow drip. No Contingencies – Fixed payments are better than ones tied to revenue, retention, or other post-closing performance metrics.

If you're the seller, make sure you’re not trading certainty today for a gamble tomorrow. And if you’re the buyer, know that the stronger the terms, the more weight the note will carry in the negotiation. 1. Security Interest in Business Assets What it does: Gives the seller a legal claim over the business’s assets (e.g., receivables, equipment, goodwill) in the event of default. How it's done: Via a Security Agreement + UCC-1 filing. Why it matters: Puts the seller ahead of unsecured creditors in bankruptcy or collection. 2. Acceleration Clause What it does: Allows the seller to demand the entire unpaid balance if the buyer defaults. Why it matters: Prevents drawn-out delinquency and gives the seller a clear enforcement path. 3. Default Interest Rate What it does: Triggers a higher interest rate (e.g., an additional 2–5%) if payments are missed or late. Why it matters: Incentivizes on-time payments and compensates for added risk after default. 4. Late Payment Penalties / Fees What it does: Adds a fixed fee or percentage (e.g., $250 or 5%) if a payment is late by more than X days. Why it matters: Reinforces the importance of timely payments and offsets admin costs. 5. Personal Guarantee (if buyer is an entity) What it does: Makes at least one individual behind the entity personally responsible for the debt. Why it matters: Reduces the risk of hiding behind a shell company or dissolving the buyer entity to dodge repayment. 6. Confession of Judgment (jurisdiction-dependent) What it does: Allows the seller to obtain a court judgment without a trial if the buyer defaults. Why it matters: Fast enforcement—but controversial and often restricted by law. See Appendix X for more detail than you ever thought you’d want on a Confession of Judgment. 7. Balloon Payment or Front-Loaded Payments What it does: Requires more money up front or a lump sum at the end to limit risk exposure and to encourage the noteholder to refinance debt to pay off the loan in a timely fashion. Why it matters: Reduces the outstanding balance quickly or provides a final incentive for full performance. 8. Reps & Warranties Tied to the Note What it does: Includes buyer promises (e.g., to maintain insurance, not transfer assets) as conditions of the note. Why it matters: Gives the seller more oversight and remedies if the buyer mismanages the business. 9. Default Triggers Beyond Nonpayment Examples include: Buyer fails to maintain licenses Buyer violates terms of the asset purchase agreement Buyer becomes insolvent or files bankruptcy Why it matters: Gives seller more grounds for acceleration and enforcement beyond missed payments. 11. Cure Periods (with limits) What it does: Gives the buyer a grace period (e.g., 10–15 days) to fix a missed payment. Why it matters: Protects buyers from technical default—but limits abuse by keeping the timeline short and defined. 3c Earnout What’s performance-based, and how do they earn it? Earnouts and purchase price retention adjustments can look similar on the surface—both involve the seller getting paid after closing—but they serve very different purposes. A retention adjustment is typically tied to the value the buyer thought they were buying—usually based on how much revenue or how many clients stick around after closing. It’s a way to protect the buyer if the business doesn’t perform as expected right out of the gate. An earnout, on the other hand, is more about upside—it’s additional money the seller can earn if the business hits certain performance targets after the deal. Think of retention adjustments as downside protection, and earnouts as performance bonuses. Structurally and emotionally, they’re very different conversations. Retention adjustments are typically assessed against a promissory note principal, whereas the earnout is more of an additional purchase price paid in a lump sum installment at a future time. [Box: Oh my goodness consult your tax people though. How Earnouts Are Taxed Earnouts can be treated as additional purchase price—which means they’re taxed as capital gains when properly structured. That’s good news for most sellers, since capital gains are usually taxed at a lower rate than ordinary income. But here’s the catch: for an earnout to qualify for capital gains treatment, it has to meet certain criteria. It must be contingent on the business’s future performance, and it should be tied directly to the sale of the business—not to the seller’s post-closing work. If the seller has to do something (like stay on and help generate that performance), the IRS may recharacterize that portion of the earnout as ordinary income—especially if it looks more like compensation than purchase price. Also, earnouts are generally taxed when received, not when the deal closes. So even though the seller may have mentally “counted” that money in the sale price, they’ll only pay taxes on it as it comes in/ If you’re a seller negotiating an earnout, structure matters—a lot. Talk to a tax advisor before the ink is dry, because how that earnout is framed can change your tax bill by thousands (or more).] Earnouts are typically tied to: Revenue milestones Client retention rates EBITDA targets Specific transition goals (like retaining key employees) From a buyer’s perspective, earnouts are a risk buffer. From the seller’s perspective, they’re often a red flag—because they’re unpredictable and subject to how the buyer runs the business. Earnouts work best when both parties agree on: The metrics The timeline The reporting process Use when: There’s uncertainty about future performance The seller is confident and wants upside You need to stretch the purchase price without a giant cash crunch Avoid when: You don’t want lingering entanglements You don’t want the seller to try to ‘control you from beyond the grave’ because they’re worried about the way you’re running their business You think post-close collaboration will be minimal or tense 3d. Equity Rollover (often referred to as a second bite at the apple) Are they retaining any stake in the business? In an equity rollover, the seller keeps a percentage of ownership in the business post-close—effectively “rolling” part of their proceeds into future equity. Think of it as saying: “Don’t take all the chips off the table—keep a few in the game.” This works well when: The seller believes in the buyer’s growth strategy There’s an eventual second exit (a re-sale, recap, or IPO) Both sides value long-term alignment Rollover equity can be: Minority, non-voting (common) Voting (rare unless there’s a joint leadership plan) Structured through a holding company or co-investment vehicle For sellers, this adds upside. For buyers, it de-risks the transition and signals confidence. Use when: You’re planning to grow and exit again You want the seller engaged long-term The seller wants more than cash—they want to ride the next wave Wrapping It Up: Crafting the Payout that Closes the Deal Every deal uses some combination of these tools. The right mix depends on: Financing options Seller’s goals Business risk profile Post-close plans But the key takeaway is this: don’t throw out a number. Build a structure that makes sense—and makes the seller say yes. Because $2.5M paid the right way will beat $3M paid the wrong way, every time. In addition to figuring out how you’ll pay the seller, a buyer needs to determine the dollars they need to run the business they’re buying. These considerations are definitely interrelated. Working capital might not be the flashiest part of a deal, but it’s one of the most quietly important—and that’s exactly why it lives under the “D” for Dollars in the STRUCTURED LOIs framework. When a buyer acquires a business, they’re not buying clients or goodwill—they’re also stepping into the day-to-day operations. That means they need enough working capital left in the business to keep it running smoothly post-close. If the seller drains the cash, runs down receivables, or lets payables pile up right before closing, the buyer can end up with a business that technically “sold” for a fair price—but functionally can't make payroll on Day 2. Working capital is how we bridge the gap between purchase price and operational reality.

Whether it’s a true working capital peg or a clean-up of timing issues, this is the spot in the LOI where the deal terms ensure the business is being handed off in usable shape—not just on paper, but in practice. [BOX Working Capital Isn’t a Mystery—It’s a Math Problem (Don’t Get Cute With It) Let’s have a quick grown-up conversation about working capital. This is one of those terms that gets thrown around in due diligence like everyone knows what it means—but when you ask people to define it or model it? You get a lot of squinting and throat clearing. So let’s make it simple: working capital is the money your business needs to function the day after closing. It covers the bills that come due before the next check hits the bank. Payroll. Rent. Software subscriptions. You know, the oxygen to keep the fire burning. Here’s the trick: working capital can be quite seasonal. If the business is cyclical—like a tax-heavy CPA firm or a holiday-dependent retail business—you need to tie the working capital estimate to the closing date, not to some theoretical “average.” Closing on March 15? You’ll need more float than if you close in August. Closing right before a big accounts receivable payday? You may need less. In other words, don’t guess. Model it. Ask the seller’s bookkeeper to pull 12-month trailing working capital snapshots. Then adjust to fit your anticipated close. And please, I say this with love: don’t try to get clever or overly “creative” with working capital math. This isn’t the place to win negotiating points or flex your Excel skills. I’ve seen buyers burn goodwill over $30K of inventory—and then lose 10x that in trust and deal fatigue. If you need working capital to close, borrow it, bake it into your financing package, and move on with your life. Deals get stuck when people haggle over things that aren’t the real issue. Don’t let working capital become a hill to die on. It’s not sexy, it’s not strategic, and if you underfund it? You’ll regret it faster than you can say “unexpected payroll gap.” ] Working Capital Checklist Check out the checklist in Appendix X for more on working capital. So that’s the STRUCTURED framework—nine deal-shaping elements designed to help you write a smarter, tighter, more thoughtful letter of intent. Why this matters is simple: the LOI sets the tone. It’s the blueprint for everything that comes next. And when you organize your thinking around the STRUCTURED elements, you’re not just filling in blanks—you’re asking the right questions, spotting the right pressure points, and heading off misunderstandings before they become expensive problems. Will every deal hit every letter perfectly? Probably not. That’s okay. The goal isn’t to rigidly follow the acronym—it’s to use it as a checklist, a conversation guide, and a gut check. It’s your way to make sure you're not just reacting—you’re leading. Because here’s the thing: people remember how a deal felt. And a well-structured LOI doesn’t make the deal better and more likely to close—it makes everyone at the table feel like they’re dealing with a professional who respects the process and is here to build something solid. That’s what STRUCTURED helps you do. Conclusion If you’ve made it this far, congratulations. You now know more about small business deals—especially the letter of intent—than 99% of people out there throwing offers around on firm they find on BizBuySell. But more importantly, you know that good deals aren’t found—they’re built. They’re shaped by clarity, structure, alignment, and human connection. They’re the product of real negotiation, thoughtful drafting, and an understanding that behind every spreadsheet is a person with a story. This book wasn’t meant to give you every answer. It was designed to arm you with better questions—the kind that lead to smarter terms, smoother closings, and fewer surprises six months later. Because here’s the truth: no deal is perfect. Every acquisition is a living, breathing negotiation between people who are (usually) doing this for the first and only time. But a deal doesn’t need to be perfect. It needs to be intentional. By focusing on structure, staying curious, managing deal fatigue, and using package bargaining and calculated empathy, you’ve got everything you need to navigate the maze. Whether you’re a seller stepping away from your life’s work or a buyer stepping into a whole new one, this isn’t a transaction—it’s a turning point. So, use the LOI not as a formality, but as a strategic foundation. Be clear. Be kind. Be specific. Protect yourself—but don’t forget that generosity and clarity often go further than gamesmanship ever will. And finally, remember this: in small business M&A, momentum matters. But so does mindset. If you stay grounded in the big picture while managing the details with intention, you’ll not only close your deal—you’ll build something you’re proud of on the other side. You’ve got this. In the world of small business acquisitions, seller financing is often the bridge that gets the deal done. The buyer gets more time and flexibility to pay, the seller walks away with interest income—and in theory, everyone wins. But the deal doesn’t end when the wire goes through. Because what comes next—especially in the note documents—can make or break how that financing plays out. Enter the Confession of Judgment. This is one of those clauses that sounds legal and boring until it suddenly becomes very, very real. So let’s unpack what it is, when it’s used, and how to handle it if it shows up in your deal. What Is a Confession of Judgment? A Confession of Judgment (COJ) is exactly what it sounds like: it’s a written agreement—usually included in or attached to a promissory note—where one party (typically the buyer) agrees in advance that if they default on a payment, the other party (the seller) can immediately enter a court judgment without a trial or even advance notice. No hearing. No chance to explain. Just an immediate judgment entered against you, enforceable like any other legal debt. It’s a powerful tool—and one that’s controversial for exactly that reason. The Seller’s Perspective: Why a COJ Might Seem Reasonable Let’s give the seller their due here. In a seller-financed deal, especially when the seller is carrying a big portion of the purchase price over time, they’re stepping into a lender’s role—but without the institutional protections a traditional lender has. If the buyer defaults, the seller might be left: Holding an unsecured note Behind a bank on collateral priority With limited visibility into how the business is being run With no guarantees of recovery in the event of bankruptcy In that light, a COJ can feel like one of the few ways the seller has leverage.

No hearing. No chance to explain. Just an immediate judgment entered against you, enforceable like any other legal debt. It’s a powerful tool—and one that’s controversial for exactly that reason. The Seller’s Perspective: Why a COJ Might Seem Reasonable Let’s give the seller their due here. In a seller-financed deal, especially when the seller is carrying a big portion of the purchase price over time, they’re stepping into a lender’s role—but without the institutional protections a traditional lender has. If the buyer defaults, the seller might be left: Holding an unsecured note Behind a bank on collateral priority With limited visibility into how the business is being run With no guarantees of recovery in the event of bankruptcy In that light, a COJ can feel like one of the few ways the seller has leverage. It gives them a fast track to collect, keeps the buyer honest, and—perhaps most importantly—puts them ahead of the “nice guy creditor” line if things go sideways. So yes, it’s a serious ask. But it’s not always an unreasonable one. The Buyer’s Perspective: What’s the Risk? The risk, simply put, is disproportionate consequence. Here’s a real-world scenario: Let’s say you’ve paid $150,000 of a $300,000 seller note over the first two years. You miss one payment—maybe you’re dealing with a short-term cash flow squeeze or a payroll surprise. With a COJ in place, the seller can immediately file for judgment on the entire note balance, not just the amount you missed. Worse still: You might not get advance notice You don’t get a hearing It becomes part of your public record and affects your credit You now have to defend yourself after a judgment is entered So yes, it's enforceable. And yes, courts do uphold these agreements in certain states. But that doesn’t mean you shouldn’t negotiate terms around it—or at the very least, understand what you’re signing. When a COJ Might Be Worth Considering (With Caveats) If you’re a seller with legitimate concerns about repayment—and especially if: The buyer has limited operating history There are other lenders in the deal (like an SBA loan) The note is unsecured You’re subordinated to bank debt or equity investors ...then a well-structured COJ, with guardrails, might be something you ask for. But here’s the catch: it must be proportionate and conditional. And if you’re the buyer, here are smart ways to manage the risk without flat-out rejecting it: Balanced Approaches: How to Structure a Fair COJ (If You Must) Limit it to specific breaches. For example: “Only applicable if buyer misses two consecutive payments without cure.” Carve out cure periods. Give the buyer 10–15 business days to catch up before triggering the judgment rights. Credit for prior payments. The COJ should only apply to the unpaid balance—not the full face value of the original note. Notice and opportunity to resolve. Build in a process that lets the buyer resolve the issue before the seller takes it to court. State-by-state rules. Remember: some states prohibit COJs entirely or require strict procedural safeguards. Know your jurisdiction. Final Word: Leverage, Yes—But Keep It Proportional A confession of judgment isn’t evil. It’s a tool. And like most tools, it can be used responsibly—or it can cause a lot of damage if misused. If you’re a buyer, don’t sign one blindly. Ask questions. Negotiate clarity. Build in reasonable protections. If you’re a seller, be honest about why you want it. If the goal is to keep the buyer from ghosting? There are other ways—like UCC filings, milestone-based defaults, or partial guarantees. The best deals are built on fair risk, not fear. A confession of judgment might have its place in the right context—but it should never be a substitute for trust, communication, and clean documentation. [Box callout. Confession of Judgment (Optional – If State Permits) [Note: This provision must be tailored to state law and may be prohibited or require specific execution formalities in some jurisdictions.] If buyer fails to cure a payment default within [15 business days] after receiving written notice from seller, and buyer has missed at least two scheduled payments in a rolling 6-month period, then buyer hereby authorizes seller, or seller’s attorney, to appear in any court of competent jurisdiction and confess judgment in favor of seller for the outstanding unpaid balance of this Note, minus any principal already paid. Seller may only confess judgment upon filing (i) a sworn affidavit of default, (ii) proof of prior payments, and (iii) a written record of the buyer’s failure to respond to the cure notice. This confession of judgment provision is not enforceable in jurisdictions where such clauses are prohibited or require separate instruments. Buyer agrees to execute such documents separately if required under applicable law.

Whether you're buying your first business or selling the business that’s been your life’s work for thirty years, here's the deal: small business buying and selling (colloquially called M&A) is a complex maze to navigate, especially for the first time. It’s emotional. It’s confusing. It’s full of people saying “on’t worry his is standard”—right before they ghost you, redline your deal to death, or casually drop a -page lease into your inbox labeled Final_Final_ActuallyFinalThisTime.pdf. Meanwhile, you’ve got one foot on the boat, one foot on the dock, with no certainty as to whether or when the losing of the deal will happen and your life as you know it will change dramatically forever. This book is your playbook. It won’t run the deal for you (nothing and no one but you should), but it is intended to give you the tactical background and practical toolkit you need to know what matters to you. Whether you’re the one writing the check or the one finally handing over the keys, you’re the expert in your business. Inside, we’ll cover what really matters in a small business deal: not the terms and timelines, but the personalities, potholes, and panic moments that make or break transactions. You’ll learn how to spot bad advice, manage deal fatigue, and push through the uncomfortable conversations most people avoid. If you want your deal to close—and not just close, but hold up after the champagne’s gone flat—this book is your manual. Let’s get into it.

metadata.title: How to Draft An Effective Privacy Policy
metadata.content: How to Draft An Effective Privacy Policy Dec 13 Written By Thomas Codevilla How I Start Drafting Privacy Policies (and I draft a lot of them). Make sure you have an accurate data map covering all personal information collected by the business, why it’s collected, what the business and its service providers do with it, who has access to it, how it’s shared, stored, and deleted. Do this not just for the client but its parent company and affiliates. Based on that data map, check which privacy laws apply. Over 25,000 consumers? Check for state privacy law applicability. Over $25m in revenue? Check California Consumer Privacy Act applicability. Child data? COPPA. Credit checks? FCRA. Health Data? HIPAA and Washington My Health My Data. Biometrics or AI? Colorado or Illinois. Text messaging and email marketing? CAN-SPAM. EU Data? GDPR. Financial data and accounts? GLBA. AI? Check California, Colorado , and the EU AI Act. And so on. Each applicable law and why it applies is now a section of your checklist. For each applicable law, check the regulations on what a privacy notice needs to contain. CCPA’s list is exhaustive, and GLBA’s is cryptic. That’s ok. List each requirement in your checklist. Use a free tool like Ghostery to see what cookies the site places. Check these against your privacy policy or cookie policy. Now check whether applicable privacy law cares about giving the consumer an opt-out or opt-in. Go through the current privacy policy and check it against what’s on your list. Then check what’s missing based on the data map. Schedule a call with your client to talk through what you’ve found. This is to soften the blow of potential red ink and double-check that you haven’t missed any big PI issues. Draft. Ditch the “we may” and old-school generic “we use everything for everything” language- try to draw a straight, plain-language line from where the data is collected to how it’s used, shared, transformed, and ultimately deleted. Can’t figure out how to phrase something? Resist the urge to copy from the big boys’ privacy policies- they could be wrong or Check for consistency across other policies and terms, like Terms of Use, Cookie Policy, EULA, and MSA. Profit ? Just kidding, keep drafting... Need assistance with this? Email Thomas Codevilla at: codevilla@skandslegal.com for help ensuring your organization is prepared for data privacy planning. metadata.title: Breaking Down The SaaS Master Services Agreement
metadata.content: Breaking Down The SaaS Master Services Agreement Jan 3 Written By Thomas Codevilla The first time I tackled a lengthy SaaS Master Services Agreement (MSA), it felt like reading a legal Ambien prescription—dense, repetitive, and designed to knock you out cold. Over the years, I’ve learned that MSAs aren’t just about legalese; they’re a mix of business reality, negotiation strategy, and practical risk management. Whether it’s ensuring the terms match the actual services provided, carving out data privacy provisions that reflect modern regulations, or negotiating fair liability limits, every clause matters. In this post, I’ll break down the key elements of SaaS MSAs into digestible chunks, showing you how to make these contracts work for your business—without the drowsiness. Business Reality Does this contract reflect the reality of the services performed? In other words, is this cloud SaaS on an old hosted SaaS form? Does the form assume the customer will own the software when they’re just getting a license? Do business and payment terms reflect your client’s deal? Leverage How much leverage does your client have to negotiate? This will dictate whether I go full Biglaw on minutiae or just hit the biggest issues. IP Think about six buckets, three for each client and customer: pre-existing IP, IP created during the agreement, and IP after termination. The agreement should say what goes in each. Data Privacy Usually, it has its own addendum with 12 pages of language related to an outdated understanding of the CCPA or GDPR. It’s important to carve out the specific uses and restrictions for the use of PII/personal data/customer data under the Agreement. Ask how much exposure your client could have in a data breach. Work directly from current regulations, not old forms, and you will amaze opposing counsel. Battle of the Forms Yeah, enormous public customer, I know you have a super detailed Statement of Work that has five levels of availability and service credits. But my client isn’t IBM and doesn’t have 24/7 support for their widget, so how about you talk with my client’s project lead and see if you can live with our SOW/SLA, ok? Super. Limitation of Liability Confidentiality, Indemnity: 90% of the time, these are either missing or one-sided. Make them mutual (if it benefits your client), and add a supercap for sensitive issues if things get sticky. My client isn’t taking on unlimited liability for a $100k software license, thank you very much. Blocking & Tackling These are the basics - defined terms, breach and cure, notice, term and termination, payment terms, entities, and signatories, all the things that make a contract actually useful and enforceable. Don’t try to do this at the same time as higher-level stuff- you’ll catch more if you put the contract down for a few hours minimum and re-read it with a clear head. Need assistance with this? If it feels like YOU just took an Ambien, I can help. Email Thomas Codevilla at: codevilla@skandslegal.com . Thomas Codevilla

metadata.title: The 90-Day Consent Rule for CPA Firm Sales: What It Covers, and What It Doesn’t
metadata.content: The 90-Day Consent Rule for CPA Firm Sales: What It Covers, and What It Doesn’t Oct 17 Written By Sara Sharp If you’re buying or selling an accounting practice, you’ve probably heard there’s a 90-day “silence means yes” rule for transferring client files. That concept exists, but it’s not a blanket permission slip. Two systems control this space: Professional ethics / state rules governing transfer of “client records” when a practice is sold or combined; and Federal tax-privacy law (IRC §7216) governing “tax return information.” Here’s the clean way to keep both happy. Part 1: The 90-day rule (client records under ethics/state rules) Under AICPA ethics guidance for practice transitions, the selling firm should send each client a written request for consent to transfer that client’s records to the successor firm. The notice may state that consent will be presumed if the client does not object within at least 90 days. Many state boards follow a similar approach; some have their own timing or notice mechanics. What to know: The 90-day presumption typically applies to client records that are not “tax return information.” State law controls the details. Some states codify a 90-day notice; others vary wording or retention requirements. Always check the board/regs where the selling practice is licensed. Part 2: §7216 shuts the door on “presumed consent” for tax return information. “Tax return information” has its own federal privacy regime. Unless a specific exception applies, a preparer needs affirmative, written taxpayer consent that meets Treas. Reg. §301.7216-3. Importantly, opt-out or “silence means yes” does not satisfy §7216. There are only two narrow sale-context allowances without taxpayer consents—and both are limited: Due diligence disclosures under a confidentiality agreement. You can share limited tax return information with a prospective buyer to evaluate the deal, under a written NDA that restricts use/disclosure strictly to that diligence purpose. That is a disclosure, not a file transfer. Transfer of a limited “taxpayer list.” In connection with selling a return-prep business, you can transfer a list containing only very basic fields (e.g., client name/contact, entity type, return form number). Anything beyond that requires signed §7216 consents. Bottom line: For any transfer of actual tax files or broader return information, you need affirmative written IRC §7216 consents. The 90-day presumed-consent idea does not apply to this category. Practical two-track playbook for your transaction Track A — Client records (ethics/state rule path): Send a client notice that (1) identifies the successor firm, (2) requests consent to transfer client records, and (3) states that if the client doesn’t object within at least 90 days, consent will be presumed (if permitted by applicable state rules). Don’t move these records until you have express consent or the 90-day period runs (again, subject to state-specific rules). Keep proof of mailing and any responses as required by your state board. Track B — Tax return information (IRC §7216 path): Use a separate consent document for each client whose files contain tax return information. Make it an affirmative opt-in (no opt-outs), include the mandated statements, and collect signatures (wet or compliant e-signature). Remember the formatting/timing rules (there are extra specifics for individual filers). Keep these consents in the file and ensure the buyer understands the permitted use/scope. During LOI & diligence (both tracks): For tax return information , share only what’s necessary under a tight NDA; treat diligence as a disclosure, not an early transfer. For non-tax client records , follow whatever your state’s ethics/board rule requires for notice and timing. Copy-ready starter language (edit to fit your state and deal) Client notice (non-tax records): We intend to transfer certain client records to in connection with the sale of our practice. Please let us know if you consent to this transfer. If we do not receive an objection from you within 90 days of the date of this letter, we may treat your non-response as consent where permitted by applicable professional rules, and transfer your client records to at that time. If you object, we will not transfer your records. §7216 consent (tax return information): By signing below, you authorize to disclose your tax return information (as defined in Treas. Reg. §301.7216-1) to for the purpose of completing the sale of and transitioning your services to . You are not required to sign this consent. This consent is valid through . You may revoke your consent at any time before we act on it by notifying us in writing. (Include all required §7216 content; use separate consents for distinct disclosures/uses.) Common pitfalls (and quick fixes) Combining notices. Don’t mash the 90-day client-record notice and the §7216 consent into one document. Different laws, different standards. Moving too soon. Don’t transfer records before (a) express consent or the end of your notice period (per your state rule) and (b) for tax info, without §7216

metadata.title: Why a 0% Seller Financing Offer Makes Your LOI Look Amateur
metadata.content: Why a 0% Seller Financing Offer Makes Your LOI Look Amateur Jan 21 Written By Sara Sharp If you are sending out letters of intent and getting nothing but polite declines or complete radio silence, you might be wondering what went wrong. Sometimes the answer is “nothing.” Deals are competitive. Sellers have options. Rejection happens. But sometimes the answer is sitting right there in your LOI, quietly waving a red flag and making the seller question whether you are ready to run their business. Let’s talk about the mythical unicorn of deal terms: 0% seller financing. The 0% Seller Note Fantasy Somewhere along the way, the internet decided that sellers regularly loan buyers hundreds of thousands of dollars for free. No interest. No upside. Just vibes. I see this all the time. Buyers genuinely believe that offering a 0% interest seller note is attractive, clever, or aggressive in a good way. It is not. If part of your purchase price is paid over time, that portion is a loan. Loans require interest. When they do not have interest, things get weird very quickly. Why Sellers Hate 0% Interest Notes Yes, sellers like interest because it pays them for the risk they are taking. That part is obvious. But the bigger problem is not emotional. It is tax related. When a seller provides a loan below market interest, the IRS steps in with something called imputed interest income. This means the seller gets taxed as if they earned interest, even if they did not actually receive it. In plain English, the seller pays taxes on money they never got. For example, if the applicable federal rate is 4% and your note pays 0%, the IRS pretends the seller earned that 4% anyway. On a large seller note, that creates a very real tax bill. You are not just asking the seller to finance your purchase. You are asking them to write a check to the IRS for the privilege of doing so. That is a tough sell. It Also Signals Inexperience Every deal has less attractive terms. That alone does not make you look unqualified. What makes sellers nervous is when a buyer clearly does not understand the risk they are pushing onto the seller. A 0% interest note tells the seller you may not understand basic deal mechanics, tax exposure, or incentives. That is not the energy you want to bring into a transaction built on trust and long term cooperation. The Simple Fix Most Buyers Miss You do not need to over engineer this. A smart LOI will at least reference the Applicable Federal Rate, often called AFR, as the minimum interest rate on any seller note. That alone tells the seller you understand the tax implications and are not asking them to absorb unnecessary risk. Even better, it keeps the conversation focused on the business, not on whether you know what you are doing. If AFR is a brand new concept to you, that is okay. But it is a sign you should pause before putting seller financing terms into your LOI and get educated first. What to Do Instead If you want your LOI to be taken seriously: Include interest on any seller note Reference AFR as a baseline Understand imputed interest income before proposing creative structures Do not outsource deal knowledge entirely to the internet Seller financing can be a powerful tool. Used poorly, it can quietly kill your deal before negotiations even begin. If you want to understand how these terms work and how to structure offers that sellers respect, subscribe to my YouTube channel . Knowing this stuff upfront will save you time, money, and a lot of awkward rejections. Smart deals are not about being aggressive. They are about being informed. metadata.title: How to Avoid a Data Breach in Your Organization
metadata.content: How to Avoid a Data Breach in Your Organization Dec 6 Written By Thomas Codevilla My all-time favorite breach involved a charismatic founder who thought he was too smart for cybersecurity requirements. He stored raw credit card data, unencrypted, in a Google sheet shared with contractors. His business was making too much money and confirmation bias is a hell of a drug. He made political taunts and managed to piss off the wrong part of the internet- the part that knew how to code. So, inevitably, he got breached and his investors started asking harder questions, like where the money for internal cyber improvements had gone. It did not end well. The Kemper Sports breach reminded me of that founder: more than 140 golf courses, private clubs, sports venues, and destination resorts nationwide storing customers' names and Social Security numbers, unencrypted and mostly unwatched. What I would tell those founders: Map Your Data. If you don’t know where your data is, you can’t protect it. Beware of individual departments maintaining their own little fiefdoms. Get Cyber Insurance. I don’t even sell cyber insurance and I’m plugging it. No serious company will give you their PI without seeing a cyber COI. Avoid Radioactive Personal Information. For the vast majority of businesses, there is no reason to collect or store customer social security numbers, government IDs, financial data, and other sensitive information. There’s usually a safer alternative. Train Incident Response. You know that one guy in IT who knows where all the bodies are buried? Imagine someone gets his password and he’s out of the office. Could your organization survive? Would you even notice a breach before it was too late? This is the point of an incident response plan and yearly training. I promise I won’t make it boring. metadata.title: Corporate Transparency Act (BOI Reporting Requirement) Blocked Nationwide
metadata.content: Corporate Transparency Act (BOI Reporting Requirement) Blocked Nationwide Dec 4 Written By Sara Sharp BREAKING: Less than one month before the federal reporting deadline for Beneficial Ownership Information (“BOI”), a federal district court in Texas issued a nationwide preliminary injunction against enforcing the beneficial ownership reporting requirements mandated by the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA). ( Texas Top Cop Shop v. Garland (December 3, 2024) U.S. Dist. Ct., Eastern Dist. Of Texas, Case No. 4:24-CV-478). The case began at the request of a family-run firearms and tactical gear retailer, called Texas Top Cop Shop Inc., as well as other co-plaintiff businesses and the Libertarian Party of Mississippi. The briefing was powerful, including such quotables as “Plaintiffs fear this flanking, quasi-Orwellian statute and its implications on our dual system of government,” a truly delightful quote from Judge Mazzant. The CTA require(d) that an estimated 32.6 million existing business entities disclose their beneficial owners to the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network before 2025. The government argued that the law’s function—to crack down on anonymous shell companies and deter money laundering, terrorism financing, and other illicit economic activity—falls within Congress’s regulatory duties. The court ruled that Congress exceeded its authority in enacting the CTA, resulting in an unconstitutional infringement on states’ rights to regulate businesses. The court granted a nationwide injunction prohibiting FinCEN from enforcing the January 1, 2025 reporting deadline for all reporting companies. The opinion was issued on December 3, 2024, and an appeal is anticipated. However, for now, businesses do not have to file beneficial ownership information reports with FinCEN. Check with your attorney for more updates. The opinion is available at: www.fullopinion.ttcsvgarland.pdf Sara Sharp I am a lawyer who advises investors and businesses in their day-to-day decision-making and through corporate transactions. https://skandslegal.com/sara-sharp

metadata.title: How to Retain Key Employees After Buying an Accounting Firm
metadata.content: How to Retain Key Employees After Buying an Accounting Firm Jan 7 Written By Sara Sharp So, you just bought an accounting firm, or you’re about to, and you're wondering how to keep the wheels turning without losing your best people. Fair question. The transition period right after a deal closes is prime time for talent loss. And spoiler alert: it's usually the high performers who leave first. Here’s what I’ve seen again and again as a deal attorney working in M&A every day. If you don’t get employee retention right, you don’t just lose people—you lose momentum, client trust, and sometimes even revenue. Here’s how to avoid all that. Start With Clarity and Confidence If you’re lucky enough to meet with employees before closing (and yes, this should be in your LOI as a condition precedent), don’t waste the opportunity. Get the seller to introduce you during a team meeting. Then, you show up an hour later and take everyone to lunch. It sounds simple, but this sequence works. It shows continuity and goodwill—and sets the tone for what’s next. Deliver Physical Offer Letters, Not Just Verbal Promises This part is crucial. When you meet the team, hand each person a printed offer letter. Not an email. Not a Slack message. A piece of paper they can take home and show their spouse. That offer letter should confirm: Their job is secure if the deal closes Pay and benefits will match or exceed their current package It’s contingent on closing, so you’re not poaching them if the deal falls through This written commitment matters because people don’t hear clearly when their livelihood is on the line. They’re too busy thinking about their mortgage, their kid’s upcoming surgery, or what happens to their vacation time. Ask This One Question Before You Even Meet the Team Before you walk into that lunch or meeting, ask the seller: “Is there anyone here who wanted to buy the business?” Because if someone on staff had their heart set on buying the firm and got passed over? You may be walking into an emotional minefield. That person could sabotage your transition faster than you can say “earnout.” It’s even trickier when it’s a family member. Think sons, daughters, or long-time right hands who were expecting to take over. Know the internal dynamics before you make your entrance. Don’t Offer Raises, Offer Retention Bonuses Everyone’s first instinct is to sweeten the pot with a salary bump. But here’s a smarter play: offer a retention bonus instead. Example: Instead of giving someone a $6,000 raise on day one, promise a $6,000 bonus if they stay for six months. That way, you’re spending the same money—but now it’s working harder to keep your team stable during the transition. You can always reward them with a raise later once you’ve had time to evaluate their role. Stability Is the Secret Sauce If there’s any uncertainty, your best employees—the ones who get recruiter calls every week—will be the first to leave. Don’t risk that. Offer written, clear, and immediate assurances. Be thoughtful in how you approach the team. And when in doubt? Bring people over. You won’t know who the real MVPs are until you’ve lived in the trenches with them. You’re not just buying processes and client lists. You’re buying trust, talent, and company culture. Get the transition right, and you’ll keep all three. Want more deal wisdom like this? Check out Deal Academy for on-demand courses on letters of intent, NDAs, diligence, and more. Or follow along on YouTube, where we break down how to actually survive buying or selling a business—with your sanity and staff intact. metadata.title: The Purchase Agreement: Your New Favorite 30-Page Romance Novel (Sort Of)
metadata.content: The Purchase Agreement: Your New Favorite 30-Page Romance Novel (Sort Of) Nov 18 Written By Sara Sharp Thinking about buying an accounting practice? Congratulations—you’re about to get intimate with one of the most thrilling documents in business law: the Purchase Agreement. Okay, thrilling might be a stretch. But if you want to avoid costly mistakes, get the deal you actually agreed to, and protect yourself when things go sideways, then yes—it should be thrilling. Or at least required reading. Let’s break it down. What Is a Purchase Agreement, Really? Think of it as the user manual for your newly acquired firm. It tells you what you’re getting, what you’re not, what happens if something goes wrong, and how everyone is supposed to behave before and after closing. Spoiler alert: you don’t want to be dusting this thing off months later and realizing it doesn’t say what you thought it did. That’s why, even though it’s not beach reading, you need to understand it before you sign. The Seven Juicy Chapters (aka Sections) of a Standard Purchase Agreement 1. Article One: The Big Stuff This is where you’ll find the purchase price, what assets are included, what’s excluded, and how you’re paying. Cash? Promissory note? Retention adjustment? It all lives here. Also important: the “disclosure schedules.” If it says “you’re buying everything unless listed otherwise,” that schedule becomes your real asset list. Pay attention to who’s playing offense here—buyers want a broad list of what they’re getting. Sellers want to limit it. 2. Article Two: Closing Mechanics This is where the bifurcated closing lives. Translation: you sign now, close later. Your agreement needs to cover both the present and the future. Think of it as drafting for time travel. I’ll dig into this more in another post, because closing mechanics are a whole topic on their own. (Hint: if closing feels anticlimactic, that’s a good thing.) 3. Article Three: Reps and Warranties from the Seller Here’s where the seller swears on their QuickBooks file that: They own what they’re selling Their financials are legit No one else secretly owns their client list They’re not being sued (or they are, and now you know about it) It’s not just about trust—it’s about claims. If something turns out to be false, this is where your breach of contract claim lives. Also, reps and warranties force sellers to disclose the weird stuff. That old wage claim? The former client is threatening a lawsuit? Better here than buried deep in “things we didn’t mention.” 4. Article Four: Buyer Reps and Warranties Much shorter. Usually just says, “Yes, I exist, and I can enter into this agreement.” If the buyer is being sued, it might show up here, too. 5. Article Five: Covenants (aka Big Future Promises) This is where we talk about non-competes, non-solicits, non-disparagement—basically, all the “please don’t ruin this for me later” clauses. If you're the buyer, make sure your non-compete language actually covers the client list you're acquiring. If you're the seller, make sure you're not signing up to be permanently unemployed in your industry. We’ll also see “further assurances” here, which is a fancy way of saying, “If we need to do another document to make this work, we’ll do it.” 6. Article Six: Indemnification Ah, yes, the "who pays for what when stuff hits the fan" section. This is where things get spicy. If a third party shows up suing the business for something that happened six months ago, this article decides who’s footing the legal bill. Buyers and sellers often haggle here over survival periods, caps, and baskets. I’ll do a deeper dive in another post, because this one is a goldmine for law nerds. 7. Article Seven: Boilerplate (aka Legal Fine Print) Don't skim this. Yes, it’s full of the classics—severability, integration, amendment clauses—but every so often, someone hides a landmine in here. Read it. And make sure the right people sign. If you’re the buyer, you want the individual seller on the hook, not just their LLC, that’s about to disappear into the night. You’re not worried about the old firm name competing—you’re worried about Jim Anderson showing up down the block with a new sign and the same clients. Final Thoughts (and One More Pro Tip) If you made it this far, you either (a) secretly love contracts or (b) are trying very hard not to get sued after you buy a business. Either way, you’re my kind of person. The purchase agreement is not just a formality. It’s the blueprint for your entire deal. Don’t treat it like a checklist item on your way to closing. metadata.title: How to meet Data Protection Addendum Criteria, 100% of the time.
metadata.content: How to meet Data Protection Addendum Criteria, 100% of the time. Nov 29 Written By Thomas Codevilla A common ask from my SaaS clients is to look over a Data Protection Addendum (DPA) to see if their system meets the DPA’s criteria out of the box. 100% of the time, it doesn’t. Company DPAs are meant to be overprotective, it’s on the attorney and company working together to make the contract reflect reality. Here are 5 of my most common changes to big company DPAs Consent for Collection Make sure your data provider reps and warrants that it has the right to give you the data AND that the consumers or data subjects have been properly notified. Data Minimization Before receiving data, always question its necessity. You don’t want HIPAA-regulated data or sensitive private information unless it’s absolutely necessary. Make sure it’s clear what you will and won’t process. De-Identification When processing data at scale , consider requesting de-identified (including differentially private) and hashed personal information from the provider; it reduces your liability in the event of a breach and, when done properly and documented on the back end, reduces your compliance workload. Third-Party Access I get it- as a small business, you’re often relying on third party service providers to host or provide key aspects of your processing. Make sure your DPA allows for processing by those third parties. Data Breach Liability Big company DPAs put all the cost and responsibility of a data breach on you by default, even if it isn’t your fault. Limit your liability to your statutory responsibilities under data privacy law. Need assistance with this? metadata.title: Why Your Letters of Intent Keep Getting Ghosted (and What to Do About It)
metadata.content: Why Your Letters of Intent Keep Getting Ghosted (and What to Do About It) Nov 7 Written By Sara Sharp Let me guess—you’ve submitted ten Letters of Intent (LOIs) to sellers of accounting firms, and the only thing you've heard in return is the sound of crickets. No rejections, no responses, just a deafening silence. Here’s the harsh truth: it’s probably not your purchase price. It’s not even the structure of your LOI. It’s that you’re ignoring the question sellers care about most: How are you going to run this business? I’m Sara Sharp, a deal attorney and buyer-seller whisperer for accounting firms nationwide. Every week, I speak with about 20 different people hoping to break into the accounting acquisition world. And this one issue comes up again and again. If you’re not answering that question—especially if you’re not a CPA—you’re wasting everyone’s time, including your own. Not All Accounting Work Is Created Equal Here’s the first distinction you need to understand: accounting ≠ CPA. Yes, they overlap, but CPA-specific work—like audit and attest services—is highly regulated. In most states (actually, 49 jurisdictions), you must be a CPA to own more than 49% of a CPA firm. In South Carolina? You’ll need a full 66.23%. Think of it like trying to buy a medical practice when you’re not a doctor. Nobody wants that. Nobody’s allowed to do that. The end. What If You’re Not a CPA? Good news: not all firms do CPA-specific work. Some are technically structured as CPA firms even though they don’t do audits or attestation. If that’s the case, we can reclassify the firm as a general accounting practice—and those can be owned by non-CPAs. But you have to know what you’re buying. If more than 10% of their revenue is coming from CPA-restricted services, you’ll need a plan. And no, that plan cannot be “I’ll just hire a tax manager.” Sellers have heard that one before, and they’re not buying it. The Real Plan Sellers Want to See You need to come in with a clear, confident strategy. Ideally, one of the following: Alternative Practice Structure (APS): Set up an LLC where 51% is owned by a CPA, and all the regulated work flows through that entity. It’s been done for decades in dental and medical roll-ups. It’s boring. It’s proven. It works. Keep the Attest Work With the Seller: Just carve it out. Buy only the general accounting work. Let them keep the rest or license it to you. Partner with a CPA: Already have a CPA on board? Great. Mention that in your LOI, loud and clear. But under no circumstances should your big reveal be: “I was looking at HVAC companies last week, and now I’m trying accounting.” These sellers spent years earning those three letters after their name. They want someone who understands—and respects—that. States Where You Absolutely Cannot Own a CPA Firm Without Being a CPA Consider this your “do not pass go” list if you’re not a licensed CPA: Delaware Hawaii New York Northern Mariana Islands U.S. Virgin Islands Why This Matters Most sellers in this industry aren’t chasing a big payout. They’re chasing peace of mind. These businesses often trade at modest multiples, not life-changing ones. Sellers want to know that their clients will be taken care of. That means your LOI has to do more than outline price and terms. It needs to say: “Here’s how I’m going to carry your legacy forward without wrecking it.” And please, for the love of all things compliant, don’t say you’re going to offshore everything or turn their client relationships into a VLOOKUP project. That’s a surefire way to get ghosted. TL;DR Want sellers to take your LOI seriously? Know whether the firm is truly required to be a CPA firm or just labeled that way. Have a plan that actually complies with state regulations. Don’t insult their intelligence by pretending hiring is easy or clients are interchangeable. Speak their language—and back it up with facts. If you’re buying an accounting firm and not talking about ownership compliance in your first outreach, you’re not just behind—you’re invisible. Ready to stop getting ghosted and start getting calls back? Check out our resources on our Dealmakers YouTube Channel here .
