metadata.title: Update on the Corporate Transparency Act in mid-2024
metadata.content: Update on the Corporate Transparency Act in mid-2024 Apr 29 Written By Sara Sharp On January 1, 2024, the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA) went into effect. The CTA requires most smaller corporations, most limited liability companies, and some other business entities to file a beneficial ownership information (BOI) report with the U.S. Department of the Treasury Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). The BOI report identifies and provides contact information for the human beings who own or control the entity. FinCEN will share this information with law enforcement to combat money laundering and other illegal activities. About 32 million existing and most new businesses are subject to this filing requirement. Since the first of the year, about 500,000 BOI reports have been filed online at the FinCEN website. But on March 1, 2024, a federal district court (federal trial court) in Alabama ruled that the Corporate Transparency Act was unconstitutional. In National Small Business United v. Yellen, No. 5:22-cv-01448 (N.D. Ala. 2024), the court issued an injunction staying enforcement of the CTA against the two plaintiffs in the case: a single individual business owner and the National Small Business Association—a 65,000-member nonprofit organization of small business owners. The district court ruling created some uncertainty among businesses subject to the CTA (termed “reporting companies”). Here’s what you need to know: If you were not a member of the National Small Business Association as of March 1, 2024, this decision has no immediate impact on you. FinCEN still expects all reporting companies to comply. As expected, the Justice Department, on behalf of the Department of the Treasury, filed a notice of appeal on March 11, 2024. In other words, this trial court decision is far from the final word on the CTA’s constitutionality. No one can predict how the courts will ultimately rule, but many legal experts believe there are strong legal grounds to reverse the trial court’s decision. If your reporting company existed before 2024, you have until January 1, 2025, to comply with your BOI filing requirement. So you can wait until late 2024 to see what happens with the pending litigation. If your reporting company was formed during 2024, you have only 90 days after your articles of incorporation, articles of organization, or similar documents were filed with the secretary of state to file your BOI report. You can’t afford to wait. Meanwhile, New York adopted its own BOI reporting law that applies only to limited liability companies formed in New York or formed out-of-state that register to do business in New York. Existing LLCs must file their reports with the New York Department of State by January 1, 2025. Newly formed LLCs will file their reports when they file their articles or registrations. Other states, such as California, are considering enacting similar laws. metadata.title: Embracing The Virginia Model Of Consumer Privacy Law
metadata.content: Embracing The Virginia Model Of Consumer Privacy Law Dec 20 Written By Thomas Codevilla Navigating changing consumer privacy laws can feel like chasing a moving target. Nineteen states have now enacted consumer privacy legislation , and while some, like California and Texas, have introduced unique thresholds, many have adopted what’s known as the "Virginia model." In this post, we’ll explore how simplifying your strategy could save you time, money, and legal headaches while setting you apart as a privacy-forward company. To be subject to a “Virginia-style” consumer privacy law, an entity (usually a for-profit, but not always- thanks Colorado) must control or process the personal data of at least 100,000 consumers from that state in a calendar year or the personal data of at least 25,000 consumers, while deriving over 50 percent of their gross revenue from the sale. This makes applicability analysis a little easier, a small relief given that a federal privacy law keeps getting squashed by big tech over targeted advertising. But a dirty secret of privacy law compliance is that, while consumers have all these new privacy rights, not many choose to exercise them . So, why not make future compliance easy on your company and offer a standard set of privacy rights to all your consumers, no matter where they live? Whenever I give this option, I can see marketing folks panic while IT sighs in relief. I’m not saying it works for every company, but if you’re feeling overwhelmed by all these new state laws, uniformity can save time and money. Need assistance with this? metadata.title: The importance of mapping the data in your organization.
metadata.content: The importance of mapping the data in your organization. Nov 22 Written By Thomas Codevilla The first thing I do with a new privacy client is map their data. We map information like: what personal information do you have, why do you have it, who do you get it from, who can see it, and how is it stored and deleted? No matter what privacy law you’re trying to comply with, your policies need to match your practices. Why? Three Reasons Why You Need to Map Your Data Your Business Suffers A Data Breach If your business suffers a data breach and you don’t know where to look to stop the bleeding, you could be underwater before you have time to call your insurance broker to ask if your General Liability policy covers cyber errors and omissions (it doesn’t). You’re Looking For Funding (Or an Acquisition) If you’re looking for funding or acquisition , one of your first calls will be from a very patient, very thorough associate asking you all the questions about your privacy compliance you were too busy with while you were building your product. If you can’t answer their questions, expect a significant purchase price reduction from your buyer or investor based on privacy risk. You Land a Big Client With Special Data Privacy Needs Trying to land a big client with special data privacy needs (HIPAA, CCPA, GDPR, Geofencing, Consumer Health Data)? Your privacy policy and security documentation have to be up to date- you can’t backfill it after you make the sale, and data mapping has to be done beforehand. So, map your data, or let me work it out with a spreadsheet and your head of engineering. Need assistance with this? metadata.title: Navigating the Business Sale Diligence Process: A Concise Guide
metadata.content: Navigating the Business Sale Diligence Process: A Concise Guide Apr 23 Written By Sara Sharp So, you're gearing up to sell your business and diving into the diligence process can feel like stepping into uncharted territory. Fear not, for we're here to guide you through the labyrinth of buyer checklists, NDA signings, and virtual data rooms (VDRs). Understanding the Flow Let's start at the beginning. Once you've found a potential buyer, they'll likely hand you a checklist. This checklist is a roadmap of sorts, outlining the information they need from you. Before divulging any details, ensure you've got a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA) in place – it's your safety net. Sorting Through the Checklist Don't panic if the checklist seems overwhelming. It's designed to cover all bases, even if some questions don't apply to your situation. Filter out the irrelevant bits, and you'll find the process more manageable. Uploading to the Virtual Data Room Now comes the fun part – uploading your documents to the VDR. Think of it as a virtual vault where all your business secrets reside. Eventually, the data you upload here will find its way into the purchase agreement. The Art of the Purchase Agreement Ah, the purchase agreement – the culmination of all your efforts. Your uploaded information will be distilled into this legal document, forming what are known as schedules. These schedules are vital for both parties to understand what's being acquired. Keeping an Eye on the Prize Remember, the end goal is for the buyer to seamlessly take over the reins of your business. This process isn't just a legal dance; it's about ensuring a smooth transition for everyone involved. Mitigating Risks and Looking Ahead But wait, there's more! As a seller, it's crucial to anticipate potential pitfalls. Not all deals go through, so keep your options open and your data room organized for the next potential buyer. Protecting Your Golden Goose Your client list – the crown jewel of your business. Treat it like the treasure it is and refrain from handing it over too soon. Keep it under wraps until the ink has dried on the deal. Seek Expert Guidance Throughout this journey, don't hesitate to lean on professionals for support. Your lawyer, in particular, can provide invaluable advice and ensure you're dotting all the i's and crossing all the t's. Conclusion Selling your business is no small feat, but with the right knowledge and preparation, you can navigate the diligence process with confidence. Stay vigilant, stay informed, and above all, keep your eye on the prize – a successful transition of ownership. Good luck! metadata.title: Starting in Privacy Law: What I Tell Law Students
metadata.content: Starting in Privacy Law: What I Tell Law Students Feb 14 Written By Thomas Codevilla After my first semester of law school went hilariously awry, I was terrified I would never get a job. I spent the rest of law school networking like crazy with practicing attorneys gracious enough to share their time. So, when law students ask me how to get into privacy law, I’m more than happy to pay it forward. Here's what I tell them: Question : Did you always know you wanted to do privacy law? Answer : Nope. I started out as a corporate generalist and noticed that the more specialized the lawyer, the better work/life balance they tended to have. My patent and tax lawyer friends seemed have better hours and nicer bosses partly because there always seemed to be enough work to go around. That realization planted the seed of looking for a niche so that, when I got the chance in-house to specialize in privacy, I took it. That said, I never would have gotten the in-house role without my corporate background, so there is something to be said for generalist training. Q: Fine, but I don’t have a job. How do I get privacy law experience? A: Privacy Law in its current form is relatively new as opposed to, for example, M&A which has decades of accumulated law and entrenched players. This is great for a student because it means there is relatively less material to absorb. With that in mind: 1. Take any and all privacy law classes at your school. 2. Consider getting a CIPP-US or CIPP-E if you can afford it. It’s not a difficult test or too expensive, and it’s a great way to show you’re serious about the field. 3. Join your local IAPP chapter as a student for free and go to all its meetups. Find local conferences on privacy law and attend them at the student rate. Show up with business cards and ask questions. 4. If you network with someone, read everything they have written and know the latest news on their specialty. For example, if we were meeting, it would be a good idea to read the SK&S blog . 5. Become familiar with CCPA and GDPR. Read the statutes, follow the excellent privacy law blogs from Husch Blackwell and Greenberg Traurig , and absorb their backlogs. 6. Set Google Alerts for “Privacy Law”, “CCPA”, “GDPR”, or whatever strikes your fancy. 7. Pick a privacy policy of a company that is subject to several privacy laws, like Airbnb or LinkedIn. The CCPA and GDPR (along with their regulations) have a list of requirements for privacy policies. Tick and tie each provision of the applicable law to a section of your chosen privacy policy. Don’t stop until you understand why each provision is in there. Bonus points if you can find an element in the regs missing from the privacy policy. 8. Don’t ask for a job, ask who else you should be talking to. 9. Folllow up about once a quarter to build a relationship and, per Brad Bernthal, give first. Q: Should I be looking at Big or Small Firms? A: When you’re looking at a job, you’re looking for a person more than a firm. Specifically, you’re looking for a mentor who will not just redline your screw-ups but talk you through a process to avoid repeating them. Talk to former associates, ask what kind of issues you’ll be working on, and accept that your job will be simple details that may not compare to the kind of high-minded content you encountered in Con Law. Look for someone with the ability and willingness to sacrifice billable time to train you. Ask associates if they’re happy; run away if they equivocate. Happy paralegals and staff are a great sign, but although they will teach you a ton about being a lawyer they should not be your sole source of training. Good luck out there, and as a random lawyer taking his fourth different state bar exam said to me in line before my bar exam, “It’s a low bar”. Thomas Codevilla

metadata.title: How to Stop Getting Your Letter of Intent Rejected: The “MAFIA” Framework for Business Buyers
metadata.content: How to Stop Getting Your Letter of Intent Rejected: The “MAFIA” Framework for Business Buyers Dec 8 Written By Sara Sharp If you’ve been putting in offers to buy a business and getting ghosted—or worse, outright rejected—you’re not alone. As a deal attorney who helps people buy and sell businesses every day, I’ve seen one letter of intent (LOI) after another get tossed aside for completely avoidable reasons. So let’s fix that. Whether you're buying your first firm or adding to an existing portfolio, you need to approach pricing with a strategy. That's where my simple acronym comes in: MAFIA . Because frankly, nobody knows how to run a tight business deal like the mafia. Here’s how to avoid the five biggest pitfalls in pricing your next deal. M – Market Demand Before you get cute with pricing, understand the temperature of the market. Is it a buyer’s market or a seller’s market in your niche? For example, accounting firms typically see strong demand in spring, but by December, it's a buyer’s playground. Understand what other buyers are likely to offer, how competitive your target is, and what leverage you actually have. Without this, you're throwing darts in the dark. A – Adjusted EBITDA Don't just look at raw profit numbers. Adjust for seller discretionary earnings and think through what that looks like for you. Are you stepping in as owner-operator, or hiring one? That decision dramatically affects profit and, by extension, what your offer should look like. F – Financing Realities This one trips up more people than I can count. Do not offer more than you can actually finance. If you’re using an SBA 7(a) loan—and most buyers under $5 million are—the bank is going to underwrite based on historical cash flow, not vibes or projections. And banks don’t care about your dreams. Their best-case scenario is getting their money back with interest. So vet your offer with your lender before submitting it. Also, no, you’re probably not getting 100 percent seller financing. That’s not a strategy. That’s a fantasy. I – Industry Multiples If you don’t know what businesses in your target industry are trading for, pause and do your homework. Seriously. Look at the NAICS code. Dig into market comps. Know whether your target is trading at 3x SDE, 7x EBITDA, or somewhere in between. And please—for the love of all things legally binding—tie your offer to that multiple. This allows flexibility if diligence reveals different profit levels than expected. A – Asking Price (The One Most People Ignore) Here’s the one buyers ignore all the time: What does the seller actually want? Not just the number—but their priorities. Do they want to lease the office space back to you? Keep their team employed? Preserve client relationships? Address that in your LOI. Refer to their own language if you’ve had conversations. Show that you listened. Because if your letter ignores what the seller cares about, you’re wasting everyone’s time. Final Thoughts You can’t control the entire M&A process, but you can control how strategic your offer is. Think like the mafia: understand the ecosystem, respect the power dynamics, and never show up to the table empty-handed. Want help building your deal instincts? Check out the courses at DealAcademy.org. You’ll go from guesswork to game plan in no time. Here’s to smarter offers that actually get accepted. metadata.title: Get Your Closing Mechanics Straight: How to Avoid Deal Disaster When Buying or Selling an Accounting Firm
metadata.content: Get Your Closing Mechanics Straight: How to Avoid Deal Disaster When Buying or Selling an Accounting Firm Dec 15 Written By Sara Sharp If you're buying or selling an accounting practice and your team can't answer the question, “So, what does closing day look like?” - you've got a problem. A big one. The closing mechanics of a deal are like the choreography in a Broadway show. Everyone (buyer, seller, attorney, lender) needs to be doing the same steps, at the same time, or the whole thing falls apart—and in deals, the curtain doesn't rise again for an encore. Let’s break down the three most common closing approaches—and why they matter—so you can avoid rookie mistakes and get your transaction across the finish line. Option 1: Simultaneous Sign and Close This is the classic, old-school method. In a simultaneous sign-and-close deal, the signature date, effective date, and closing date are all the same. You sign the documents, the money moves, and voilà—you own the business. But here's the kicker: you can't sign anything in advance. Once that pen hits paper, you're legally committed. While this method is neat and tidy, it can also be totally impractical if: You need a tax clearance from a state agency Your lender won’t schedule a closing until they see a signed agreement Spoiler alert: that’s most of the time. Option 2: Delayed Closing with Conditions (a.k.a. “Let’s keep everything on track”) Most of my deals are delayed sign-and-close. Why? Because instead of waiting for everything to line up exactly right in a single moment so you can close, it lets you ease into it and start marking things off your list before the closing date. You can sign the purchase agreement and the seller can get comfortable enough to introduce you to a key employee. Plus, strategically you want to take things off the table once they’re agreed to. By signing the purchase agreement, you make sure everyone has put their pens down on the major deal points. But what happens if something important changes after the signing but before closing? Like the bank pulls its funding or a critical employee quits? To avoid that nightmare, your purchase agreement should include conditions precedent—fancy legalese for “if X doesn’t happen, we’re not closing.” At the top of that list? Financing. This is the structure I use to create what I call an anticlimactic closing. That’s right—boring is good. No drama. No surprises. Just a solid, methodical transfer of a business with: A signed purchase agreement Clearly defined conditions precedent A firm closing date triggered only when financing, documents, and logistics are all lined up So, What Is Closing Then? If you’ve already signed the purchase agreement, what happens at closing? Glad you asked. That’s when the money moves, and key deal documents get executed: Promissory Note Bill of Sale Assignment and Assumption Agreement Closing Certificate These are the documents that actually transfer ownership and liability, and they need to reflect the reality of that day, not what everyone thought might happen a month ago. A closing certificate, in particular, is your way of saying: “Everything I promised in the purchase agreement is still true, today.” So it’s great for closing the gap. Option 3: The (Misunderstood) Escrow Signature Strategy Ever hear someone say they want to “hold signatures in escrow” and nod politely while wondering what on earth that actually means? Here’s the deal: there’s no official escrow agency involved. It’s not tied to title companies. It’s just a mutual agreement that both parties will sign the documents, but not make them effective until everyone agrees via email to “release” them. It’s a legal fiction—but sometimes a useful one. Especially when you’re close to agreement but still working through the deal checklist. I don’t recommend it in hostile or highly contested situations, but it can buy you breathing room in a friendly transaction. Choose Your Mechanics Early or Risk a Meltdown Here’s the bottom line: your deal documents must match your closing plan. If you’re not aligned on how and when you're signing and closing, you’re setting yourself up for confusion, delays, and potentially catastrophic legal exposure. And the worst part? Fixing a closing mechanic mistake after the fact is like trying to put toothpaste back in the tube—technically possible, but very, very messy. metadata.title: Navigating the Colorado Privacy Act Amendments: Biometrics and Child Data
metadata.content: Navigating the Colorado Privacy Act Amendments: Biometrics and Child Data Oct 23 Written By Thomas Codevilla The Colorado Privacy Act (CPA) is emerging as a model for state-level privacy regulation. Recent amendments focus on biometric information and children’s privacy, which when combined with Colorado’s AI Act (more on this in later posts), arguably put Colorado ahead of California in the race to shame the feds on privacy law. This issue-spotting guide will help you understand the amendments and the steps businesses subject to the CPA must take to comply. Biometrics: Enhanced Protections for Unique Identifiers Under HB-1130 , biometric data—such as fingerprints, facial recognition data, and retinal scans—are categorized as sensitive personal information under the CPA, when those pieces of information are or can be used to identify an individual. Starting July 1, 2025 , businesses will need to implement additional safeguards when collecting or processing this type of data, particularly ensuring explicit consumer consent. The qualifier in HB-1130 that a biometric needs to be capable of identifying a person is important; photographs, by themselves, are not biometric information. However, given Harvard students’ recent hacking of Meta glasses to identify people from just a passing glance , the CPA may soon become broader than intended. Key requirements: Consent must be explicit : Businesses must obtain clear, specific, affirmative consent before collecting or selling biometric data. This differs from Illinois’ BIPA, under which selling biometrics is illegal even with consumer consent. Limited use : Businesses are restricted in how they can use biometric data. It should only be used for specific, legitimate purposes with non-discriminatory effect. Data Protection Assessments (DPAs) : Before processing biometric data, businesses are required to conduct Data Protection Assessments (DPAs). Think of a DPA as an internal CYA measure; if something goes wrong and you’re asked to explain yourself, your DPA is where you start. Steps to take: Update consent mechanisms : Ensure you have an explicit consent process in place before collecting biometric data. I follow GDPR’s model here- no blanket consents, no general checkboxes, plain language, description of use. Conduct DPAs : Perform DPAs when introducing new technologies that utilize biometrics OR when expanding existing processes or uses. Revisit data storage practices : Ensure that biometric data is encrypted and securely stored. Consider retention policies to delete biometric data as soon as it is no longer needed​​​. Children’s Privacy: Stronger Protections for Minors SB-041 sets higher standards for handling data concerning minors (under 18) and children (under 13), similar to the protections under the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) but adding further clarity and responsibilities for online businesses. As of October 1, 2025 , online businesses will need to meet stringent requirements when collecting, storing, and using children's personal data: Parental consent : For any data collection involving minors, businesses must obtain consent from minors (under 18), including verifiable parental consent (as defined under COPPA) for children. This cannot be a passive consent process—parents must take an active role in approving data collection. Restrictions on data processing: Without consent, a business cannot collect child information for sale, target advertising, or profiling. Geolocation: Use of geolocation is restricted to the specific purpose and time for which it is necessary, with notification required the entire time. Design . The amendment prohibits use of any system or design feature to significantly increase, sustain, or extend a minor’s use of the system. In other words, every social media app and game ever. I expect the regulations on this one will be fun to read. What businesses should do: Verify parental consent : Implement parental verification systems that confirm the identity and consent of parents or guardians before collecting any data from children. Review profiling practices : If your business uses AI or data analytics to target children, ensure you have mechanisms to turn off profiling for children’s accounts unless express parental consent is provided. Update privacy policies : Clearly outline how children’s data is processed, and ensure your privacy policies reflect the parental rights and consent requirements​​. Data Protection Assessment . As with biometrics, before collecting or using any child data, document the purpose, categories of data collected, uses of the data, and how the risks to minors are addressed under your process. The new CPA amendments raise the bar for businesses collecting or processing child or biometric data in Colorado. Privacy Policies, process reviews, and Data Protection Assessments take time and real thought; email codevilla@skandslegal.com for help and war stories about COPPA compliance. Thomas Codevilla

metadata.title: BOI Reporting is Back in time for Christmas
metadata.content: BOI Reporting is Back in time for Christmas Dec 24 Written By Sara Sharp Just when you thought your Christmas list couldn’t get any longer, FinCen steps in to help. As of December 23, 2024, the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in Texas Top Cop Shop, Inc. v. Garland, 5th Cir. Appeal No. 24-40792 (Dec. 23, 2024), has reversed the U.S. District Court and dissolved the preliminary injunction. Don’t worry, in their generous wisdom, the powers that be have lso granted us a 12-day extension so BOI filings are now due by January 13, 2025. The Fifth Circuit's opinion is short to the point of adorableness and you can read it for yourself here . The most annoying portion of the Fifth Circuit's opinion is the discussion that the Corporate Transparency Act, which gives rise to the FINCEN BOI requirements, is very likely a constitutional exercise of Congress' powers under the Commerce Clause. Since we’ve all been waiting and wondering whether this whole thing will be ultimately be found constitutional, the review of this little post-it note size opinion is revealing (okay it’s 7 pages long, but that’s very short for these things). Basically noting that the CTA operates to gather information to fight money laundering, the financing of terrorism, tax fraud and other crimes, this opinion indicates the US Supreme Court may in fact find that the BOI reporting is safely considered a proper exercise of the Commerce Clause powers. In short, a classic Happy Holidays from the Federal Government. metadata.title: What does the FTC’s vote to ban non-competes mean for my deal?
metadata.content: What does the FTC’s vote to ban non-competes mean for my deal? Apr 24 Written By Sara Sharp On April 23, 2024, following a 90-day public comment period, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) voted 3-2 to issue a final rule reflecting their vote to classify non-compete clauses as a violation of Section 5 of the FTC Act, thereby banning most non-compete clauses for workers nationwide. While enforcement will likely be delayed by legal challenges— the U.S. Chamber of Commerce has stated its intention to file a legal challenge as early as today—companies that have traditionally used non-competes should begin preparing for the final rule’s effectiveness. This would include identifying existing agreements affected by the final rule, identifying which of the existing agreements will require rescission, and which will remain enforceable. Companies should also begin exploring alternatives to non-competes that may satisfy the company’s legitimate business objectives, including the protection of trade secrets and other confidential information, without violating the FTC’s rule. *It's not effective yet, and substantial delays are expected from business groups who are likely to challenge it legally. It has to be published and then 120 days need to pass first. *It does carve out pretty much one exception: for the sale of business-what that means is currently in flux, but it is likely going to be limited to owners *If you have non-competes out there, you have an affirmative obligation to notify those people that they're no longer valid (click the blogpost below for standard approve language for this notice) Key Points: The ban applies to new non-compete agreements for all workers, except senior executives with existing non-competes in place. Existing non-compete agreements for non-executive workers become unenforceable. The ban doesn’t cover non-competes outside the U.S. or in franchisor/franchisee relationships. Nonprofits and healthcare organizations may be exempt. Employers must notify affected workers about the unenforceability of existing agreements. The ban doesn’t affect non-disclosure or non-solicitation agreements, but overly broad ones may be considered non-compete clauses. There’s an exception for non-competes in bona fide business sales. The proposed rule stated the exception applied to owners of at least 25% of a business, but this part was removed from the final rule. State non-compete laws not in conflict with the FTC rule remain valid. Challenges and Uncertainty: Legal challenges against the FTC rule are likely due to questions about its authority. A temporary restraining order or injunction may delay the rule’s implementation. Employers should monitor legal developments and consider adjusting their agreements accordingly. Recommendation: Employers should wait for legal challenges to unfold. If the rule stands, they have 120 days to comply. In the meantime, reviewing non-compete agreements and considering narrower alternatives like NDAs is advisable. We’ll keep you updated on any changes. Extra credit: Model language provided by the FTC at this website is here and (currently states): A new rule enforced by the Federal Trade Commission makes it unlawful for us to enforce a non-compete clause. As of ,  will not enforce any non-compete clause against you. This means that as of : · You may seek or accept a job with any company or any person—even if they compete with . · You may run your own business—even if it competes with . · You may compete with  following your employment with . 96 Please don’t wrap up your deal like a last-minute gift Hi Sara, If you're feeling the December crunch, you're not alone. Buyers and sellers alike are trying to close before the year ends. But here's your friendly deal attorney PSA: Rushing a transaction like it’s a last-minute gift run is how you end up with a deal that looks great on the outside and falls apart the second you open it. The cure for regret in January? Diligence. Real, boring, document-heavy diligence. Make sure the financials make sense. Make sure the people in the business actually work there. Make sure the seller owns what they’re selling. It’s not festive. But it’s necessary. If you want to go into the new year with a deal you can actually live with, take the time now. Even if it slows things down. 96 Selling Your Business? Keep Diligence From Killing Your Deal Hi Sara, Thinking about selling your business? Buckle up – because the diligence process is where deals are made…or broken. But don’t worry, I’m here to break it down into real talk – no corporate jargon, no stress headaches (well, fewer of those, anyway). Step1: Sign That NDA – Seriously Before you share anything, get an NDA in place. That client list you built with sweat and caffeine? You don’t want it floating around. Protect it. Step 2: The Buyer’s Checklist – AKA, Your New Homework Once you find a buyer, they’ll hand you a checklist that looks like it was written by someone with a PhD in Overwhelming You. Don’t freak out. It’s a catch-all list. Some stuff won’t apply to you. Drop “n/a” on the things that don’t apply like environmental concerns and tackle the rest. Completing the checklist should be a collaborative process, so delegate everything to the Buyer where you can. Weekly calls can help keep momentum. Step 3: The Virtual Data Room – Less of a Vault, More of a Beat Up Filing Cabinet Upload your docs to a Virtual Data Room (VDR). Think of it as a digital safe deposit box for your business secrets. This is what the buyer will comb through to build the purchase agreement later. Step 4: The Purchase Agreement – Your Business, in Legalese Everything you upload becomes part of this holy grail document – complete with “schedules” (fancy term for all the details). This is what locks in the deal. The Schedules are very protective for you, you want to add as much detail as you can to them. This is the one easy thing too many sellers leave on the table. Pro Tip: Keep Your Golden Goose Safe Your client list? That’s your crown jewel. Don’t hand it over until the deal is signed, sealed, and delivered. No early peeks. Deals Fall Through – Stay Ready Not every deal closes. Keep your data room organized and maintain a good copy so you’re prepped for the next buyer if needed. I promise the second round is easier! Call in the Pros (That’s What We’re Here For) Lean on your lawyer and other experts to avoid expensive mistakes. You don’t want to be the person who sells their business only to get sued when you were supposed to be sailing off into the sunset. Selling your business is a long elaborate process. It’s part paperwork, part poker face, and a lot of “Why is this checklist so long?” But with the right team and the right prep, you’ll get to that smooth transition – and maybe even a celebratory drink after. Got questions? Thinking about selling? Check out our courses here on Deal Academy to help you get started. 96 The #1 Closing Mistake That Could Wreck Your Deal (And How to Avoid It) Hi Sara, Let’s talk about a sneaky little deal-killer: closing mechanics. I know, I know—sounds like something only lawyers and escrow agents should care about. But if you’re buying or selling an accounting firm (or any business, really), this is the one thing you cannot afford to mess up. See, your agreements are written based on a plan for closing. If everyone (buyer, seller, and lawyers) isn’t on the same page about what that looks like, things can go sideways—fast. Two Ways to Close a Deal (And Why It Matters) Most people assume that when you sign a purchase agreement, boom! The deal is done. That’s the old-school, “simultaneous sign and close” approach. No difference between the signing date, closing date, and effective date—it’s all one and the same. Simple, right? Except when it’s not. Banks and state agencies love to complicate things. Okay okay, so do lawyers! But get a load of this chicken and egg situation: Most lenders won’t schedule your closing until they see a final approved (and sometimes) signed purchase agreement. Sometimes the lender won’t close until you get a state agency’s sign off, but in order to get that sign off, the state requires a signed agreement. So somehow you need to sign the purchase agreement BEFORE you can actually confirm you have the money to purchase the business. So if you’re relying on financing, you’d better believe you need an escape hatch in case the bank pulls the plug at the last second (which certainly happened in 2020). That’s why we almost always structure deals as a delayed sign-and-close. The idea? You sign the purchase agreement as soon as both parties are ready. You close at a later date, once financing, tax clearances, and other conditions are met. There are built-in escape clauses (a.k.a. “conditions precedent”) so nobody gets stuck in a deal they can’t afford to close. What Actually Happens on Closing Day? So if you’ve already signed the purchase agreement, what’s left to do at closing? Glad you asked. On closing day, you’ll finalize: ✔ The Wire Transfer – Because sellers don’t work on the honor system. ✔ The Promissory Note – A legally binding “I.O.U.” that shouldn’t be signed until we are really sure things are going the distance. ✔ The Bill of Sale – Officially transfers ownership. ✔ Assignment & Assumption Agreements – Ensures the buyer is stepping into the seller’s legal shoes. ✔ The Closing Certificate – A final “truth check” that confirms everything the seller promised originally is still true on closing day. Mess this up, and you could be in for a world of legal and financial headaches. The Bottom Line If you’re buying or selling an accounting practice, get clear on your closing mechanics early. A sloppy approach can lead to unnecessary risk, frustrated buyers and sellers, and even lawsuits. 96 The Contract Clause That Could Outlive Your Deal Hi Sara, Let’s talk about a contract term that’s as exciting as it sounds- in fact, this is one of the only contract terms with a name that sounds more like it belongs in a dystopian thriller than a 40 page purchase agreement: Survival. Sounds intense, right? That’s because it kind of is. And let me tell you—if you’re negotiating a purchase agreement and glossing over the survival clause, you’re making a rookie mistake. What is “Survival”? No, it’s not a Hunger Games reference. In a contract, “survival” refers to how long your reps and warranties live on after closing. Here’s why it matters: If the agreement says nothing about survival? Those reps may hang around indefinitely (or until your local statute of limitations gives them the boot). That’s great for the buyer, not so great for the seller. The Seller’s Dilemma: If you're the seller, you don’t want to be on the hook forever. You want a survival period that caps your liability—12, 18, maybe 24 months. The Buyer’s Balancing Act: From the buyer’s perspective, you need some amount of time. You maybe won’t uncover shady vendor arrangements, ghost clients, or mysteriously disappearing revenue until you’ve gone through at least one full operating cycle. That’s why most buyers push for 18+ months—to uncover issues and have time to act on them. Pro Tip: If your contract says nothing about survival and you're the seller—fix that. Immediately. If it says nothing and you're the buyer—enjoy the gift that keeps on giving–at least through the applicable statute of limitations. Survival may sound like a footnote, but it’s actually a battleground in disguise. And if you want to fight smart, you better understand what you’re agreeing to. 96 The Side Letter: Secret Weapon or Legal Landmine? Hi Sara, Ever heard someone say, “Let’s just handle that in a side letter,” and thought—that sounds... shady? You’re not alone. Today, I’m here to clear the air on side letters—what they are, why they matter, and how one wrong sentence can blow up your whole deal. So, What’s a Side Letter? It’s not a mysterious loophole. A side letter is simply a short agreement that supplements your main contract—like a post-it note stuck to your big purchase agreement. Used well, it’s a tool of precision. Used poorly? It’s chaos. Here’s when I see side letters most: To handle last-minute terms without reopening the whole contract When one selling partner wants something unique—like special payment terms or a carveout on a non-compete To avoid dragging board members or lenders into review mode over every oddball term When the parties want to keep some things private, like an individual guarantee or a post-closing referral arrangement All of that is totally legit—if you do it right. Now Here’s Where It Can All Go Sideways The #1 mistake I see with side letters? Forgetting about the integration clause in the main agreement. That’s the boring boilerplate at the end that says, “This is the entire agreement. It overrides anything else we’ve ever said—out loud or in writing.” Translation: if your side letter contradicts the main agreement and doesn’t reference it properly, you could accidentally override the whole thing—or worse, make your side letter completely unenforceable. Pro tip: Make sure your side letter references the purchase agreement and says it’s intended to supplement, not replace it. If you get that wrong, it could be like swapping the batteries in a smoke alarm… with raisins. Useless. Want to Learn More? 96 How Skipping a Lawyer Cost This Buyer Big Time (Don’t Be Like John) Hi Sara, Let me tell you about John. John bought an accounting practice. He thought he did his homework – checked the books, met the clients, even pictured himself finally taking an Alaskan cruise with his wife after tax season. What he didn’t do? Hire a lawyer. Big mistake. Turns out, the previous owner had been fabricating write-offs for clients. After the sale closed, John had to spend hours—with every single client—breaking the bad news. Clients were furious, some left, and John was stuck paying off a 10-year SBA loan for a practice that was now hemorrhaging revenue. All because he skipped legal counsel. Here’s what a lawyer would have done for john: Helped him structure his deal with greater retention mechanics so he could ensure the Seller kept some skin in the game Added protections in the purchase agreement (like warranties and indemnities) to shield him from the fallout of past misdeeds Instead, John was left footing the bill—both financially and emotionally. Don't be like John. When you’re buying an accounting practice (or any business, really), you need more than Google and good intentions. You need a lawyer who knows the deal landscape—someone who can: Draft a purchase agreement that actually protects you Ensure you’re not inheriting someone else’s mess and that you have solutions to help if you do The cost of hiring an attorney? A fraction of what John lost trying to fix someone else’s mistakes. Thinking of buying a firm? Let’s make sure your success story doesn’t start like John’s. To smart deals (and zero client write-off scandals), Sara Sharp Partner, SK&S Law Group Business Consultant & Founder, Deal Academy P.S. 96 Don’t Let Red Lines Derail Your Deal Hi Sara, Let’s talk about a universal truth in deal-making: everyone’s happy with the first draft of a purchase agreement...until those dreaded red lines show up. The initial draft goes out, and spirits are high. It’s a moment of optimism, closing seems within reach and simple. But the second round of edits between the parties’ attorneys? If you’re not careful, that’s when the wheels come off, and chaos ensues. Resentment brews. Tempers flare. Attorneys fees mount and people blame the other side. Why does this happen? Sticker Shock on Legal Fees: Those mounting invoices don’t exactly inspire goodwill. Rejection Stings: When your carefully crafted offer gets marked up or outright rejected, it can feel very personal. The Lawyer Factor: Let’s face it, some attorneys are more sandpaper than silk—grating and uncooperative. Add in the “telephone game” between two parties, and it’s a recipe for escalation. By this point, the excitement of the deal is a distant memory, replaced by glares across the negotiation table. But it doesn’t have to be this way. How to Keep Your Deal on Track: Start Fair: A balanced initial agreement minimizes the back-and-forth drama. Nail the LOI: A solid Letter of intent sets the stage for smoother negotiations in the definitive agreements. Choose the Right Attorney: A collaborative, experienced deal attorney can save your deal—and your sanity. If you choose a combative attorney or a lawyer who doesn’t primarily work in deals, you may be throwing a wildcard into the mix that the deal can’t recover from. The bottom line? A little upfront effort and the right professionals can keep your deal moving forward, even through those inevitable red-line edits. 96 TL;DR - We are off the hook permanently for BOI reporting. The Final Act in the BOI Saga Hi Sara, Well the toxic ex-boyfriend saga has finally come to a conclusion-and no dateline reenactments are expected. The long and the short of it is: Yesterday FinCEN reversed the court that reversed the court that reversed the law that reversed the agency that reversed the executive action that reversed the regulation that reversed the other court that reversed the initial action. The Treasury Department is announcing today (March 2, 2025) that, with respect to the Corporate Transparency Act, not only will it not enforce any penalties or fines associated with the beneficial ownership information reporting rule under the existing regulatory deadlines, but it will further not enforce any penalties or fines against U.S. citizens or domestic reporting companies or their beneficial owners after the forthcoming rule changes take effect either. The Treasury Department will further be issuing a proposed rule making that will narrow the scope of the rule to foreign reporting companies only. The most bored among us can see the full Treasury Department press release here. TL;DR - We are off the hook permanently for BOI reporting. 96 The hidden cost of selling too soon Hi Sara, Here’s a hot take from a deal attorney: Selling your firm is not always the smartest financial move. At least not right away. Say your firm brings in $1 million topline and you net $400,000 a year. You get an offer to sell for $1 million. That is ~2.5 years of income. It’s tempting. But it’s also worth asking…could you just keep working and earn the same money? The answer is yes. But here’s the catch Most people don’t stop after 2.5 years. They keep going. Then they do the math again later, and again after that. Suddenly, 20 years have gone by, and they still don’t have an exit plan. Eventually, the real question becomes: How much longer do you want to be doing this? When you sell, it’s not just about price It is about timing. It is about freedom. It is about getting out before you’re burned out. So if you're thinking about selling, take a minute to run the numbers honestly. Then decide what kind of exit is actually worth it. 96 What’s Actually Killing Your Deal (Spoiler: It’s Not the Market) Hi Sara, Let’s play a little game. What do you think kills more accounting firm deals than anything else? A) Market conditions B) Financing hurdles C) Ghosting buyers D) Lawyers being unreasonable and not knowing the first thing about business If you guessed “all of the above,” congratulations, you’ve either bought a firm before or you’ve cried into a spreadsheet trying. 96 The Compliance Mistake That Could Tank Your Deal (and No One’s Talking About It) Hi Sara, Ever heard of Section 7216? No? Well, if you're in the business of buying or running an accounting firm, you probably should. I recently sat down with my colleague Tom Codevilla—our in-house privacy law whiz—and we dug into the legal landmine that is data compliance. This one’s especially for the folks planning to “buy a boring business” and then offshore all their labor while sipping cocktails. If that’s your plan... buckle up. Here’s the short version: Section 7216 is a federal regulation that applies to tax preparers. It requires informed, written consent from clients before you can share their data, even with your own contractors. That consent has to be in a specific format. Spoiler: your engagement letter with some 7216 language buried in the middle does not cut it. Even if 7216 doesn’t apply to you (because maybe you’re doing payroll or advisory work), don’t relax just yet. There’s an entire ecosystem of privacy laws that do apply. And no, “who’s going to know?” isn’t a great defense, especially when: A buyer is doing diligence, and your lack of compliance slashes your valuation A breach occurs, and you get hit with state-level notification requirements and expensive credit monitoring Your offshore contractor leaves a gaping security hole wide open, and your client data winds up floating on the dark web Yeah. Not ideal. What You Should Be Thinking About: Have you mapped how data enters, moves, and leaves your business? Do your third-party contractors have proper confidentiality agreements? Are you applying data minimization and least access principles? (Fancy terms for "don’t share more than you have to.") Are you training your team to spot phishing and social engineering scams? None of this is meant to scare you. (Okay, maybe just a little.) But this is the stuff buyers care about. It affects deal value, liability, and your ability to exit cleanly. 96 Corporate Transparency Act (BOI Reporting Requirement) Blocked Nationwide BREAKING NEWS: Corporate Transparency Act (BOI Reporting Requirement) Blocked Nationwide Hi Everyone, Less than one month before the federal reporting deadline for Beneficial Ownership Information (“BOI”), a federal district court in Texas issued a nationwide preliminary injunction against enforcing the beneficial ownership reporting requirements mandated by the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA). (Texas Top Cop Shop v. Garland (December 3, 2024) U.S. Dist. Ct., Eastern Dist. Of Texas, Case No. 4:24-CV-478). The case began at the request of a family-run firearms and tactical gear retailer, called Texas Top Cop Shop Inc., as well as other co-plaintiff businesses and the Libertarian Party of Mississippi. The briefing was powerful, including such quotables as “Plaintiffs fear this flanking, quasi-Orwellian statute and its implications on our dual system of government,” -a truly delightful and borderline sassy statement from Judge Mazzant. As you may know, the CTA require(d) that an estimated 32.6 million existing business entities disclose their beneficial owners to the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network before 2025. The government argued that the law’s function—to crack down on anonymous shell companies and deter money laundering, terrorism financing, and other illicit economic activity—falls within Congress’s regulatory duties. The court ruled that Congress exceeded its authority in enacting the CTA, resulting in an unconstitutional infringement on states’ rights to regulate businesses. The court granted a nationwide injunction prohibiting FinCEN from enforcing the January 1, 2025, reporting deadline for all reporting companies. The opinion was issued on December 3, 2024, and an appeal is anticipated. However, for now, businesses do not have to file beneficial ownership information reports with FinCEN. Check with your attorney for more updates. The opinion is available at: www.fullopinion.ttcsvgarland.pdf Best, Sara Sharp Deal Attorney, Business Consultant SK&S Law Group Copyright © 2024 Someday Consultants, All rights reserved. 96 The One Due Diligence Mistake That Could Tank Your Business Acquisition Hi Sara, Buying a business? You’re probably knee-deep in financial statements, debt service coverage ratios, and making sure the numbers check out. But do you know what most buyers completely ignore? The employee handbook. Yes, that legally questionable 70-page document no one—including the seller—has ever actually read. And yet, skipping it nearly torpedoed a deal I worked on last week. The Landmine Hiding in Plain Sight A buyer was acquiring a small business—just five employees, all women. Everyone was excited. I casually asked for the employment handbook, mostly as a formality. They sent it over as a joke, like, “Sure, if you really want to waste your time.” Well, guess what I found? The seller had unknowingly adopted big-company policies (think FMLA, ADA) that didn’t even apply to them. Buried in the fine print? A 12-week paid maternity leave policy—which the seller had no idea existed. The five employees? They definitely knew. Now the buyer had a tough choice: ➝ Match the policy and take a financial hit. ➝ Cut it and risk losing the entire team post-close. Oh, and they weren’t allowed to talk to employees before closing—so they had to make the call blind. Why This Matters (Even in an Asset Purchase) "It’s an asset purchase—I’m not taking on liabilities, so who cares?" Because you’re not just buying assets, you’re buying people. Employees don’t magically reset their expectations just because ownership changes hands. If you don’t honor policies they were promised, they’ll leave. What You Should Be Checking (That You’re Probably Not) ➝ The employee handbook (yes, really—just skim it). ➝ Hidden liabilities in PTO, benefits, or outdated workplace policies that could become your problem. ➝ Anything that might make employees feel like they got a raw deal when you take over. Most buyers only realize this after key employees start quitting—or when they find themselves stuck with unexpected financial obligations. Don’t be that buyer. 96 The Hidden Culture Clues Buyers Miss (And Why They Matter) Hi Sara, You can’t put company culture on a spreadsheet. But that doesn’t mean you should ignore it. 96 What Really Happens If You Default on an SBA Loan (and Why It’s Not as Scary as You Think) Hi Sara, “I’ve got a 7(a) loan… what happens if I default?” It’s the question everyone wants to ask—but no one actually asks their banker. And honestly, I get it. Walking into a loan meeting and saying, “Hey, what happens if this all goes sideways?” isn’t exactly confidence-inspiring. So I asked for you. Recently, I sat down with Eric Rabinovich from Live Oak Bank—an SBA lender who actually knows his stuff. And we dug into the unspoken anxiety a lot of small business buyers carry: what if I can’t make my payments? Here’s what you should know (but probably won’t hear from your loan officer): Default isn’t common. SBA 7(a) loans are underwritten carefully, especially in industries like professional services. So before you panic, know that defaults are rare—and you’re likely not alone if you’re just feeling nervous rather than actually in trouble. There is a big difference between “I’m anxious” and “I’m about to miss a payment.” If it’s the latter—call the bank. Early. Not calling won’t help, and lenders often have options like maturity extensions or forbearance tools they may be willing to explore—especially before you miss a payment. If you’re within the first 18 months? The stakes may be higher. A default in that window can trigger an audit of the loan by the SBA, and if the bank didn’t follow the SOPs to a tee, they could lose the government guarantee. So yes—they might feel extra motivated to work something out early on. The “personal guarantee” isn’t just a scary phrase. If you do default, banks aren’t always trying to squeeze value from your business (especially if it’s mostly goodwill and a copier on lease). Instead, they go for your personal assets. Yes, that includes your house if it's tied to the loan—and exemptions vary wildly by state. (California’s, for instance, is laughably low.) Bottom line? Don’t stick your head in the sand. If you’re feeling the squeeze, talk to your lender. If you’re about to close and just realized your second home could become part of the SBA’s repo wish list… definitely know what you’re signing. And if you’re doing a smaller deal (under $500K)? Live Oak has a killer Express Loan product that’s actually made for your world. Want more real talk about real deals—without the sugar coating? 96 The End of the Family Business (and What That Means for Your Deal) Hi Sara, I’m a real deal attorney. I help people buy and sell businesses every day—especially in the accounting world, where things are getting a little... complicated. Here’s a trend I’ve been seeing, and spoiler: it’s kind of a bummer. Private equity has entered the room. And with it? Some serious downstream effects most people aren’t talking about—especially for family-run businesses. Once upon a time, an accounting firm owner could slowly hand off the business to their child. A junior partner would earn their stripes, buy in over a decade, and one day—after a gold watch and a sentimental dinner—the torch would be passed. That’s cute. It also doesn’t happen anymore. Why not? Because valuations are up, interest rates are high, and most 25-year-olds working in their parent’s firm aren’t sitting on $3.5M in cash (shocking, I know). Meanwhile, sellers aren’t exactly eager to leave that kind of money on the table—especially when they can get 90% up front through SBA financing. So what happens? Do the parents forego millions of dollars prior to their retirement? Do they put that kind of debt on the shoulders of their children? I’ve now seen it five times in one year: parents skipping over their own kids and selling to third parties. The result? Adult children still working in the firm—except now they report to someone they’re not related to. Someone who bought their legacy. It’s often a little bit sad. It’s messy. And if you’re buying one of these businesses, you need to tread carefully. Here’s why it matters for you as a buyer: Family dynamics are tricky. You’re stepping into the middle of a deeply personal transition. Be ready to manage with a lot of emotional intelligence. Client loyalty often sticks to the family. If Josh Williams III has been the familiar face for 15 years, clients may not take kindly to your new ownership—even if you paid top dollar. Legal vulnerability. You can get the seller to sign a non-compete, but their adult child? Depending on the state, you might not be able to get them under one at all. And if they’re not? They’re free to walk out and compete. So no, you’re not just buying a practice. You’re buying a set of relationships, and some of them may walk out the door on Day 1. Bottom line: If you’re buying a family business, dig deeper than the P&L. Understand the people. Secure the key team. 96 That LOI Term That’s Screaming “I Have No Idea What I’m Doing” Hi Sara, If you've been firing off Letters of Intent (LOIs) like you're entering a sweepstakes—only to get ghosted, politely declined, or hit with the classic “we’ve decided to go another direction”... this one’s for you. Let’s talk about the one deal term that’s making smart sellers everywhere roll their eyes and move on: Zero. Percent. Interest. Seller. Notes. Yup, someone on YouTube (or maybe LinkedIn) made them sound like a genius move. But here’s the truth, straight from the trenches: it’s not savvy, it’s not strategic—it’s just a huge red flag. Why? Let me count the ways. Sellers aren’t ATMs. They’re not in the business of financing your acquisition for free. They want to get paid—and that includes interest on the money they’re essentially loaning you. Zero percent doesn’t incentivize payoff. If you’re the buyer, why would you pay early? There’s no financial benefit. You’d ride that note out to the bitter end. Not great for the seller. Here’s the kicker: The IRS hates it, too. They’ll treat that sweet 0% note as if it did have interest—thanks to a lovely concept called imputed interest income. That means the seller gets taxed as if they earned interest, even when they didn’t. Sounds fun, right? So when you throw a 0% seller note into your offer, you’re not just lowballing—you’re broadcasting that you don’t understand deal structure or tax implications. Not exactly confidence-inspiring. Bottom line: if you want sellers to take your LOI seriously, treat seller financing like the loan it is. Include a real interest rate, preferably one that aligns with the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR)—Google it. Want to stop making rookie mistakes that tank your offers before you even get to diligence? 96 Good Firms vs. Good Deals – They’re Not the Same (and Why That Matters) Hi Sara, If you’re on the hunt for an accounting firm to buy, you’ve probably caught yourself scrolling listings like it’s late-night Zillow—dreaming of that perfect cloud-based beauty with remote staff and sky-high margins. But here’s a little reality check: the “perfect” firm doesn’t always mean the “perfect” deal. And if you mix those up? You could end up with a cash flow nightmare instead of your next big win. Let’s break down why terms matter just as much as the firm—and how knowing the difference could save you from overpaying your way into buyer’s remorse. I spent most of my week talking to buyers—and when Letter of Intent season is in full swing, you know it feels a lot like musical chairs: Tax season slows things down. May and June? Buyers flood in, offers fly. July and August? Closings heat up. September 15 & October 15 deadlines creep up—panic. Then it’s holidays, and boom, back to tax season. When this happens, buyers are scanning listings, making snap judgments: ✅ Cloud-based firm, great margins? Good deal. ❌ Local, paper-based, not remote? Bad deal. Except… that’s not how this works. A good firm doesn’t always equal a good deal. Why? Because a good deal is the firm + the terms. You need both to make the math work: Good firm, bad terms? Overpay, and it won’t cash flow. You’re toast. Less desirable firm, great terms? Might be your best deal yet. I hear this all the time: “But this firm is perfect—remote team, owner works on the business, not in it.” (Yes, we should all drink every time someone says that.) But if you’re paying 10x earnings? That’s not a dream. That’s a future bankruptcy filing. On the flip side, a “meh” firm—local clients, paper-based—might be a home run if you negotiate seller financing, a lower price, or better transition support. 96 Promissory Notes: Boring Name, Sexy Deal Tool Hi Sara, If you’re buying or selling a business, you’ve probably met our friend: the promissory note. Sounds dull. It’s anything but. A promissory note is a promise to pay. Groundbreaking, I know. But before you tune out, here’s why it matters: when used right, it can make the difference between a deadlocked deal and one that gets across the finish line. Here’s what you need to know—without needing a law degree: You want $1.2 million for your business. The buyer’s stuck on $1 million. Enter: the promissory note. That extra $200K? It can live in a note, payable if the business performs post-closing. It’s called a retention adjustment, and it’s basically the deal version of “let’s see who’s right.” But don’t stop there. You can slice and dice a note like a Vegas card shark. $500K note? Make $50K of it the SBA-required “equity injection” (hello, 24-month standby). Carve the rest into separate notes with different terms. The bank cares about how the equity portion of the Note is structured, but may have different (and more lenient) thoughts on the other parts. Why I Like Notes More Than Earn-Outs if I’m the Buyer Earn-outs are needy. They involve escrow agents, agreements, arguments, and fees. Notes? You just draft them, sign them, and boom—you’re off to the races. They’re elegant. They’re manageable. And they don’t come with a customer service line. If you’re a busy business owner—and most of my clients are—this kind of simplicity matters. Notes let you build in conditional payments without the administrative circus of a full-blown earn-out. We love that. *But ON THE OTHER HAND, if I’m the seller, I certainly like the fact that my money is sitting in an escrow account somewhere. One Last Note (Get It?) Don't treat notes like a monolith. Be strategic. Use multiple notes. Tailor the terms. And above all: stop pretending like “standard terms” are your only option. You can (and should) get creative. 96 Why That 0% Interest Offer Could Backfire—Big Time Hi Sara, Let’s talk about something that gets ignored way too often in deal negotiations: interest rates on seller financing. Yes, I know. Not exactly a crowd-pleaser at cocktail hour. But if you’re buying or selling a business and you throw out a 0% interest promissory note thinking it’s no big deal… you might want to sit down. Here’s the deal: The IRS has this little thing called the Applicable Federal Rate (AFR). It's their way of saying, “If you lend someone money, we expect you to earn a certain minimum interest—or we’ll tax you like you did.” So what happens if the AFR is 4% and your deal includes a 2% interest rate on a $100,000 note? The seller only pockets $2,000 in actual interest—but Uncle Sam taxes them like they made $4,000. That phantom $2,000? Still taxed. That’s called imputed interest income, and it’s about as fun as it sounds. Now imagine that same problem with a 0% loan on, say, a $500,000 balance. The tax hit alone can be thousands of dollars… for income the seller never actually received. Why This Matters: When buyers pitch 0% interest seller notes, they’re not just asking for a sweet deal—they’re handing the seller a tax bill on top of the loan risk and inflation erosion. It’s like borrowing their car, returning it with no gas, and handing them a parking ticket for good measure. You can do better. Savvy buyers will either: Offer interest at the current AFR (Google it—rates are public), Or at least understand the risk they’re asking the seller to shoulder and explain why the structure makes sense. And if this is the first time you’re hearing about AFR or imputed interest? Please don’t toss a 0% loan in your LOI like it’s a hot tip from a Reddit thread. Bottom line: If you want seller financing to actually work, make it fair. Or at the very least, don’t make it tax-punitive. Ready to structure smarter offers that actually get accepted? 96 The SBA Just Rolled Over on Rollover Equity Sara, Heads up, buyers and sellers—especially the ones eyeing a little equity rollover in your next deal. The SBA’s latest revision to SOP 50 10 8 (effective June 1, 2025) just dropped, and it comes with a curveball that could change the way deals are structured. Here’s the big news: If a seller keeps any equity—yes, even 1%—they now have to personally guarantee the entire SBA 7(a) loan. Not just their sliver of the pie. The whole thing. And that personal guarantee sticks around for two years after the deal closes. Previously, this only kicked in if you owned 20% or more. So yes, this is a big shift. One that could make some sellers think twice before hanging onto a small piece of the business. What does this mean for deals? Well, we’re likely going to see: More caution with rollover equity. If you thought you’d keep a toe in the water without getting soaked—surprise! You're swimming in the deep end now. A stronger push for outside capital. Think investor-backed deals, seller notes structured outside SBA guidelines, or other creative financing workarounds. This also means SBA lenders are going to be extra nosy about your deal structure. So if you're the buyer, make sure your legal and lending teams are in sync. And if you’re the seller—know what you’re signing up for. Of course, we’ve seen SOPs evolve before. It’s entirely possible this gets softened or reinterpreted later. But for now, this is theoretically going to be the rule. Need help navigating SBA rules or deal structuring? That’s kind of our thing. Until next time—make smart deals and skip the surprises, Sara Sharp Partner, SK&S Law Group Business Consultant & Founder of Deal Academy P.S. 96 Want to Sell Your Firm? Here’s What It’s Actually Worth Hi Sara, Selling your accounting firm is a big move – but let’s be honest, the first thing you’re probably wondering is: How much can I actually get for this thing? I get it. You’ve spent years (decades?) building this practice. You’ve navigated tax seasons, client emergencies, and maybe even the occasional panic attack over an IRS notice. Now, you want to be sure you’re getting what it’s worth when you sell. Here’s what you need to know about valuing your firm for an external sale – no sugarcoating, just the real talk: 1. Cash Upfront: Show Me the Money (Or… Not) Spoiler alert: Most buyers are not showing up with a briefcase of cash like in the movies. Expect a down payment between 60-80% (90% is excellent). The rest? That’s where retention periods and payout plans (Seller Notes) come in. 2. Retention Period: What You Get Depends on What They Collect Brace yourself—most deals in this industry are at least partially based on collections. Translation: You get paid a percentage of what the buyer actually collects from your clients over time. This could be great—or frustrating—depending on how smoothly your clients transition. (Hint: It’s why you want to train your clients to stop showing up with shoeboxes of receipts to chat with you for 2 hours.) 3. Firm Size: Bigger Isn’t Always Better That fancy office and extra staff? It might look good on paper, but a smaller firm with low overhead can sometimes be worth more to a buyer. Why? Profit margins. Buyers love a lean, efficient firm that’s not weighed down by rent and payroll. Remote practices go for the highest multiples. 4. Payout Period: Get Ready for the Long Game Most sales get fully paid out over 3-10 years. Smaller firms: Usually 4-6 years. Larger firms: Could stretch to 10. If an SBA loan is involved? You’ll likely get more money upfront, but the buyer will be repaying that loan for the next decade. What Does This All Mean for You? The value of your firm isn’t just about revenue. It’s about the terms of the deal, the buyer’s risk tolerance, and how smoothly your clients transition. Bottom Line: The biggest deals aren’t always the ones with the highest sticker price – they’re the ones that pay out (and let you actually enjoy retirement). Thinking about selling? People have feelings and emergencies and generally require a lot of resources. Customer Service Isn’t Optional Whether it’s an HVAC technician or a car wash attendant, businesses that serve homeowners demand excellent customer service. And “excellent” doesn’t happen without constant oversight. Equipment breaks. Complaints roll in. Someone has to manage it all. A few negative reviews can quite literally bankrupt you. Employees Fear Change After an acquisition, employees often worry about layoffs or pay cuts. Stabilizing operations and winning their trust takes time—and money. 96 Make This Your Last Tax Season Ever - Start the Process of Selling Now Hi Sara, I know. You’re buried under tax returns, clients are panicking over 1099s, and your coffee consumption is at “dangerous levels.” Selling your firm? That feels like a problem for Future You – maybe May You, or July You, sipping a margarita on a cruise deck somewhere. But here’s the thing: Tax Season is actually the best time to prep for a sale – without adding to your tax-season chaos. Why? Because the little steps you take now can mean a much bigger payday (and a smoother exit) when you’re ready to hand over the keys. Here’s what you can do – in between e-filing battles – to set yourself up for success: 1. Raise Your Rates (Yes, Even Now) Most firms sell based on a multiple of gross revenue. Translation: Higher rates = Higher value. Even a 10% bump this year could boost your sale price dollar-for-dollar. And if you don’t do it, your buyer will – and that could lead to client attrition that messes with your earn-out later. 2. Write Down What’s in Your Head You know those “special” clients—the ones with odd filing quirks or that “one-off” rate you gave them in 2008? That’s all in your brain… and nowhere else. Document it now while you’re dealing with each client one by one anyways: client notes, billing nuances, or anything only you know. This makes your firm easier to sell and transition, plus it saves you from frantic, post-sale “Did we file the Johnsons’ extension?” texts from your buyer. 3. Start (Secretly) Planning for Staff Changes Tax season isn’t the time to replace anyone, but it is the time to think ahead. If you know you’ll need staffing changes before selling, start mapping it out now. The last thing you want is staffing drama when you’re trying to close a deal. 4. Clean Up Your Expenses (Your Buyer Will Notice) Your profit margin – or Seller’s Discretionary Earnings (SDE) – is everything when it comes to your sale price. Be honest: Are you paying Cousin Bob $50/hour to “handle tech stuff” (aka watch YouTube)? Writing off that golf membership as “client entertainment”? That’s crunching your profit margin in a way you need to be ready to explain. Make a list of expenses that could (or should) be adjusted later. It could mean the difference between a good sale and a great one. 5. Find Your Deal Team – Before You Need Them Good brokers and attorneys who know financial firms? They get busy fast. Start building those relationships now – during tax season when they’re often a little quieter. By the time you’re ready to sell, you’ll have the right people in your corner. The Bottom Line: Prepping your firm for sale doesn’t have to mean taking on “one more thing” during tax season. These steps fit right into your day-to-day. And they’ll put you miles ahead when you’re ready to move on – whether that’s next year or five years down the road. Thinking about selling (even just hypothetically)? Curious how this all works? 96 The 7 Things You Must Check in a Purchase Agreement Before Buying an Accounting Firm Hi Sara, If you’re buying an accounting practice, you’re going to come across a purchase agreement—and let’s be real, it will probably look like a 20-page legal maze designed to put you to sleep. But here’s the thing: this document controls everything about your deal. It’s your business’s user manual, your playbook, and, if something goes wrong, your only protection. So today, I’m breaking down the seven key sections you must understand before signing on the dotted line. 1. What Exactly Are You Buying? (And What’s Excluded?) This is where you find out if you’re getting all the assets you expect—or if the seller conveniently forgot to include key client lists, software, or equipment. If you’re the buyer, you want the contract to say everything is included unless specifically excluded. If you’re the seller? You want the opposite. 2. The Money Details (a.k.a. The Purchase Price) How much are you paying? Is it all cash, or is there a promissory note? Are there any earnout term or price adjustments based on client retention or revenue? Miss something here, and you might be in for a nasty surprise later. 3. Closing Mechanics: When Does This Deal Actually Happen? Most deals aren’t “sign today, close today.” They involve a bifurcated sign-and-close, meaning: ✔ You sign the agreement now. ✔ The deal officially closes later—after financing, approvals, or other conditions are met. If you don’t structure this properly, you could be legally obligated to buy before securing funding. (Yes, I’ve seen this happen. Yes, it got ugly.) 4. The Seller’s Promises (And Why They Matter) Reps and warranties are the seller’s legal promises about the business. Things like: “Our financial statements are accurate.” “We actually own the assets we’re selling.” “We haven’t secretly sold the client list to someone else.” If any of these turn out to be false, you’ve got a breach of contract claim. But only if you made sure they were included in writing. These are SUPER important. 5. What Happens If Something Goes Wrong? This is where indemnification comes in—it decides who pays if a lawsuit shows up later. Example: A client sues over work done before closing. Who’s responsible—you or the seller? Get this section wrong, and you could be on the hook for past problems you had nothing to do with. 6. Non-Compete Clauses (The Fine Print That Matters) If you’re the buyer, you don’t want the seller setting up shop across the street and poaching clients. If you’re the seller, you don’t want to be banned from your entire profession for the next decade. The right non-compete is a balance—clear, enforceable, and specific. If it’s too broad, courts might throw it out. If it’s too narrow, it won’t protect you. If you’re the one under a non-compete, you’re going to want it to be specific enough that you can tell whether or not a business opportunity will violate it. 7. The Boilerplate (Yes, You Still Have to Read It) The last section might seem like legal fluff, but I’ve found some wild clauses buried in here—like secret fees, weird assignment rules, and even clauses that completely contradict earlier sections. So read it. The Bottom Line A purchase agreement is more than just paperwork—it’s the foundation of your deal. If you don’t understand what’s in it, you’re flying blind. 96 Why Your Letters of Intent Are Being Ignored Hi Sara, Submitting letters of intent (LOIs) but getting crickets in response? You’re not alone. I’ve talked to hundreds of buyers in the accounting industry, and there’s one big reason LOIs often end up in the seller’s trash bin: you’re not answering the one question sellers care about most. “How Are You Going to Take Care of My Business?” It seems obvious, but for sellers—especially those running CPA firms—it’s the dealbreaker. If your LOI doesn’t explain how you’ll manage their highly regulated and sophisticated practice, especially if you’re not a CPA yourself, you’re unlikely to get a call back. Here’s why: CPA-Specific Work Matters: Not all accounting is created equal. While bookkeeping, payroll, and general tax prep fall under “accounting,” CPA-specific tasks—like audit and attestation work—require that coveted CPA designation. Regulatory Hurdles Exist: In most jurisdictions, CPA firms must be majority-owned by CPAs (51% or more). In some states, like South Carolina, the threshold is even higher at 66.6%. Without a CPA designation, you can’t own these businesses outright. Sellers Care About Their Legacy: Sellers work hard to build their practices. They’re not just selling a business; they’re entrusting their clients to you and sometimes their employees as well. If your plan doesn’t inspire confidence, they’ll pass. How to Fix Your LOI Here’s how to address sellers’ concerns upfront: Have a Clear Ownership Plan: If you’re not a CPA, acknowledge the regulatory requirements and provide a solution that answers their question before they can ask it. Options include: Partnering with a CPA to co-own the firm. Structuring the deal as a general accounting practice (if audit work isn’t involved). Using an alternative practice structure (APS) to spin off CPA-specific tasks into a separate CPA-owned entity. Don’t Default to “I’ll Hire Someone”: Hiring a tax manager or offshoring CPA-specific tasks might sound plenty fine to you, but sellers are understandably very skeptical of this pie in the sky solution. Show you’ve done the homework by (at the very least) identifying or partnering with qualified talent. Even still, you should know that some sellers are simply not going to consider a non-CPA buyer. Prioritize Client Care: Sellers want assurance that their clients will be taken care of. Your LOI should show empathy for their concerns and confidence in your ability to maintain those relationships. At the end of the day, sellers aren’t just chasing the highest offer. They want a buyer who understands the industry, respects their hard work, and has a realistic plan for the future.
