96 Selling Your Accounting Practice? Don’t Overlook This Crucial Step Hi Sara, So, you’ve decided to sell your accounting practice—congratulations! Now, let’s talk about a little wrinkle you might not have anticipated: the AICPA’s 90-day notice requirement for transferring client records. If you’re unfamiliar with this rule, here’s the gist: even after you’ve sold your business (stock or asset sale—it doesn’t matter), you’re required to notify clients and obtain their consent before transferring their records to the buyer. And if they don’t respond at all, you have to wait 90 days before assuming it’s okay. Sounds simple? Sure, until you realize: That’s 90 days of your buyer paying overhead on a business they can’t fully operate. It’s also 90 days of dwindling working capital and potentially frustrated clients. So, how are people navigating this tricky requirement? Creative Solutions Sellers Are Using (not necessarily solutions I recommend!) Pre-Closing Partnership: Sellers make the buyer a partner just before closing, transforming the transaction into an internal transfer and sidestepping the 90-day rule entirely. All Hands on Deck: For smaller client lists, sellers personally call each client, requesting consent and singing the praises of the incoming buyer. Contractor Stopgap: Sellers retain their LLC post-sale and hire the buyer as a contractor, allowing access to records under the seller’s umbrella until consents are in place. Each of these options has pros and cons, and some are more feasible than others depending on the size of your client list and the timing of your sale. They are all in the gray area of compliance and may not meet the risk profile of you or your counterparty. Why This Matters The rule aims to protect sensitive client data—a noble goal. But its implementation can feel like a logistical headache, especially during tax season when delays could be disastrous. What You Should Do If you’re selling your practice: Understand your client relationships. Do you have an email relationship with your clients? If not, securing consent might be harder than expected and take an enormous amount of effort. Plan ahead with your buyer. Discuss how you’ll tackle the 90-day hurdle early in the process. Stay informed about compliance options and be ready to get creative. At the end of the day, selling your accounting practice is a huge milestone. The right plan—and the right team—can make the process smoother. Have questions about selling your practice or navigating the AICPA’s notice requirements? 96 Think Your Non-Compete Doesn’t Matter? Think Again. Hi Sara, Let’s talk about the number one clause that gets glossed over, shrugged off, and misunderstood in nearly every deal I touch: the non-compete. Every day, I hear some version of: “Non-competes aren’t enforceable, right? So who cares?” Oh, just the buyer, the seller, the bank, and your entire deal. That’s who. The Non-Compete Myth That Won’t Die Thanks to headlines (and let’s be honest, a few clickbaity TikToks), people think non-competes are dead. But here’s the truth: they’re very much alive—especially when you’re buying or selling a business. Even when the FTC tried to come for them, they carved out a big juicy exception for business sales. Why? Because you can’t buy an accounting firm and then let the seller open a competing firm across the street the next day. That's not a business deal. That's a mess. Where Your Non-Compete Lives Matters It’s not just what your non-compete says, but where it lives. Stick it in the wrong agreement—say, a consulting agreement instead of a purchase agreement—and you may find out the hard way it doesn’t hold up. And don’t forget: Geographic scope needs to be defined (50 miles from where, exactly?) Time frame needs to make sense (hint: 5 years might not cover a 10-year SBA loan) Actual clarity matters (your lawyer should be able to look at it and say, “Yes, you can do this” or “No, you absolutely cannot”) But Wait, There’s More (Nuance) Let’s say your seller still wants to do their grandkid’s taxes. Or help their favorite client until one of them dies (yes, that’s a real quote I’ve heard). That’s fine. Just write it down. Include exceptions. Carve it out. Make it clear. Because a good non-compete shouldn’t feel like a straitjacket. It should feel like a well-fitting suit. Fits like a glove. 96 Want to Make a Seller Hate You? Put This in Your LOI Hi Sara, Let’s play a game. What’s one thing you can put in your Letter of Intent that instantly makes a seller question your ability to run anything, much less their business? Answer: A 0% interest seller note. Yikes. I see this all the time. Some eager buyer (probably fresh off a YouTube binge) sends in an LOI offering seller financing at 0% interest—as if that’s a totally normal, savvy move. Spoiler: it’s not usually. Here’s why that “interest-free” offer makes sellers cringe (and quietly blacklist you): It’s a tax trap. Even if the seller agrees to 0%, the IRS doesn’t. Imputed interest means the seller still pays taxes as if they earned interest. So you're not just offering a bad deal—you're offering one that costs them. It signals you don’t understand deals. Or at least, you haven't Googled “applicable federal rate.” Offering a loan below that rate without understanding the tax consequences doesn’t scream "trustworthy operator of a tax firm." It kills motivation to repay. Would you rush to pay off an interest-free loan? Neither would your seller. That’s why they’re unlikely to love the idea of giving you one. It’s not 2010. Inflation is real. Cost of capital is real. And unless your seller is feeling wildly philanthropic, they need a very good reason why they should finance your dream at 0%. The fix? At a minimum, offer AFR (Applicable Federal Rate) on seller notes. Show the seller that you understand basic finance, tax implications, and how not to look like a rookie. 96 The Most Expensive Mistake I See Buyers Make (And How to Avoid It) Hi Sara, Guys, please stop handing out your equity ownership like it’s candy. I spend a good chunk of my workweek trying to un-mess partnership disasters. So here’s the one thing I wish every business owner, buyer, and entrepreneur would stop doing this year: 👉 Bringing on a “partner” too early or too thoughtlessly. Sounds harmless, right? You find someone smart, they’re excited, you click. Why not share the load? You split the risk, you gain a sounding board, you finally stop annoying your spouse with endless business talk. What could go wrong? Well…everything. The Problem with Equity Promises Most people give away ownership based on potential: “If we build this together, we’ll win together.” But what actually happens is this: one person ends up doing the heavy lifting while the other disappears to become a rock-climbing, kombucha-making, off-the-grid nomad who still collects 50% of the profits forever. It’s not just frustrating—it’s legally sticky. You can’t just “unpartner” someone because they stopped showing up. You’ll need a court order or a written agreement (that they’re willing to sign), and those aren’t easy to get. It’s often referred to as a business divorce—and not just for the emotional mess it leaves behind. What Disgruntled Founders Try Instead: Spin up a competing business and channel all your energy there (not without risk). Crank up your salary to minimize profit distributions (not without risk and also taxable). Sell the business anyway and watch half the money go to your absentee co-founder (infuriating). Sound familiar? There’s a Better Way If you must bring in a co-owner, treat it like a prenup. Set clear expectations, outline exit terms, and protect the business if things go sideways. (Yes, I draft those kinds of documents all the time.) But if you’re early in the game—building or buying a business—try literally anything else before giving away equity. Gift cards. Cash. Consulting fees. Free snacks. Future bonuses. Whatever. Just don’t give away the whole farm because you’re short on cash. You’ll thank me later. Your lawyer will thank you now. 96 The Hidden Deal Killer You’re Probably Ignoring Hi Sara, Want to know one of the top reasons business sales die at the last minute? The landlord. No one thinks about them until they’re the only thing standing between you and closing—and by then, you have zero leverage. This week, I saw a deal collapse days before closing because of a lease issue. The buyers were relocating, everything was lined up… and then they realized they had to personally guarantee the lease. Just like that, the deal was dead. Why Landlords Hold All the Cards If your business is in a prime location, the landlord knows they can fill that space instantly. So why should they rush to approve a new tenant? They don’t need to play ball, and if you wait too long to negotiate, they’ll have all the power. How to Avoid This Mess Get the landlord involved early. Yes, confidentiality matters, but waiting until the end gives them every reason to say no. Know that personal guarantees are standard. If you’re hoping to avoid one, be prepared to prepay rent or put up extra security. If you’re a seller, don’t assume the lease transfer will be easy. Buyers might be excited to take over your business, but if the landlord refuses to assign the lease, the deal is dead. Lessons from the Trenches I’ve seen deals where landlords have: Refused to assign a lease because they liked the current tenant and didn’t want to risk a change. Rejected SBA-required lease terms, which make the bank the first priority if the business defaults. Landlords hate this. Changed their mind at the last second, leaving the buyer stranded. If you’re in a transaction right now, consider this your warning shot—figure out the lease situation before you’re deep into due diligence. 96 That five year clause? Meet reality Hi Sara, Here’s a fun surprise I see way too often: A non-compete that says, “No competing for five years from closing.” Sounds strong. Looks good on paper. 96 A tale of timelines, lawsuits, and bundles of sticks. Want to Limit Risk? Start with This One Contract Clause. Hi Sara, Let’s talk about timelines. Specifically, how long your reps and warranties should stick around after your business deal closes. If you’re selling, you probably don’t want a buyer showing up three years later saying, “Surprise! You owe me money for that thing I just discovered.” If you’re buying, you absolutely want that runway—because you won’t know everything about the business until you’ve lived through a full annual cycle (or two). Enter: the survival clause. This clause limits how long certain representations and warranties survive after closing. In other words, it’s a contractual expiration date on how long you can be sued for stuff you promised. Sellers want shorter. Buyers want longer. Welcome to the eternal tug-of-war that is deal negotiation. What’s typical? I’ve seen 12 months, 18 months, 24, even 36. Personally, I like 18 months for buyers—it gives you a year to uncover issues, plus a little breathing room to hire a lawyer and actually do something about it. Sellers? You’re gunning for 12. Anything longer gives the buyer time to discover problems and get their legal ducks in a row. Also—let’s not forget about the statute of limitations. Just because the contract doesn’t say how long reps survive doesn’t mean there’s no limit. But it does mean that limit could be a looooong time. And unless you’re trying to fund your lawyer’s next vacation home, I recommend putting something in writing. The New Thought: Exclusivity is Can Be Pretty Powerful You've heard me talk about the narrow sales window in these deals-spoiler it's SHORT. As the deal is waning in day 30, you suddenly have a motivation to let the other side know you're calling it so you can get your money back. 96 The Hidden LOI Clause That Could Slash Your Purchase Price Hi Sara, Let’s play a quick game of “Which Offer Would You Choose?” You’re selling your accounting practice. Two buyers show up: Buyer A offers $3M Buyer B offers $2.9M Easy choice, right? Spoiler: Buyer A’s offer might not actually be $3M. 96 When to Call Your Bank—and When to Just Breathe Hi Sara, Let’s talk about something fun. Debt. Stress. SBA audits. Okay, so maybe not fun—but definitely important. If you’ve bought a business (especially an accounting firm), odds are you used SBA financing. And in those first 12–18 months, the transition is often messy. Cash flow is tight. Clients are adjusting. You’re adjusting. And that loan payment starts to feel… heavy. So here’s the million-dollar question I hear all the time: When should I call the bank if I think I might miss a payment? Here’s the truth: 👉 If you’re just anxious, but still able to pay, breathe. No need to call the bank just to talk about your feelings. 👉 But if it’s looking likely that you’ll miss a payment? Talk to them before it happens. Silence kills options. Banks can work with you if the circumstances are right, modify terms, offer temporary forbearance, or extend maturity dates, but only if there’s communication before the problem becomes a disaster. And if you’re in the first 18 months of your loan, listen up: That’s the danger zone. A missed payment triggers an audit by the SBA that puts the bank’s loan guarantee at risk. So yes, they’re extra sensitive during this time. And yes, communication matters more than ever. Buying a firm is hard enough. Don’t make it harder by ghosting your lender. 96 Is Your Non-Compete Worthless? Here's How to Fix It Hi Sara, Let’s talk about non-competes—a favorite topic for business owners, and one of the most misunderstood legal documents in existence. I see it all the time: non-competes that sound airtight but, when tested, are about as useful as a screen door on a submarine. The Big Mistake Everyone’s Making The question everyone asks is ‘is this even enforceable’? And the answer is usually at least partially yes. But the question people SHOULD be asking is ‘does this even help me’ and the answer to that is often ‘nope, not a bit.’ Most non-competes include a geographical restriction. They say something like: “You can’t compete within 20 miles of this business location.” That might have worked when businesses were local, and horse-drawn carriages were all the rage. But in 2024, when services are offered nationwide (hello, internet!), a 20-mile radius is laughably ineffective. Why It Matters If your clients are scattered across the country, what good is a non-compete that only covers a tiny local area? It’s a loophole big enough to drive a semi-truck through. And trust me, if a former employee or buyer wants to compete with you, they will drive through it. How to Fix It Your non-compete needs to reflect where your clients actually are. If your business operates nationwide, then your non-compete should restrict competitors from providing services to your client base, wherever they’re located. Of course, you do have to balance that against federal and state laws relating to enforceability which is where all the nuance comes in and is why lawyers still have a job. Don’t Let Your Non-Compete Work Against You Non-competes are meant to protect your business, not give you a false sense of security. If your current agreement isn’t built for the way your business operates today, it’s time for a rewrite. Have questions about making your non-compete actually enforceable? 96 Before you drop a number on a business, learn to think like the original deal pros. Make Them an Offer They Can’t Refuse Hi Sara, When it comes to making offers on a business, you don’t want to come off like a clueless rookie. You want to come in cool, calculated, and compelling. So I created a framework to help you do exactly that. And yes, it’s called M.A.F.I.A.—because who understands business negotiation better than the original entrepreneurs in pinstripes? Here’s how to make your offer bulletproof (and maybe a little intimidating—in a good way): M – Market Demand: Is it a buyer’s market or a seller’s market? That shiny accounting firm might look unreasonably expensive in May but be 80% of the cost by December. Timing is everything. A – Adjusted EBITDA: This isn’t just about the profit number in the listing. You need to adjust for reality—like whether you’ll be replacing an owner-operator. Because spoiler: hiring someone who knows what they’re doing is not simple and if you do pull it off, it costs money, and that affects your real returns. F – Financing Realities: Please, I beg you—don’t offer a price you can’t actually fund. You need to know if you’re using SBA, cash, seller finance (rare), or investor capital. Pitching a fantasy offer just wastes everyone’s time. Bonus points if you don’t offer terms the bank won’t allow. I – Industry Multiples: If this is the first time you’re hearing “industry multiple,” stop reading and go Google it. Every industry has them. Don’t offer based on gross revenue unless you want zero leverage when the actual profit numbers look different in diligence. Tie your offer to EBITDA or SDE and show your work. A – Asking Price: Buyers often obsess over financials but forget the most important number in the deal: the seller’s real asking price—which has just as much to do with emotions and legacy as dollars. If your offer doesn’t reflect what the seller actually cares about, don’t be surprised when you lose the deal to someone who simply paid more attention. Follow these steps, and you’ll go from looking like a hopeful buyer to a serious contender. Ready to learn how the deal game really works? Check out Deal Academy. 96 How to Buy a Business with $0 Down (No, Really) Hi Sara, Want to buy a business without spending a dime of your own money? It sounds like a scam, right? Like some late-night infomercial: “This one weird trick will make you a millionaire!” I promise you—it’s not. But before we get ahead of ourselves, let’s start with what doesn’t work: ❌ Convincing a seller to finance 100% of the deal (good luck with that). ❌ Finding a “free” business (if you’ve found one, it’s probably a terrible deal). ❌ Manifesting a business into existence (if only it were that easy). What does work is using an SBA 7(a) loan strategically. This program is already a game-changer in business acquisitions, offering financing up to 90%. But what if I told you that, in some cases, you can finance 100% of a deal—without putting in a single dollar of your own cash? Here’s the play: ➝ The SBA requires buyers to put down 10%, right? Well, some lenders will accept a seller note—a loan from the seller themselves—as that 10%. ➝ If structured correctly (meaning the note follows SBA rules, like a 24-month standby period), the bank treats it like a cash down payment. ➝ Result? You just bought a business with no money out of pocket. But Here’s the Catch... ➝ Not all banks do this. You need a preferred SBA lender who actually understands these deals. ➝ Your Letter of Intent (LOI) matters. If you try to sneak this in last minute, the seller will be less than thrilled. Transparency is key. ➝ “$0 down” doesn’t mean “free.” You still need funds for closing costs, loan origination fees, legal fees, and diligence expenses. The Takeaway? There’s an absolute wave of business owners looking to retire—millions of them, in fact. The opportunity is massive. But the people who win? They’re the ones who get creative with financing, work with the right banks, and structure deals that actually close. 96 Purchase Agreements: Your (Not-So-Boring) Deal Survival Guide Hi Sara, If you're buying an accounting firm, you’re going to meet a purchase agreement. And by “meet,” I mean it’s going to sit on your desk like a 40-page foreign language exam. Let’s change that. Purchase agreements can look intimidating, but under all that legal lingo, there’s a pattern. A structure. Dare I say... a method to the madness. And understanding it can save you from signing something that quietly sets your hair on fire. Here’s the cheat sheet I share with clients: Article 1: What You’re Actually Buying Assets, price, terms. It's all in here. Read it like your career depends on it (because it might). Bonus tip: Make sure you understand what's excluded, not just what you're getting. Because if it’s not listed clearly, you’re probably not getting it. Article 3: The Great List of Promises These are the seller’s (and your) reps and warranties. Think of this as the “are you telling the truth and nothing but the truth?” section. The hidden magic? These reps force sellers to disclose things they “forgot” to mention—like pending lawsuits or unpaid wage claims. That’s not just legal housekeeping. That’s gold. Article 5: Covenants, aka The Thou Shalt Nots This is where the non-competes, non-solicits, and general behavior clauses live. Are they enforceable? Reasonable? Clear enough that you won’t accidentally trip over them just by breathing in the wrong ZIP code? Let’s hope so. Article 6: Indemnification Also known as “who’s cleaning up the mess if something goes wrong?” This section matters a lot more than people think, especially when a third party crashes the party with a lawsuit. Miscellaneous: The Sneaky Stuff Boilerplate doesn’t mean unimportant. I’ve found all kinds of landmines hiding in those standard-seeming sections. Read them. All of them. Yes, even the severability clause. Signature Lines: Who’s Actually on the Hook Make sure individuals are signing, not just LLCs. You can’t hold “ABC Accounting, LLC” accountable when it vanishes six months after closing. You want Jim Anderson’s signature if Jim Anderson is the one making promises. Still awake? Then you, my friend, are the exact kind of person I want reading these emails. 96 How to make sure you get a good deal when buying or selling and accounting practice The Stages of a Deal: A Step-by-Step Guide From Sara Sharp: Navigating the Process of Buying an Accounting Firm Hi Everyone, I’m Sara Sharp, and I help people buy and sell accounting firms. Buying a firm can seem like a daunting process, but if you break it down into clear steps, it’s much easier to manage. Here’s a simple guide to help you understand each stage of the deal-making process. 1. Determining Your Deal Box Before you start looking for a firm to buy, you need to define your “deal box.” This means figuring out what kind of firm you’re looking for. Consider the size, location, client base, and services offered. Knowing exactly what you want will help you focus your search. Location Asking Price Types of Clients Services Offered Firm Size by Revenue or Employee Count Sellers Discretionary Earnings aka Cashflow 2. Searching Online Marketplaces Once you know what you’re looking for, start searching online marketplaces. There are many websites that specialize in listing accounting practices for sale. You can filter the search results to match your deal box criteria, ie List Price, Revenue, Cashflow, Location, etc. Examples: BizBuySell.com Accountingpracticeexchange.com 3. Submitting an NDA, Personal Financial Statement, and Resume When you find a firm that fits, the next step is to submit a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA). The NDA ensures that all information shared between you and the seller remains confidential. Pair the NDA with a Personal Financial Statement (PFS). The Personal Financial Statement shows the seller that you have the financial ability to buy the firm. It may include proof of funds or an SBA Pre-Qualification letter. Attach your resume. This outlines your experience and qualifications to show the seller you're prepared to run the firm. SBA Personal Financial Statement 4. Seller Meeting If the seller is interested in moving forward, you’ll have a meeting to discuss the firm in more detail. First impressions are EVERYTHING. So take great care with this call. This is your chance to ask questions, learn more about the business, and see if it’s a good fit for you. But most importantly, remember this firm is their baby. Don’t call their baby ugly the first time you meet. It’s an opportunity to build rapport with the seller, which will be essential as you move forward. 5. Submitting an LOI (Letter of Intent) After the seller meeting, if you decide you want to buy the firm, you’ll submit a Letter of Intent (LOI). The LOI outlines the basic terms of the deal, such as the purchase price, payment terms, and any conditions that need to be met. It’s not legally binding, but it shows the seller that you’re serious about moving forward. Become an LOI Expert here 6. Due Diligence Once the LOI is signed, the due diligence process begins. This is where you carefully review all aspects of the business. This includes financial statements, client contracts, and operations. Due diligence helps you confirm that the business is as it was represented and identify any potential risks. Sample Due Diligence Document Request List: Last 3 years Income Statements Last 3 years Tax Returns Current Balance Sheet AR Aging Summary Bank Statements General Ledger Employee List Vendor List Client List Contracts Consider hiring a CPA who specializes in due diligence to perform a Quality of Earnings assessment. 7. Securing Funding While in due diligence, you’ll want to start the process to secure funding for the deal. This could involve getting a loan from a bank, finding investors, or using your own savings. It’s important to have your financing in place before you move on to the final steps. If you plan to apply for an SBA 7(a) loan, make sure you’re working with an SBA Preferred Lender. That can save you months in processing time! 8. Closing the Deal After securing funding, you’re ready to close the deal. This is where all the final paperwork is signed, and the business officially changes hands. Closing the deal usually involves working with attorneys to ensure everything is done correctly. 9. Transitioning Ownership Finally, after the deal closes, you’ll need to transition ownership. This includes training from the previous owner. Introducing yourself to clients and employees. Making necessary changes to the business operations. A smooth transition is key to maintaining the firm’s success and keeping clients and staff happy. Buying an accounting firm isn't easy. But follow these stages, and you can navigate the process with confidence. Remember, each step is important. Take your time to get things right. It will pay off in the long run. If you ever have any questions or need guidance, I’m here to help you through each stage of the deal. I hope this guide helps you feel more prepared for your next big move. When you’re buying a firm, everyone talks about the profit, but not everyone agrees on what that actually means. Some buyers use SDE (Seller’s Discretionary Earnings), others throw around EBITDA, and both can be right; it just depends on the type of buyer you are. Here’s the cheat sheet: SDE is what matters when you’re going to run the firm yourself. It includes all the ways the seller was paying themselves: salary, car, retirement, maybe even “employing” their teenage son. EBITDA is what you look at when you’re not running it yourself. You’ll have to hire someone to do the work, so you'll have to back out all those perks and look at what’s left. But here’s the catch: replacing a good owner-operator isn't easy. They’re usually doing the work of two people, and they know the business inside and out. So if you're planning to go full absentee owner, be ready to build a team, not just hire a body. And if you're buying a firm with multiple partners and stepping in as a solo owner? That's when we start doing a little math magic to normalize things. 96 One Thing You Shouldn’t Skip in Your Diligence Checklist Hi Sara, What if I told you skipping one simple step in your diligence checklist could cause you to lose your business—Too dramatic? How about missing this one thing that could cause you to go bankrupt? The world to end! - How’s that for drama? In my role as a deal attorney, I am pretty much just a perpetual buzzkill when it comes to cutting corners in business deals. Yesterday, someone asked me if they could delete a certain section from their diligence checklist because it didn’t seem relevant. I get it, it’s usually in the first few lines of the list and those lists are long. As a human person and business person, I empathize a great deal with people wanting to cut down a very very long list of things to do, but unfortunately you really really should do it. Spoiler alert: it’s very relevant. The Diligence Detail You Can’t Overlook At the top of every diligence checklist is something that sounds boring but is absolutely critical: Articles of Organization, Incorporation, and Organizational Documents. Why does this matter? As many people have asked me, “Why do I need this if this is an asset purchase?” Because these documents tell you who owns the business and what its assets are. If you don’t verify ownership, you could end up in a nightmare scenario where: The seller isn’t actually the owner (GASP) You paid for assets that legally belong to someone else (LOUDER GASP) And guess what? Whether it’s a stock or an asset purchase, that’s your problem to untangle after the deal closes. Don’t Take the Seller’s Word for It Even in an asset purchase—where you’re buying the stuff, not the company itself—you need to know who legally owns the assets you think you’re buying. These documents give you that clarity. Skipping them is a big risk and you probably don’t like taking risks. Let this be your friendly reminder: keep those organizational documents on your checklist. I see this mistake constantly. A buyer does all the right things—market research, adjusted EBITDA, checks financing, studies industry multiples—and then they drop a number without ever asking... “What does the seller actually care about?” Here are some things to consider: Is the seller trying to lease you the building they own? Do they want to make sure their team stays employed? Are they emotionally attached to their client base? These things matter a lot. And if your LOI doesn’t speak to them, you’ll lose to someone whose offer is lower but smarter. Here’s how to fix it: Use the seller’s language in your LOI. 96 Why Your Next Deal Could Be Killed By a Data Breach Hi Sara, Let’s talk about something way scarier than IRS audits, angry clients, or even running out of LaCroix at the office: data breaches. I recently sat down with my colleague Tom Codevilla, who’s our in-house privacy law guru, and we got real about the mess that can follow when small businesses get too relaxed about compliance—especially in the age of offshoring and automating everything. What triggered this discussion? It all started with Section 7216—an IRS rule that applies to tax preparers and requires explicit client consent before you share tax data with contractors. Sounds simple. It’s not. The rule is specific. And it has criminal penalties. (Yes, it talks about prison time. For real.) But here’s the kicker: Even if 7216 doesn’t apply to you, there are a whole slew of other privacy laws that might. State laws. Federal laws. International laws (hello GDPR). It’s a buffet of liability. Offshoring? Read This Twice. Thinking of sending work to a third-party provider in another country? You need a contract. One that protects you. One that holds them responsible if they mess up. And one that complies with your clients’ privacy obligations—not just your own. Why This Matters for M&A Even if you’ve skated by without an incident, here’s where it catches up to you: when you try to sell. Buyers will dig into your data practices. If you’ve been winging it? Expect price reductions, insurance headaches, expensive indemnification carveouts, and in worst-case scenarios, canceled deals. And if there’s a data breach… That’s when things really go off the rails: Expensive credit monitoring costs Mandatory AG notifications Disgruntled clients (with lawyers) And months of distraction from actually running your business One client lost their deal entirely after a breach. Another had to recreate years of client files from scratch. If that doesn’t make your palms sweat, I don’t know what will. Simple Steps That Save Deals Here’s your “not getting sued” starter pack: Use data minimization: Only share what’s needed Implement least-access policies: Keep sensitive info on a need-to-know basis Audit your contractors: Regularly and in writing Get tailored cyber insurance: Generic policies don’t cut it Train your team: Social engineering scams are real, and your receptionist is a prime target The truth is, none of this is optional anymore. Privacy is part of business. Period. Want to listen to the full episode with Tom? Click here to tune in.
